sections.heading: What IGCSE maths help costs, starting from zero
paragraphs: Put the options in price order and the decision becomes much easier. At zero cost there is the school's own revision provision, which is already funded through fees and which a surprising number of students use patchily. Also at zero cost there are past papers from the correct board, available through the school's exams officer, which when sat under timing and marked honestly tell you more about where the marks are going than any conversation with a tutor will.

Above that sit the paid options, and the published market bands for Abu Dhabi read in October 2026 are these. Budget online tutoring, typically a university student, runs AED 45 to 150 an hour. A qualified subject tutor working online runs AED 150 to 300. An in-home one-to-one visit runs AED 180 to 500 with the journey inside the fee. A named IGCSE or A-Level specialist runs AED 200 to 450 and above. Premium examiner-led provision reaches AED 650 at the top of this market.

What changes between those bands is not enthusiasm. It is whether the person can look at a marked 0580 or 4MA1 script and name the four things costing marks, and then teach against them. A budget tutor will help a student complete homework correctly. A subject specialist will tell you that the real problem is three steps done mentally on every algebra question and a calculator in the wrong angle mode. Those are different products and they are priced accordingly.

IB Gram publishes no hourly figure on this page. We offer a free trial lesson and a consultation, and the number follows once the board, the tier and the frequency are known. The table below is the market, not us.

sections.heading: 0580 or 4MA1: the code decides what the money buys
paragraphs: A maths tutor is only worth a specialist rate if they are teaching the right qualification. Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics is syllabus 0580. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A is 4MA1. They cover overlapping content with different papers, different tiering language, different question phrasing and different mark schemes, and the calculator policy across the papers is not the same.

Ask the school for the code rather than the subject name. It takes one email and it removes all ambiguity. Then give the code to any tutor you speak to. If they ask which tier and which paper pattern applies to your child's exam year, they know the qualification. If they say "IGCSE maths is IGCSE maths", you have learned something useful for AED 0.

The tiering language differs too, and it confuses families comparing providers. Cambridge 0580 is Core and Extended. Pearson 4MA1 is Foundation and Higher. They are not identical in content or in grade ceiling, so a tutor who talks about Foundation when your child is entered for Cambridge Core is working from the wrong map.

One operational point with real consequences, especially for private candidates. Cambridge allocates every exam centre to one of six administrative zones, states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, and says it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong timetable. If your child is entered through the school that is the school's job. If they are a private candidate it is yours.

sections.heading: The tier decision is the most expensive thing nobody charges for
paragraphs: In maths, more than any other IGCSE subject, the tier your child is entered for sets a ceiling. A Core or Foundation entry limits the available grade. An Extended or Higher entry does not, but it puts harder algebra, trigonometry and problem solving in front of a student who may not be ready, with a genuine risk of a worse result than a secure lower-tier entry would have produced.

The cost appears later. A Level Mathematics and IB Higher Level maths courses normally require an Extended or Higher grade at a reasonable level, and sixth forms set their own thresholds. A student capped in Year 10 can find a door closed in Year 11 by a decision taken eighteen months earlier, and reopening it means a resit series, another year's planning, and sometimes a different sixth form.

This is where a small amount of money does the most work. Four to six sessions in Year 10, aimed squarely at the algebra, trigonometry and multi-step problem solving that separate the tiers, is a defined cost protecting an expensive decision. The same spend in Year 11 on general revision buys much less, because the entry is already made.

Ask the department two questions: which tier is my child provisionally entered for, and what specifically would have to improve for the other tier to be viable. Any maths department will answer both, and the second answer is a precise tutoring brief that costs nothing to obtain.

sections.heading: The four things that eat most IGCSE maths marks
paragraphs: Across marked scripts from both boards, the losses concentrate. The biggest is working that the marker cannot see. A student performs three steps mentally, writes a single line, arrives at the right answer, and collects a fraction of the method marks the question offered. This is not a knowledge problem and it is not expensive to fix: roughly three weeks of a tutor refusing to accept unshown steps changes it permanently. Families paying for topic re-teaching while this habit persists are paying for the wrong thing.

The second is algebraic manipulation under pressure. Almost every multi-step question at Extended or Higher tier routes through a rearrangement, and an error there propagates into everything after it, so one slip costs a whole question rather than a mark. Fluency here is drilled rather than understood, and it responds to short, frequent practice better than to long sessions.

The third is the diagram. Bearings, 3D trigonometry, circle theorems and compound-shape mensuration are all routinely attempted without drawing or annotating anything, and all are routinely lost for exactly that reason. The instruction is almost absurdly simple — draw it, label it, then calculate — and it recovers marks immediately.

The fourth is the calculator: unset angle modes, fraction entry producing decimals, statistical functions used without recording the inputs, and correct displayed answers written down with nothing to support them. A single session on calculator discipline often returns more marks than a topic block. It is the cheapest item on any maths tutoring menu and the one least likely to be offered to you, because it does not sound like teaching.
bullets: Invisible working: the largest loss, fixable in about three weeks

sections.heading: Calculator and non-calculator papers are different skills
paragraphs: Families treat maths revision as one activity, and the papers do not. Where a non-calculator component is sat, it examines arithmetic fluency, surd and fraction handling, estimation and mental method, and a student who has revised exclusively with a calculator to hand will be slower and less accurate on it than their topic knowledge predicts. Where a calculator is allowed, the examination shifts towards efficient use of the machine and towards recording enough working that a correct display earns full credit.

The revision implication is that the two need separating. A week of non-calculator practice, deliberately done without the machine on the desk, builds something a week of mixed practice does not. Equally, a session spent entirely on calculator technique — modes, fraction entry, statistical functions, how much working to show alongside a display — is not a waste of a specialist hour, it is one of the highest-return hours available.

Paper patterns differ between the boards and are revised by them, so the only safe source is the syllabus or specification for your child's actual exam year, obtained through the school. What is stable is the principle: find out which of your child's papers permit a calculator and which do not, and make sure the revision for each looks different.

This is also where a cheap tutor and an expensive one diverge most visibly. Asked to improve a non-calculator score, a budget tutor will set more questions. A specialist will set fewer questions, remove the calculator from the room, and work on method and estimation.

sections.heading: Price per grade point: where maths money goes furthest
paragraphs: Hourly rate is a poor way to compare tutoring purchases. A better one is how much it costs to move the grade, and on that measure the ranking is consistent and slightly counter-intuitive. The cheapest grade movement comes from the unglamorous items: working presentation, calculator discipline, and a diagram habit. Two or three sessions, a visible change on the next marked paper.

Next cheapest is a targeted topic block of four to six sessions aimed at named weaknesses from a real script. It is defined, testable and finite. After that comes a tier-protection block in Year 10, which is cheap in itself and prevents a very expensive downstream problem. Weekly one-to-one across a year is the most expensive option and the right one when the gap is genuinely broad rather than specific.

The worst value in this market is a weekly open-ended hour with no diagnosis behind it, bought at a specialist rate and spent on whatever homework is due. It is also the single most commonly purchased product, because it is the easiest to sell and the easiest to agree to. A family that insists on a diagnosis first and a named topic list second will spend less and get more, whichever provider they use.

An honest note on what tutoring cannot buy: it cannot guarantee a grade, it is not required for Ministry of Education equivalency or for university admission, and no provider should suggest otherwise. What it buys is hours of specialist attention on identified weaknesses, and it should be budgeted and reviewed as the finite purchase it is.

sections.heading: Resit economics: when November is worth it
paragraphs: A maths grade below what the sixth form requires raises a resit question, and it is a financial decision as much as an academic one. For a Cambridge candidate the resit route is the November series, since the February and March series is offered to India only and is not available in Abu Dhabi. For a Pearson candidate November is also available, alongside the May/June window.

The costs are three. The entry fee, which is set by the board and administered through a centre and which you should price before deciding. The tutoring, which for a resit should be short and targeted rather than a full re-teach, because the student has already covered the syllabus once. And the time cost, which families underestimate: a November resit runs through the first term of sixth form, competing with new courses at exactly the point a student needs to establish themselves.

The timings are knowable. Pearson's published history shows a November window running from late October to mid-November and results reaching students the following January — November 2025 results landed on 22 January 2026. That means a resit grade arrives part-way through the sixth-form year, which is useful for a conditional place and not useful for an application already decided.

Weigh it accordingly. A resit is worth it when a specific, named threshold is missed by a small margin and a defined block of work can close it. It is poor value when the gap is broad, when the student is already stretched by new courses, or when the receiving school has indicated it will take the original grade anyway. Ask the sixth form directly before spending anything.

sections.heading: Why there is no in-home option here, and what replaces it
paragraphs: Stated plainly, because this page targets a local maths-tutor search: IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE. No tutor will travel to an Al Maryah Island address. In-home tutoring is a service we run in India only. Every UAE lesson is live one-to-one video with a subject specialist, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time.

The honest case for that is a cost case, which suits this page. On an island with no school inside it and few resident maths specialists, an in-home match comes from the mainland. The published gap between the online and in-home bands in this market is roughly AED 30 to 200 an hour, and on this island that gap pays for a journey across a bridge at the hour the roads are worst. Across a school year of weekly sessions that is a substantial sum spent on driving rather than on teaching.

What replaces it, for maths specifically, is not a compromise. A shared digital whiteboard keeps every worked line, so last week's quadratic can be reopened rather than reconstructed from a notebook. The exact past-paper question can be pasted onto the board. The student works on their own paper, in their own handwriting, with a camera on it — which is precisely what the exam will ask of them. The one requirement is that camera, and we set it up in the first session.

The practical gain is selection. Instead of asking who can reach the island by five o'clock, we ask who teaches 0580 Extended or 4MA1 Higher and can read a marked script. On Al Maryah Island that reordering is the whole of the advantage.

faqs.question: What is the cheapest useful way to improve IGCSE maths on Al Maryah Island?
faqs.answer: Two things that cost nothing. Use the school's own revision provision properly, since it is already funded through fees and most students use it patchily. Then sit a past paper from the correct board under exam timing and mark it honestly against the real mark scheme. That single exercise identifies where marks are going more precisely than any conversation with a tutor. Only after that does paid help become efficient, because you now know what to buy. Families who reverse this order pay specialist rates for homework supervision, which is the commonest waste in this market.

faqs.question: How much does an IGCSE maths tutor cost in Abu Dhabi in AED?
faqs.answer: Published market figures read in October 2026: budget online tutoring at AED 45 to 150 an hour, a qualified subject tutor online at AED 150 to 300, an in-home one-to-one visit at AED 180 to 500 with the journey inside the rate, and a named IGCSE or A-Level specialist at AED 200 to 450 and above, reaching AED 650 for premium examiner-led provision. On a monthly basis Bestimate's 2026 estimates give AED 240 to 600 for budget weekly sessions and AED 600 to 1,200 mid-range. Those are the market's numbers; ours follow a free trial and a consultation.

faqs.question: Why is an in-home maths rate higher than an online one on this island?
faqs.answer: Because you are buying a journey as well as an hour. Al Maryah Island is roughly half a square kilometre of towers with no school inside it and few resident maths specialists, so an in-home match travels from the mainland across a bridge at the busiest part of the afternoon. The published gap between the bands is roughly AED 30 to 200 an hour, which across a school year of weekly sessions is a substantial sum spent on driving. IB Gram offers no home visits in the UAE at all, so the gap does not arise for us.

faqs.question: Which maths syllabus code is my child sitting, and why does the code matter?
faqs.answer: Ask the school: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics is 0580 and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A is 4MA1. The content overlaps but the papers, tier names, command terms, mark schemes and calculator policies differ. Cambridge tiers as Core and Extended; Pearson as Foundation and Higher. A tutor drilling the wrong board's past papers is teaching useful mathematics and wasting the specificity a specialist rate is supposed to buy. Give the code to anyone you speak to; whether they ask about the tier and paper pattern tells you a lot for nothing.

faqs.question: Is the Core or Foundation entry going to cost us money later?
faqs.answer: Potentially a great deal. A lower-tier maths entry caps the available grade, and A Level Mathematics and IB Higher Level maths courses normally require an Extended or Higher grade at a reasonable level, with each sixth form setting its own threshold. A student capped in Year 10 can find a door closed in Year 11 by a decision made eighteen months earlier, and reopening it means a resit series and another year of planning. Four to six sessions in Year 10 aimed at the content separating the tiers is the cheapest insurance available in this subject.

faqs.question: Which single maths fix gives the fastest visible return?
faqs.answer: Making the working visible. Students routinely do three steps mentally, write one line, reach the right answer and collect a fraction of the method marks available. It is a habit rather than a knowledge gap, roughly three weeks of a tutor refusing to accept unshown steps changes it permanently, and the gain appears on the very next marked paper. Close behind it is one session on calculator discipline — angle modes, fraction entry, statistical functions, and recording enough alongside a display to earn full credit. Neither is impressive to advertise, which is why neither gets offered.

faqs.question: How should revision differ between a calculator and a non-calculator paper?
faqs.answer: They examine different skills, so they need separating. A non-calculator component rewards arithmetic fluency, fraction and surd handling, estimation and mental method, and a student who has only ever revised with the machine on the desk will underperform their topic knowledge. A calculator component rewards efficient machine use plus enough recorded working to support the display. Practise each in its own sessions, with the calculator deliberately removed or deliberately foregrounded. Paper patterns are revised by the boards, so confirm which of your child's papers permit a calculator through the school.

faqs.question: Do you hand over past papers and mark schemes with the fee?
faqs.answer: No. We reference them and point to the official source. Board syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables are copyrighted material belonging to Cambridge or Pearson, and bundling scanned copies into a tutoring package is redistributing somebody else's property rather than adding value for you. Papers come through your school's exams officer or the board. What a tutor adds is not the paper but the marking of your child's attempt at it against the real rubric, and the naming of what went wrong, which a downloaded folder cannot do.

faqs.question: Is a November resit in maths worth the money?
faqs.answer: It depends on the size of the gap and on a question you can ask for free. For Cambridge candidates November is the resit route, since the February and March series is India-only and unavailable in Abu Dhabi; Pearson offers November too. Price three things: the entry fee from your centre, a short targeted tutoring block rather than a full re-teach, and the time cost of revising through the first sixth-form term. Pearson's history shows November results reaching students the following January. Before any of that, ask the receiving sixth form whether they will accept the original grade.

faqs.question: How many sessions does a maths topic block normally take?
faqs.answer: Four to six for a named weakness, which is enough to teach the method, drill it, and test it under timing without the arrangement drifting into open-ended supervision. Algebraic manipulation sometimes needs more because it is fluency rather than knowledge and responds to short frequent practice. Calculator discipline and working presentation need one or two. The important feature is not the number but the endpoint: a block has a defined topic list, a defined session count and a named assessment to review against, which is what stops a maths budget becoming a subscription.

faqs.question: Should we fund maths and another subject at the same time?
faqs.answer: Rarely, and maths is usually the one to fund. It gates the sixth-form choice more tightly than any other IGCSE subject, so a grade there has consequences a science grade may not. Funding two subjects weekly roughly doubles the monthly figure and splits the student's attention in the term they can least afford it, which tends to produce two small nudges rather than one changed grade. The exception is a genuine emergency where two subjects are both at risk of closing a specific door. Otherwise take maths properly and reassess with the next marked assessment.

faqs.question: Which maths topics should we actually pay someone to teach?
faqs.answer: The ones a marked script shows, which in practice cluster. Algebraic manipulation, because almost every multi-step question at the higher tiers routes through it and one slip loses a whole question. Trigonometry and bearings, because they are attempted without diagrams and lost for that reason. Histograms with unequal class widths and conditional probability, because they recur every series and are under-practised. And multi-step problem solving at the top of the higher tier, where the skill is planning a route rather than any single technique. Everything else, the school is already covering.

faqs.question: Can a tutor guarantee my child a particular IGCSE maths grade?
faqs.answer: No, and a provider offering one is telling you something about themselves rather than about your child. What tutoring buys is hours of specialist attention aimed at identified weaknesses, and the outcome depends on the student's work between sessions, the starting point, the tier they are entered for and the paper on the day. We publish no grade guarantees, no success percentages and no self-generated statistics, because we could not evidence them with a sample size, a date and a method. Review the spend against the next marked assessment instead; that is a real measure.

faqs.question: Do private maths tutors in Abu Dhabi need a permit, and does it cost them?
faqs.answer: Yes to the permit, no to the cost. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued through MoHRE, and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Applications go through the MoHRE smart app, website or e-services system. Tutoring without a permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and since no fine schedule is published you should distrust any figure quoted at you.

faqs.question: What should we send before a free IGCSE maths trial on Al Maryah Island?
faqs.answer: The syllabus code and tier, so the tutor is board-correct from the first minute. The last two marked maths assessments with the teacher's comments, ideally including a past paper sat under timing. And the time your child is actually home, since a commute from Al Reem is twenty minutes and one from the mainland can be fifty, which decides which slots are real. With those three, the trial hour works on evidence and you can ask the tutor at the end to name the four errors they found and what each one costs.

faqs.question: Will anyone come to our Al Maryah Island address for the maths lessons?

intro.heading: Al Muroor's school day decides when maths tuition can happen
paragraphs: Al Muroor is a dense inland district of apartment blocks behind Muroor Road, with Airport Road along one flank and the Al Mushrif and Al Nahyan school cluster a few minutes away. Almost nobody here attends a school on their own street. Children leave in several directions each morning and come back in several directions each afternoon, and the gap between those two facts is why so many maths tuition arrangements in this neighbourhood collapse in the second month.

The arithmetic is simple and rarely done. A British-curriculum secondary day in Abu Dhabi typically ends between 2.50pm and 3.30pm. Add fifteen to twenty-five minutes for a car park and a pick-up queue, then the drive. From Al Mushrif that is short. From Al Reem Island it is a bridge crossing at the worst hour of the day. From the Al Raha corridor or Khalifa City it is twenty-five to forty minutes on a good afternoon. A Year 11 student who left school at 3.15pm is through the door of an Al Muroor flat somewhere between 3.45pm and 4.50pm, and is not ready to think about quadratics for another half hour after that. None of that is unusual; it is simply rarely written down before a tuition slot is agreed.

Which means the 4pm slot that every tuition timetable offers is the wrong slot for this neighbourhood, and the 5pm one is marginal. The first genuinely workable weekday window for an Al Muroor IGCSE student is 6pm, and 6.30pm or 7pm is better. That is a problem for an in-home arrangement, because the tutor now has to cross the same city at the same hour and that journey appears in the fee: in-home one-to-one visits in this market are quoted at AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel included, against AED 150 to 300 online for comparable teaching.

IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE. Visits to a family's address are something we run only in India. For an Al Muroor family, every maths lesson is one-to-one over live video, which is the reason a 7pm Tuesday slot can be held for forty weeks without anyone renegotiating it in October. There is no drive to absorb, no parking, and no cascade when a pick-up runs late.

The second half of this page is about the maths itself, because the timetable only matters if the hour is well spent. Your child sits either Cambridge 0580 or Pearson Edexcel 4MA1, at two papers each, at a tier the school chose. Which code, which tier, and which paper is non-calculator are the three facts that should shape every session, and a surprising number of families reach February of Year 11 without being told any of them.

abu-dhabi/igcse-maths-tutor-in-al-muroor.programmesIntro: An Al Muroor family usually meets IGCSE maths as part of a longer British-curriculum sequence, and the maths decisions made at each stage constrain the next one. These are the three stages that matter around Years 9 to 13.

programmes.name: Key Stage 3, Years 7 to 9
programmes.description: The years in which the tier decision is quietly being made. Schools set maths from Year 7 or 8, and set movement after Year 9 is uncommon. A student comfortable with negative indices, fraction arithmetic without a calculator and algebraic rearrangement by the end of Year 9 is an Extended or Higher candidate; one who is not will usually be entered for Core or Foundation unless something changes early.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Muroor this stage frequently coincides with a change of school or curriculum, because families arriving in Abu Dhabi often move children into the Al Mushrif and Al Nahyan cluster mid-stage. A student arriving from a CBSE or American system meets different notation and a different expectation about showing method, and three or four sessions in Year 9 is cheaper than two years of tier recovery.

programmes.name: IGCSE Mathematics, Years 10 and 11
programmes.description: Two years, one syllabus code, two papers and a tier. Cambridge 0580 splits into Core, grades C to G, and Extended, grades A* to E. Pearson Edexcel 4MA1 splits into Foundation, grades 5 to 1, and Higher, grades 9 to 4. Tuition in Year 10 is cheaper and more effective than tuition in Year 11, because Year 10 can still change the entry.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi centres sit the June and November series for Cambridge; the February and March series is offered in India only. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May/June and November. Schools in the Al Mushrif cluster commonly enter the main cohort in June, which makes the February half-term the last point at which a Year 11 can meaningfully change direction.

programmes.name: Post-16 maths routes
programmes.description: An IGCSE maths grade is the gate to everything afterwards. A-Level Mathematics typically expects a grade 7 or A at Higher or Extended, and IB Analysis and Approaches assumes the same algebraic fluency from week one. A Core or Foundation entry closes both routes, which is why the tier conversation in Year 10 is about options rather than about this year's report.
programmes.countryNote: Al Muroor students continuing into the IB Diploma mostly move to campuses on Al Reem Island, Saadiyat Island or the Al Raha corridor, where Analysis and Approaches cohorts are small. abu-dhabi/igcse-maths-tutor-in-al-muroor.subjectsIntro: These are the components an IGCSE maths tutor working with an Al Muroor student is actually dealing with, named by paper and by topic rather than by chapter.

subjects.name: Cambridge 0580 Extended, Paper 3
subjects.description: Shorter structured questions sat without a calculator, worth half the Extended grade. Marks go missing on fraction arithmetic, standard form, surds and index laws, all of which school practice tends to do with a calculator in hand. This is the most recoverable paper in the subject and the one most tuition plans ignore.

subjects.name: Cambridge 0580 Extended, Paper 4
subjects.description: Longer multi-step questions worth the other half of the grade, with the heavier algebra, trigonometry, vectors and probability content. The failure mode is method marks lost to unshown working on questions a student can answer. Training here is about writing, not about knowing.

subjects.name: Pearson Edexcel 4MA1 Papers 1 and 2
subjects.description: Two papers, both calculator-permitted, 50% each, which makes the Edexcel route feel different from Cambridge in practice even where the content overlaps. Higher tier covers grades 9 to 4 and expects confident algebraic manipulation, functions and transformations of graphs.

subjects.name: Algebra: rearrangement, factorising and quadratics
subjects.description: The spine of the subject and the single best predictor of a grade. Completing the square, the quadratic formula, simultaneous equations with one non-linear, algebraic fractions and the factor theorem. A student who is insecure here loses marks in topics that look unrelated, such as mensuration and probability.

subjects.name: Trigonometry beyond right-angled triangles
subjects.description: Sine and cosine rules, area of a triangle, bearings and three-dimensional problems. Students lose marks by choosing the wrong rule rather than by applying it badly, so the useful practice is identification under timing rather than repetition of worked examples.

subjects.name: Graphs, functions and transformations
subjects.description: Sketching quadratics, cubics and reciprocals, reading gradients and intercepts, transformations of curves, and inverse and composite functions on the Edexcel Higher route. The common gap is reading a graph for information rather than plotting one, which is what the papers mostly ask.

subjects.name: Probability and set notation
subjects.description: Tree diagrams, conditional probability and Venn notation, where the arithmetic is easy and the structure is not. Marks are lost in setting the problem out, not in the multiplication, which makes this topic unusually responsive to a few well-aimed sessions.

subjects.name: Mensuration, similarity and bounds
subjects.description: Volume and surface area of composite solids, similar shapes with area and volume scale factors, and upper and lower bounds. Scale factors applied to the wrong power is the classic Extended error and costs several marks on a single question.

subjects.name: Non-calculator number fluency
subjects.description: Fractions, decimals, percentages, standard form, surds and index laws performed by hand at speed. It is a trained motor skill rather than an understanding, and six short sessions on it reliably move more grade than six hours of topic revision in the spring.

subjects.name: Past-paper technique and timing
subjects.description: Whole papers under exam conditions, then dissected mark by mark against the published mark scheme's demands. The aim is a student who knows how long a six-mark question is allowed to take and what the examiner expects to see written down.

sections.heading: The Al Muroor afternoon, hour by hour
paragraphs: A workable IGCSE maths slot for an Al Muroor student starts at 6pm. That is the practical answer, and it comes out of the school run rather than out of any theory about concentration. Secondary schools serving this neighbourhood finish between roughly 2.50pm and 3.30pm. Pick-up adds fifteen to twenty-five minutes before a car moves. Then the drive, which ranges from five minutes within Al Mushrif to forty on the Al Raha run at the wrong hour.

The table sets out the main directions an Al Muroor family travels and what each does to the evening. The figures are typical drive times rather than measurements, and they vary with the day; what does not vary is the ordering. Families on the island cluster have options before six. Families crossing a bridge or heading to the mainland communities do not, and a tuition plan that pretends otherwise produces a cancelled session in week four and an abandoned arrangement by half term.

This is where online delivery stops being a compromise and becomes the reason the arrangement survives. A tutor who must physically arrive at a flat behind Muroor Road at 6.30pm is making the same journey the family just made, in the same traffic, and that journey is paid for in the hourly rate. Removing it means the slot can be late enough to be realistic, long enough to be useful, and stable enough to hold through a whole academic year.

sections.heading: Which maths syllabus is your child actually sitting?
paragraphs: Three families in ten arrive at a first maths session without knowing whether their child sits Cambridge 0580 or Pearson Edexcel 4MA1. It is not a trivial distinction and it is printed on every past paper the school hands out. The two specifications cover similar mathematics and assess it differently, and a tutor working from the wrong one will give sound teaching and the wrong exam preparation.

Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 splits into Core and Extended. On the current structure, Core students sit a non-calculator paper and a calculator paper; Extended students sit their own non-calculator and calculator pair, each worth half the grade. Core is graded C to G, Extended A* to E. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics Specification A, code 4MA1, sets two papers of equal weight at Foundation or Higher tier, both with a calculator permitted, with Higher covering grades 9 to 4 and Foundation 5 to 1.

The practical consequences are specific. A Cambridge Extended student needs trained non-calculator fluency because half the grade depends on it, and most school practice does not provide that. An Edexcel Higher student needs calculator discipline and strong algebraic manipulation across two long papers. A student who changes schools mid-course can change boards mid-course, which happens more often in Abu Dhabi than anywhere, and the overlap is close enough to hide the gaps until a mock paper exposes them. Ask the school for the specification code in writing. It takes one email, it costs nothing, and it is the piece of information every subsequent decision about past papers, tier and timing depends on.

sections.heading: Core, Extended and the ceiling nobody mentions at parents' evening
paragraphs: The tier your child is entered for sets the highest grade available to them, and that fact is often communicated quietly or not at all. A Cambridge Core entry caps the grade at C. A Pearson Foundation entry caps it at 5. Those are respectable outcomes and the right call for plenty of students, but they close doors that a family may not know are closing.

The doors are post-16 ones. A-Level Mathematics commonly expects a grade 7 or an A, which a Core or Foundation entry cannot produce. IB Analysis and Approaches assumes Extended-level algebra from the first week. Science A-Levels expect confident maths. So the tier decision in Year 10 is not about this year's grade; it is about which subjects are available in Year 12, and it is worth asking the school directly which tier your child is on and what it caps.

Where a student is borderline, the useful question is narrower than it sounds: can they do non-calculator number and algebra reliably? Not quickly, not elegantly, reliably. Students placed in Core who could have held Extended almost always fail that one test rather than the broader syllabus. It is also the most trainable thing in the subject, which is why a short Year 10 block aimed at exactly that is the best value available in IGCSE maths and why it is worth buying before the entry is submitted rather than after. One further warning: a school can move a student down a tier late in Year 11 and present it as protecting the grade. Sometimes that is correct. Ask what the ceiling becomes and what it closes, and ask before the entry is submitted rather than after.

sections.heading: Where IGCSE maths marks actually go missing
paragraphs: Mark loss in IGCSE maths is unusually predictable, which makes it cheap to fix if anyone looks. The dominant cause is not ignorance of a topic. It is unshown working on questions the student can do, followed by arithmetic slips in non-calculator work, followed by choosing the wrong method on a question that signals its method clearly to a trained reader.

Unshown working is the biggest and the easiest. On a multi-step question most of the marks are method marks, and a correct final answer with no visible route earns fewer of them than an incorrect answer with a clear one. Students who have been praised for doing things in their heads lose most to this, and it takes about three sessions of nagging and one mock paper to break the habit. Scale-factor errors in similar shapes are the classic Extended trap: area scales by the square, volume by the cube, and a student who applies the linear factor loses an entire question.

The rest cluster into a short list. Bearings measured from the wrong direction. Probability trees drawn correctly then multiplied along the wrong branch. Standard form handled confidently on a calculator and not at all by hand. Rounding applied too early, so a correct method produces a wrong answer. None of these needs new mathematics taught. They need diagnosis against the student's own scripts, which is why a tutor who asks to see the last mock paper before the first session is doing the job properly.

sections.heading: The June and November series, counted backwards
paragraphs: Cambridge International runs IGCSE exams in a June series and a November series. UAE centres sit those two; the February and March series is offered to India only, so any advice built around a February exam window does not apply to a child sitting in Abu Dhabi. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states plainly that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after the wrong zone timetable was used, which is a detail worth checking with the school rather than assuming.

The deadlines that matter sit months before the papers. Final entries are submitted by the school, not the family, and once submitted the tier is fixed. Mock papers usually sit in the winter term and drive predicted grades. For the November route, the Pearson November 2026 final timetable ran to 19 November 2026 and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026, which shows how long the gap between paper and result can be.

Work backwards from those fixed points. If the June series is the target, the tier conversation belongs in the autumn of Year 10, non-calculator fluency work belongs in the winter of Year 10, and whole-paper timing belongs from February of Year 11. Starting the sequence in April of Year 11 is the single commonest mistake in this market, and it is also when every specialist with capacity has already been booked by somebody else.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies sitting alongside the IGCSE timetable
paragraphs: An Abu Dhabi family planning a maths tutoring schedule is planning around a timetable that is fuller than the British curriculum alone. Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific national curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. Those subjects sit on top of the IGCSE programme, not instead of part of it, and they consume real hours in the school week and in homework.

The published requirements give a sense of scale. KHDA's mandatory-subject guidance for Dubai, the most detailed document of its kind in the country, calculates instructional time in forty-minute lesson units, requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and prohibits combined classes for the two groups outright. It also requires that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold the appropriate KHDA permission to teach those subjects, and states that using different or additional content for the mandatory subjects without prior permission from the Ministry is not allowed.

For a maths tuition plan in Al Muroor, the point is practical. A Year 11 student is carrying eight or nine IGCSE subjects plus Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and the week has no slack in it. That is an argument for one well-aimed maths session rather than two vague ones, for sixty minutes rather than two hours, and for weekend mornings when a long past paper needs doing. It is also worth knowing that for Ministry of Education equivalency, Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five required IGCSE subjects.

sections.heading: Ramadan, half terms and the rhythm of an Abu Dhabi school year
paragraphs: A weekly tutoring arrangement that ignores the Abu Dhabi calendar breaks three or four times a year, and each break costs more than a missed session because restarting is slower than continuing. Planning for the interruptions in advance is the difference between a plan that lasts a year and one that lasts a term.

Ramadan shortens the school day across the UAE and moves the whole family's energy to the evening. Sessions that worked at 6.30pm often work better after iftar, and students revising for a June series during Ramadan generally do better with shorter, more frequent sessions than with the usual ninety-minute block. Saying this in advance and moving the slot deliberately works far better than cancelling week by week and hoping to catch up.

The other interruptions are predictable too. The winter break lands shortly after mocks, which makes it either the most valuable fortnight of Year 11 or a complete loss, depending on whether anything was planned. Spring break sits uncomfortably close to the June series. Al Muroor families also travel in the long summer, and a Year 10 student who stops maths entirely for ten weeks returns measurably weaker in exactly the non-calculator fluency that decides the tier. Two sessions a month over the summer prevents that, and online delivery means they happen wherever the family is. Plan the year's interruptions once, in September, on a single sheet. Ramadan, the winter break, spring break, the exam series and the family's own travel. A plan drawn in September survives; a plan renegotiated in each of those four weeks does not, and in Year 11 there is no spare term to recover a lost one.
bullets: Move the slot after iftar during Ramadan rather than cancelling week to week
Shorter and more frequent beats long blocks during a shortened school day
The winter break after mocks is the highest-value fortnight in Year 11
Two summer sessions a month protect the fluency that decides the tier

sections.heading: ADEK, tutor permits and what you can check for yourself
paragraphs: Private schools in Abu Dhabi are overseen by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate and publishes its own inspection outcomes. It is worth reading your child's school report from ADEK alongside the school's own, because the two are written for different audiences and an inspection report comments on teaching quality by subject in a way a school newsletter does not.

Private tutoring sits under a separate, federal rule. Anyone giving private lessons in the UAE needs a private tuition work permit from MoHRE, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered at government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's own service page for the permit lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time, applied for through its app, website or e-services. Those tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and because no fine schedule has been published, any specific amount circulating online is unverified.

Two checks are available to any Al Muroor parent and cost nothing. Ask the tutor whether they hold a current private tuition permit, and treat the answer as a legal clearance rather than as evidence of teaching quality or of any regulator endorsing anybody. Second, be aware that ADEK's professional-ethics rules bar private and charter school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit carries a comparable condition. An offer of private lessons from your child's own classroom teacher is an offer to breach that, which is press-reported policy worth verifying against ADEK's current document.

process.title: Tell us the board, the tier and the school run
process.description: Cambridge 0580 or Pearson Edexcel 4MA1, Core or Extended, Foundation or Higher, plus which direction the afternoon drive goes. The tier tells us who should teach your child; the drive tells us honestly which evening slots are worth offering.

process.title: Send the last mock paper, marked
process.description: A marked script is worth more than any description of the problem, because mark loss in IGCSE maths is visible on the page. Send the paper and the latest report, and the trial lesson begins with diagnosis rather than with introductions.

process.title: Take the free trial in the slot you intend to keep
process.description: Book the trial at the time you would really hold each week, not at a convenient one-off hour. A 5pm trial that works once and a 5pm weekly slot that never works again is the commonest reason an arrangement fails. The tutor is named before the lesson.

process.title: Fix the slot and track the school's sequence
process.description: Once a workable time is agreed it stays fixed, and the sessions follow your child's own scheme of work so nothing is taught twice in two versions. Notes and the shared whiteboard are saved after every lesson.

process.title: Shift to whole papers from February of Year 11
process.description: In the final stretch the plan changes shape: fewer topic sessions, more whole papers under timing, dissected against the mark scheme. Weekend mornings usually replace one weekday slot at this point, because a fresh brain sits a paper better than a tired one.

whyPoints.title: Slots built around the real school run
whyPoints.description: Sessions start from 6pm Gulf Standard Time because that is when an Al Muroor household is actually home and settled, whether the drive came from Al Mushrif or from the Al Raha corridor. A slot nobody can sustain is not a cheaper slot, it is a cancelled one.

whyPoints.title: Both boards, by paper
whyPoints.description: Cambridge 0580 and Pearson Edexcel 4MA1 are taught by their actual paper structure, including which paper permits a calculator. A tutor working from the wrong specification gives sound maths teaching and the wrong exam preparation.

whyPoints.title: The tier conversation in Year 10
whyPoints.description: Entry tier sets the grade ceiling and the post-16 options, and it is decided while there is still time to change the inputs. A short diagnostic block in Year 10 is worth more than a term of Year 11 intervention.

whyPoints.description: The first session works from a marked mock paper rather than a chapter list, because unshown working, premature rounding and scale-factor errors are visible on the page and invisible in a report.

whyPoints.title: A calendar that survives Ramadan and the summer

faqs.question: What is the earliest a maths session can realistically start for a child living in Al Muroor?
faqs.answer: Six in the evening, and 6.30pm or 7pm on the longer runs. Secondary schools serving this neighbourhood finish between about 2.50pm and 3.30pm, pick-up takes another fifteen to twenty-five minutes, and the drive back ranges from five minutes within Al Mushrif to forty from the Al Raha corridor at that hour. A child home at 4.45pm is not ready for algebra at five. Booking the trial at the time you actually intend to keep, rather than at a convenient one-off hour, is the single best way to avoid an arrangement that quietly dies in November.

faqs.question: Where is the syllabus code printed, and why does the board matter so much?
faqs.answer: The code is printed on every past paper the school issues and on the specification the maths department works from, so the fastest route is to look at a recent past paper or ask the head of maths directly. It matters more than it sounds. Cambridge 0580 Extended includes a non-calculator paper worth half the grade; Edexcel 4MA1 permits a calculator on both papers. A tutor working from the wrong specification can teach excellent mathematics and prepare your child for the wrong assessment, and the overlap is close enough to hide that until a mock paper exposes it.

faqs.question: Can a tutor come to our flat in Al Muroor for maths lessons?
faqs.answer: Some Abu Dhabi providers do offer that, and market rates for in-home one-to-one sit at AED 180 to 500 an hour precisely because the figure absorbs the tutor's journey. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; visits to a family's address are something we run only in India. Al Muroor lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. The practical gain is a slot late enough to be realistic after a long school run, and an hour that contains sixty minutes of teaching rather than forty plus somebody's drive down Airport Road.

faqs.question: Is Extended tier worth pushing for if my child is borderline in Year 10?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, because the tier sets the grade ceiling and therefore the post-16 options. Cambridge Core caps at grade C and Edexcel Foundation at grade 5, which effectively closes A-Level Mathematics and makes IB Analysis and Approaches very hard to enter. The decision almost always turns on one narrow question: can the student do non-calculator number and algebra reliably? That is the most trainable thing in the subject. A four to eight session block in Year 10 aimed squarely at it is the best value purchase available in IGCSE maths, because it happens before the entry is submitted.

faqs.question: Why does my child lose marks on questions they clearly know how to do?
faqs.answer: Almost always unshown working. On a multi-step IGCSE question most of the marks are method marks, so a correct final answer with no visible route scores less than an incorrect answer with a clear one. Students praised for working things out in their heads are the worst affected. The habit takes roughly three sessions of consistent correction and one dissected mock paper to break. The other repeat offenders are rounding applied too early, which turns a correct method into a wrong answer, and area or volume scale factors applied as if they were linear.

faqs.question: Which maths topics cost Abu Dhabi IGCSE students the most marks?
faqs.answer: Non-calculator number work leads, because half the Cambridge Extended grade depends on it and most school practice happens with a calculator to hand. Fractions, standard form, surds and index laws by hand are the specific gaps. After that come similar shapes, where area scales by the square and volume by the cube and students apply the linear factor; trigonometry, where the error is choosing between the sine and cosine rules rather than applying either; and probability trees, which are usually drawn correctly and then multiplied along the wrong branch.

faqs.question: Should we use weekday evenings or weekend mornings for maths?
faqs.answer: Both, for different jobs. A fixed weekday evening slot from 6pm is right for topic teaching and for keeping pace with the school's scheme of work. Weekend mornings are the only realistic window for whole papers under exam timing, which cannot be done properly after a long school day and a forty-minute drive. From February of Year 11 most Al Muroor families end up swapping one weekday session for a longer weekend morning, with the paper sat first and the session spent on the dissection.

faqs.question: When should a Year 11 maths plan switch from topics to past papers?
faqs.answer: February, or immediately after mocks if those sit later. Before that point, topic teaching and non-calculator fluency work give the better return because there is still time to change what the student knows. After it, the limiting factor is usually technique rather than knowledge: timing, working shown, question-type recognition and choosing what to attempt first. The switch should be deliberate and visible. If a tutor is still working chapter by chapter in April of Year 11, ask what the plan is for whole papers.

faqs.question: Does Ramadan mean pausing maths tuition until after the holiday?
faqs.answer: No, though it usually means moving it. The school day shortens across the UAE during Ramadan and household energy moves to the evening, so a session that worked at 6.30pm often works better after iftar. Shorter and more frequent sessions tend to suit a shortened day better than the usual ninety-minute block. Deciding the new slot in advance works considerably better than cancelling week by week, because restarting a maths arrangement costs more than continuing one, particularly for a Year 11 facing the June series.

faqs.question: My child changed schools and the maths looks different. What usually goes wrong?
faqs.answer: Board changes hide inside curriculum similarity. A student moving between Abu Dhabi schools can move from Cambridge 0580 to Edexcel 4MA1 mid-course, and the content overlaps enough that nothing looks wrong until a mock paper arrives with an unfamiliar structure. The gaps are usually in paper format rather than mathematics: a Cambridge Extended student who has never sat a non-calculator paper, or an Edexcel student unfamiliar with Cambridge question phrasing. A diagnostic session against a past paper from the new board identifies that in an hour.

faqs.question: Do private maths tutors in Abu Dhabi need a government permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Individuals offering private lessons in the UAE need a private tuition work permit from MoHRE, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18, and MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day turnaround. Tutoring without one carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no official fine schedule is published, so quoted amounts online are unverified.

faqs.question: Can my child's own school maths teacher tutor them privately in the evening?
faqs.answer: They should not. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff bar teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE private tuition permit carries a comparable condition in its code of conduct. This has been reported in the press rather than quoted here from the policy document itself, so verify the current wording with ADEK or the school before acting on it. The practical point stands either way: an offer of private lessons from your child's own classroom teacher is an offer to breach a professional rule.

faqs.question: Will five IGCSE passes be enough when my child applies to a UAE university?
faqs.answer: On the British track, the Ministry of Education requires a pass in five accredited subjects at GCSE or IGCSE with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or better, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. One competitor page in this market states six subjects, which is wrong. Equivalency is handled by the Ministry, not by any tutoring provider, so verify the current requirement on moe.gov.ae before relying on it.

faqs.question: Which schools do your IGCSE maths students near Muroor Road attend?
faqs.answer: Students we support in this part of Abu Dhabi island come from the British-curriculum schools in Al Mushrif and Al Nahyan and from campuses on Al Reem Island, in Khalifa City and along the Al Raha corridor, including The British School Al Khubairat, International Community School Abu Dhabi, Al Yasmina Academy, Reach British School and Repton School Abu Dhabi. Those names describe the local school map only. IB Gram has no affiliation, partnership or endorsement relationship with any school named, and none of them is a client.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week does an Al Muroor Year 11 usually need for maths?
faqs.answer: One, for most students, held consistently for two or three terms. One well-aimed weekly session that tracks the school's sequence beats two vague ones, particularly for a child already carrying eight or nine subjects plus Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies. A second session earns its place for about six to eight weeks around mocks or in the final run to the June series, usually as a weekend morning for whole-paper work. More than two a week is rarely a teaching decision; it is usually a sign the diagnosis was never done.

Lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, and if the match is wrong we change it.

intro.heading: Nobody in Al Mushrif advertises a syllabus code, and that is the whole problem
paragraphs: Al Mushrif sits inland from the Corniche, bounded roughly by Airport Road, Karamah Street and the long run of villa blocks behind Mushrif Mall. It is one of the older residential districts on the island, and it has something most newer Abu Dhabi communities do not: a settled population of families who have had children in the same British-curriculum school for a decade. That stability is why the search for an IGCSE maths tutor here is rarely a panic search. It is usually a considered one, made by a parent who already knows which teacher their child gets on and which they do not.

What that parent cannot find out from a listings site is the thing that decides whether tuition works. Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A 4MA1 are not the same course. They do not use the same tiering language, they do not weight their papers the same way, and they do not reward the same exam habits. A tutor who has spent three years on 4MA1 Higher and is handed a 0580 Extended student will teach competently and still miss the specific places that syllabus takes marks off. The fix is not more hours. It is a tutor matched to the code.

The second thing a local search cannot tell you is availability. Al Mushrif is a twenty-minute drive from almost everywhere on the island, which sounds convenient until you count how many adults within that radius have taught Extended maths to grade 8 and 9 standard, are free at five in the afternoon, and hold a valid private tuition work permit. That pool is thin, and it gets thinner in the weeks before a series. Agencies handle the shortage by sending whoever is free. We handle it by widening the geography instead of lowering the bar.

So the page you are reading does not open with a promise. It opens with the position: IB Gram does not send a tutor to an Al Mushrif address, because home visits are a service we run only in India. For UAE families the lesson is delivered online, one-to-one, over live video, with a shared whiteboard and the student's own past papers on screen. That is a narrower offer than the local market makes, and it is the reason a Mushrif family can work with somebody who has taught the exact paper their child is sitting rather than somebody who happens to live off Karamah Street.

Below you will find the syllabus structures side by side, the places students actually drop marks in each, what the Abu Dhabi market charges in AED with every figure attributed, the Cambridge and Pearson session calendar counted backwards from results day, the permit rules that decide who may legally teach your child, and an honest account of what happens in the weeks when no specialist has a free slot. If one section is all you need, take it and leave the rest.

abu-dhabi/igcse-maths-tutor-in-al-mushri.programmesIntro: Al Mushrif children are spread across three qualification tracks, and the maths teaching a student needs depends more on the track than on the year group. These are the three IB Gram covers for families in this district, with the part that is specific to Abu Dhabi noted on each.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Two examined years ending in a terminal series. Mathematics is compulsory in every British-curriculum school in Abu Dhabi, and it is the subject most likely to be the reason a student is pulled out of a triple-science or an additional-language option. Tiering is decided by the school, usually late in Year 10, and reversing that decision later is possible but awkward. Tuition at this stage is paper practice against the mark scheme, not re-teaching from the textbook.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi private schools are licensed and inspected by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. Entry for IGCSE maths is made by the school as an exam centre, and Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones with its own timetable version. Ask your school's exams officer which zone it sits in before you plan revision around any published date.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus the core. Maths splits into Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation, each at two levels, and the choice is made at the end of Year 11 on the strength of IGCSE performance. A student who scraped a 6 on 0580 Extended will find Analysis and Approaches Higher Level unforgiving, and that conversation is better had in March of Year 11 than in October of Year 12.
programmes.countryNote: Several schools within reach of Al Mushrif run the Diploma alongside A Levels, so a Year 11 student here often has a genuine choice rather than a default. UAE candidates sit the May session. We do not publish IB exam or results dates on these pages, because the IB's own site blocks automated checking and a date a parent plans around has to come from the school's IB coordinator or ibo.org directly.

programmes.name: AS and A Level mathematics
programmes.description: The linear route most British-curriculum schools in the emirate still offer. Pure maths dominates, with mechanics or statistics as the applied component depending on the board. Students arriving from a comfortable 0580 Extended grade are often surprised by the proof and algebraic fluency demanded in the first term, and that gap is the single most common reason a Year 12 asks for help in October.
programmes.countryNote: For UAE Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track, a student must show five accredited subjects at GCSE or IGCSE with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or better, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. Verify the current wording with the Ministry before you rely on it.

abu-dhabi/igcse-maths-tutor-in-al-mushri.subjectsIntro: Maths is the page's subject, but it is not one subject. These are the strands an IGCSE maths tutor working with an Al Mushrif student actually teaches, and the place each one tends to cost marks. A diagnostic session usually finds the problem in two or three of them, not all nine.

subjects.name: Number, ratio and percentage change
subjects.description: Reverse percentages, compound growth and repeated proportional change. Marks go on the method line, and students who do the arithmetic mentally lose them even when the final figure is right. Standard form and bounds appear here too, and upper and lower bound questions are among the most reliably mishandled on the non-calculator paper.

subjects.name: Algebraic manipulation and rearrangement
subjects.description: Factorising quadratics, algebraic fractions, changing the subject of a formula with the subject appearing twice. This is the strand that determines whether the rest of the paper is accessible. A student who cannot rearrange confidently will lose marks in mensuration, in kinematics graphs and in trigonometry without ever meeting an algebra question.

subjects.name: Equations, inequalities and simultaneous systems
subjects.description: Linear and quadratic simultaneous equations, inequality regions, and the quadratic formula applied without a calculator. Extended candidates meet non-linear pairs that need substitution, and the usual failure is an arithmetic slip in the discriminant rather than any misunderstanding of the method.

subjects.name: Coordinate geometry and graphs
subjects.description: Gradients, midpoints, parallel and perpendicular lines, and sketching cubics, reciprocals and exponentials. Transformations of graphs are a common Extended question and are usually answered by guesswork. Reading a gradient from a distance-time or speed-time graph belongs here and is worth practising against real mark schemes.

subjects.name: Mensuration and compound solids
subjects.description: Arc length, sector area, surface area and volume of cones, spheres and frustums, and the similar-shape scale factors for area and volume. Candidates routinely apply a length scale factor to a volume. The formulae that are given on the paper and the ones that must be recalled differ by board, which is worth checking early.

subjects.name: Trigonometry in two and three dimensions
subjects.description: Sine and cosine rules, area of a triangle, bearings, and angles between a line and a plane. Three-dimensional trigonometry is where Extended students lose most heavily, because the question demands a correct sketch before any calculation. Teaching the sketch, not the formula, is what moves the mark.

subjects.name: Probability and set notation
subjects.description: Tree diagrams, conditional probability without replacement, Venn notation and complements. The arithmetic is easy and the reading is not: a question that changes from with replacement to without in its second clause is the standard trap, and students lose two marks for a correct method applied to the wrong denominator.

subjects.name: Statistics, averages and cumulative frequency
subjects.description: Grouped data, estimated means, histograms with unequal class widths and cumulative frequency curves read for quartiles. Frequency density is the single most common technical error on this strand. Interpretation marks also sit here, and they reward a sentence in plain English rather than a number.

subjects.name: Vectors and transformations
subjects.description: Column vectors, magnitude, and geometric proof using vector paths. Students who are fluent elsewhere often treat vector proof as unteachable. It is a short, learnable routine: express every needed path in terms of the given vectors, then compare. Two sessions usually settles it.

subjects.name: Functions and the additional maths bridge
subjects.description: Composite and inverse functions, domain and range, and the early calculus that Cambridge Additional Mathematics 0606 introduces for students heading to A Level or Higher Level. Schools near Al Mushrif that offer 0606 usually run it as a twilight option, which makes it the subject most likely to need outside support.

regions.note: The apartment strip along the northern shore. Flats here mean less study space than a Mushrif villa, which makes a quiet, fixed, forty-five-minute online slot more valuable than a longer session squeezed around family life.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: A bridge and a causeway away, and a much younger population. Al Reem's school-age children are mostly in primary and lower secondary, so the IGCSE cohort there is small and the tutoring demand is concentrated on Years 7 to 9 maths foundations.

regions.note: Ten to fifteen minutes from Al Mushrif outside peak, considerably more at pickup. Saadiyat schools finish late and run heavy co-curricular programmes, so weekday sessions for students there realistically start at six rather than four.

sections.heading: What a search for an IGCSE maths tutor in Al Mushrif is really asking
paragraphs: The search means two things at once: does somebody near me know this syllabus, and can they start this week. The honest answer in Al Mushrif is that proximity and syllabus depth seldom arrive in the same person, and when they do, that person is already booked. So IB Gram matches the other way round. The tutor is selected on the syllabus code, the tier and the paper your child is weakest in, and the lesson is delivered online over live video at a time that fits the Abu Dhabi school day.

That is a narrower claim than the local market makes, and it is deliberate. A tutor who drives to a Mushrif villa has to be inside a sensible radius, has to have a free evening after traffic, and has to charge enough to make the journey worth making. Each of those filters removes candidates, and none of them has anything to do with whether the person has taught Extended Paper 4 recently. Drop the geography filter and the remaining pool is selected on teaching alone.

The table below is the version of this answer we would want to read as a parent: what coverage actually looks like by subject and level, how long a match usually takes, and what happens when nobody suitable is free. sections.heading: Which maths syllabus your child is actually sitting
paragraphs: Three codes dominate Abu Dhabi British-curriculum maths entries, and they behave differently in the exam hall. Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 splits candidates into Core and Extended, with a non-calculator paper and a calculator paper in each route and the calculator paper carrying the larger share of the marks. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A 4MA1 runs two papers of equal weight, allows a calculator in both, and tiers as Foundation and Higher. Cambridge International Mathematics 0607 is a different animal again, built around a graphic display calculator and, in its extended route, an investigation-style paper.

The practical consequence is that revision advice copied from the wrong board actively harms. A 4MA1 Higher student drilled on non-calculator arithmetic is spending time on a skill that paper does not test in isolation. A 0580 Extended student who has only ever practised with a calculator to hand walks into Paper 2 unprepared for the mental arithmetic load. This is the single most common thing we find in a first session, and it costs nothing to fix beyond knowing which code is on the entry.

Find the code before you book anything. It is on the statement of entry the school issues, on the front of every past paper the department hands out, and the exams officer will confirm it in a sentence. Then check the tier. Core and Foundation cap the grade available, and a student working comfortably at the top of Core is in the wrong route rather than doing well. Tier decisions are usually taken late in Year 10, which means a Year 10 parent reading this still has a say.

sections.heading: Where Al Mushrif students lose marks, in order of how many
paragraphs: Across diagnostic sessions with students from the central island schools, the losses cluster in the same handful of places, and almost none of them are about not knowing the topic. The largest single category is method marks forfeited by doing arithmetic in the head. A correct answer with no visible working scores the answer mark and nothing else; a wrong answer with full working often scores most of the question. Students who are quick at maths lose more marks this way than students who are slow at it.

Second is the unit and rounding instruction. Give your answer to three significant figures, leave your answer in terms of pi, give the answer in centimetres when the diagram is in millimetres. These are not maths errors and they are not accidents either: they are the result of reading the question once. Third is three-dimensional trigonometry, where the failure is geometric rather than computational. The student who cannot draw the right triangle out of the solid cannot start, and no amount of sine-rule practice helps.

Fourth, and particular to the non-calculator paper, is surd and exact-form confidence. A Mushrif student who has had a calculator available since Year 7 often has no working relationship with surds at all. Fifth is frequency density on histograms, which is a one-session fix that nobody seems to make. A diagnostic session is spent finding which of these five a particular student owns, because teaching all five to everybody is how tuition becomes expensive and slow.

sections.heading: What the Abu Dhabi market charges, and what the travel premium actually buys
paragraphs: Start with the monthly figure, because that is the number that decides whether tuition continues past February. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table puts a weekly one-hour arrangement at roughly AED 240 to 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. Published monthly packages in this market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home visits. Those are market figures from the providers named, not an IB Gram price list.

Converted to hourly, the bands are these. Budget online tuition, typically a university student, runs AED 45 to 150: EdFlik advertises from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52. A qualified subject tutor online sits at AED 150 to 300, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. An in-home one-to-one visit, travel included, is quoted at AED 180 to 500, with Bestimate at 180 to 350 and independent home tutors at 200 to 500. Named specialists reach AED 200 to 450 and beyond, with TutorChase publishing AED 270, and premium examiner-branded tuition at AED 500 to 650, where BartyED quotes AED 650.

The interesting gap is between the online qualified band and the in-home band for the same person. The difference is travel: an hour in the car, fuel, and the risk of a cancelled session that cannot be refilled. In Al Mushrif that premium buys a short drive, which is why in-home rates on the central island sit at the lower end of the quoted range. It buys nothing in Khalifa City, where the same tutor loses ninety minutes to the round trip. Nobody in this market publishes an AED figure with a source attached, which is why every number on this page has one.

sections.heading: Why nobody within ten minutes of Mushrif Park is the right filter
paragraphs: Set the radius at ten minutes from Mushrif Mall and you have drawn a circle around a few thousand households. Now apply the real requirements: has taught IGCSE maths to Extended standard in the last two years, knows which board your child's school enters, is free between four and seven on a weekday in term time, and holds a valid MoHRE private tuition work permit. Each condition is reasonable. Together they empty the circle, and what fills it instead is whoever is available.

This is the mechanism behind a complaint we hear often: the first tutor was lovely and nothing changed. A patient, pleasant graduate who did maths at university is not the same as a teacher who knows that question 19 on Extended Paper 4 is where the grade is decided. The first will supervise homework competently. The second will look at a mock paper and say, in one sentence, which three things are costing seven marks. Those are different services at a similar hourly price.

Widening the geography is not a compromise, it is the point. A Mushrif family working online can be matched to someone who has taught 0580 Extended through four series rather than someone who lives off Karamah Street, and the lesson still starts at five. What is lost is the physical presence of an adult in the room, which matters most for younger children and least for a Year 11 working through timed papers. That trade is worth naming honestly rather than selling around.

sections.heading: The June and November series, counted backwards from results day
paragraphs: UAE candidates sit two series. Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level exams in a June series and a November series, and offers the February/March series to India only, which is why a timetable found on a general revision blog may be useless here. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May/June and November. Both boards publish provisional timetables well ahead, and both revise them, so the only safe source is the live timetable on the board's own site.

What a parent can plan on is the shape rather than the dates. Entry closes months before the paper is sat. Mock windows fall roughly a term earlier. Results follow the exam window by weeks, not days: Pearson's June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, while November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026, and the November 2026 International GCSE timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. Those are dated citations, and they are the right way to understand the rhythm without quoting a future date that will go stale.

One Cambridge detail is worth more than any date. Every exam centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, each with its own version of the timetable, and Cambridge states that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after the wrong zone timetable was used. Ask your school's exams officer which zone it is in and plan revision from that version. The table below is the sequence counted backwards, which is the order a family actually experiences it.
