subjects.description: Should be automatic before the Year 11 autumn, because almost every upper-tier question routes through it. A student rearranging slowly loses time in every question rather than marks in one topic, which is why this is the first thing a calendar-led plan secures.

subjects.name: Percentages and reverse percentages
subjects.description: Appears in some form in most series and is the most reliably mishandled topic at this level: students multiply where they should divide. Fix it by the Year 11 autumn and it stays fixed; leave it to the spring and it competes with everything else for attention.

subjects.name: Similar shapes and scale factors
subjects.description: Length, area and volume scale by different powers of the ratio and the length factor gets used for all three. A one-week fix at any point in the calendar, which makes it the ideal topic to clear in the fortnight after mocks.

subjects.name: Trigonometry and bearings
subjects.description: Sine and cosine rules, three-figure bearings measured clockwise from north, and the ambiguous case of the sine rule, which many students do not know exists. Needs to be secure by the mock cycle because it rewards practice over several weeks.

subjects.name: Cumulative frequency, box plots and histograms
subjects.description: Histograms with unequal class widths require frequency density and students plot raw frequency instead. Statistics topics are good late-calendar work, because they are self-contained and do not depend on earlier material being secure.

subjects.name: Upper and lower bounds
subjects.description: Choosing which bound to use in a division or subtraction. Taught once in Year 10 and rarely revisited, so it is nearly always worth one deliberate week in the Year 11 autumn before anybody starts past papers seriously.

subjects.name: Simultaneous equations including a quadratic
subjects.description: Substituting a linear equation into a quadratic and tracking two solution pairs. Depends on algebraic fluency, so it cannot be fixed before manipulation is secure, which puts it in the Year 11 autumn rather than the spring.

subjects.name: Vectors and transformations
subjects.description: Column vector arithmetic and fully described transformations: a rotation needs centre and direction, an enlargement needs scale factor and centre. Descriptive precision is the mark, and it is a two-week fix at any point in the year.

subjects.name: Probability trees and conditional probability
subjects.description: Without replacement is where the marks sit, because the second branch denominators change. Self-contained enough to be worth doing in the final twelve weeks, and reliable once drilled with denominators annotated every time.

subjects.name: Functions, composite and inverse
subjects.description: Composite order is the recurring error, with students evaluating the outer function first. Inverse functions return the question to algebraic rearrangement, so this topic is a good late check on whether the manipulation work actually held.

sections.heading: Where a mathematics student should be, term by term
paragraphs: Almost every family that feels behind is behind against a schedule rather than against their child's ability, and the schedule is knowable. The table below sets out what should be true at each stage of the two examined years in mathematics specifically. It is a ten-minute checklist rather than a counsel of perfection, and it usually identifies two or three concrete things that are missing.

The failure pattern is consistent across this part of Abu Dhabi. A manipulation gap opens in Year 9 or the Year 10 autumn. Nobody notices, because Year 10 reports are not read as examination results. The gap is carried into Year 11, where the school is teaching new content and has no time to go back, and by the winter mocks the student is being examined on two years of material with one year genuinely fluent.

Catching that early is dramatically cheaper. One weekly hour from the Year 10 autumn, aimed at manipulation and then at the recurring topics, costs a fraction of a spring intensive and does not compete for the student's hours with mock revision and other subjects' coursework. The families who spend least overall are the ones who started earliest, not the ones who held out longest.

If you are reading this in the Year 11 spring, the checklist still works; it simply tells you which stages to skip. Secure manipulation if it is not secure, clear the two or three self-contained topics that can be fixed in a week each, and then spend everything remaining on conversion rather than coverage.

sections.heading: The series counted backwards for mathematics
paragraphs: Counting backwards in weeks is what makes a plan usable, because a student can hold a week in their head and cannot hold a term. The table below works back from the first mathematics paper. The weeks are approximate because each Abu Dhabi school sets its own mock and study-leave dates, so take the structure and insert your school's calendar into it.

Two items on the list are not negotiable and are easy to miss because they are administrative rather than academic. Final entries are submitted months before the papers, and the tier is fixed at that point for that series. Access arrangements, where a student needs them, must be applied for with supporting evidence before the entry deadline and cannot be arranged retrospectively. Both are a single email to the school office away.

The stage families most often misjudge is sixteen weeks out, which is usually just after mocks. That is the moment the plan should change character, from learning content to converting it. Students still working through a revision guide cover to cover at eight weeks out are the ones who never made that switch, and the switch is a decision rather than a skill.

Always check the live official timetable on the board's own site. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series and they can be revised, and Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, stating that it is essential to use the correct version for your zone and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one.

sections.heading: The tier entry is a calendar event, not an opinion
paragraphs: Parents tend to treat tiering as a judgement the school has made about their child. It is more useful to treat it as a dated administrative decision with a deadline attached. A Cambridge Core entry means the Core papers and a maximum grade of C. A Pearson Foundation entry caps at 5. Once entries are submitted for a series, that ceiling is fixed for that series whatever happens afterwards.

The school is usually right about the tier, and the problem is not the judgement. The problem is that it is communicated as administration, so a family discovers the cap at confirmation. A student who worked hard through Year 10 and outgrew a provisional Core judgement may have no straightforward route up by then, because the upper-tier content was never taught to them.

The downstream calendar consequence is the part that stings. Post-16 applications happen in the Year 11 winter and spring, and a mathematics ceiling of C or 5 can remove A Level Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry and Economics from the options. Nobody conceals this; it simply never gets said out loud while the entry can still be changed, because nobody owns that conversation.

The action is small and dated. In the Year 10 spring, email the school and ask for three things in writing: the tier in each examined subject, the maximum grade it allows, and the last date on which a change can be submitted. Then, if the answer is uncomfortable, two diagnostic sessions against the upper-tier specification will tell you whether pressing the point is realistic.

sections.heading: Mock season is the mathematics diagnostic
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi British-curriculum schools generally run mocks in the winter term, and most families read the result as a progress report. Read as a progress report it yields a grade. Read as a diagnostic, the same script tells you precisely which of four things is wrong, and the four have completely different remedies and timescales.

Go through it mark by mark. Every lost mark falls into one of four categories: content not known, command term or question wording misread, working not shown, or time ran out. Count them. A student with most losses in the timing column does not need more content teaching at all, and a student with most in the working column needs a habit installed rather than a topic taught.

In mathematics specifically, the working category is usually larger than families expect. Multi-stage questions award method marks for visible steps, so a student who computes mentally and writes a single line collects the answer mark and forfeits the rest. Across a paper with several such questions that habit alone can be worth a grade boundary, and it is the cheapest item on the list to change.

Al Raha Gardens has a practical advantage during mock season. Schools across Abu Dhabi release students for parts of it, and for students commuting to Khalifa City or the inner city that fortnight removes the journey as well. Three or four sessions in that window, working from a fresh script, reliably outperform twelve sessions in October working from a syllabus checklist.

sections.heading: November as the mathematics repair series
paragraphs: If June goes badly, three options exist and the window to choose between them is short. Pearson June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, which gives a sense of how little time sits between a result and the start of a post-16 course. The conversation is better had in the spring than in the week the grade arrives.

The first option is an enquiry about results, submitted by the school within a deadline set by the board. It is a clerical and marking review with defined grounds rather than a general appeal, and it is worth considering where a grade sits a mark or two below a boundary on a paper the student felt went well. Mathematics is a reasonable candidate because the marking is comparatively objective.

The second is the November series, which produces a grade the following January. November 2025 Pearson results reached students on 22 January 2026. For mathematics specifically a November resit is often a good bet, because the subject responds to a focused three-month build in a way that content-heavy subjects do not: the topics are known, the gap is usually technique, and technique improves quickly with timed practice.

The third is a full retake in the following June series, which suits a student several boundaries short where the content genuinely needs rebuilding rather than converting. Cambridge candidates in the UAE use June and November for all of this; the February and March series is offered to India only and is not available here, whatever a generic revision site suggests.

sections.heading: A twelve-week mathematics build when the weeks are counted
paragraphs: Twelve weeks is the window most families arrive with, usually just after mocks, and it is enough for a real change if it is spent on conversion rather than coverage. The decision that makes it work is to stop trying to learn the parts of the specification never understood and to secure marks on the parts that were.

The structure below runs in four phases of three weeks. The first three weeks establish a baseline, produce the error list and clear the self-contained topics that can each be fixed in a week: similar shapes, bounds, probability without replacement. The next three attack the highest-frequency errors on the list, which in mathematics are usually unshown working and reverse percentages rather than topics. The next three rehearse full papers under timing. The last three reduce to pacing and short daily recall.

Two things should be dropped deliberately, and dropping them is harder than adding anything. Topics that appear rarely and are not understood should be abandoned rather than learned badly, because the hours they consume are worth more elsewhere. And re-reading notes should stop entirely, since at this stage it produces a feeling of progress with almost no measurable return.

The honest limit: twelve focused weeks can move a grade boundary and sometimes two in mathematics, which responds better than most subjects to technique work. It will not move four. No provider can guarantee a grade or an improvement, and anyone offering one is selling. What a diagnostic session produces is an estimate you can hold us to, based on the script in front of us.

sections.heading: Ramadan, the spring break and the weeks that are not there
paragraphs: A plan built on calendar weeks rather than teaching weeks will break, and in the UAE the gap between the two is substantial. Most Abu Dhabi private schools run three terms with a winter break around the turn of the year and a spring break towards the end of March, and that spring break lands squarely in the period when examination revision should be at its most intense.

Ramadan moves roughly eleven days earlier each year and currently falls in the spring, which means it increasingly overlaps the weeks before the May and June papers. Schools shorten the day during Ramadan, which frees the afternoon, but the freed afternoon is a weak teaching window because the household is fasting and preparing. A post-Iftar slot, commonly between 20:30 and 22:00, works much better and is easy to staff on video because nobody is driving.

Some families would rather pause for the month and resume afterwards. That is a legitimate choice we would rather you made deliberately than drifted into, because paying for sessions nobody attends is the worst outcome available. What matters is deciding in advance: a month lost by accident at that point in the year is expensive, and a month paused on purpose is manageable.

Do the arithmetic before agreeing any plan. Take the paper date, subtract the spring break, subtract the weeks your school has reserved for study leave, subtract Ramadan if your household reduces sessions then, and subtract travel you already know about. Most Abu Dhabi families find the real number is four to six weeks lower than their first estimate, and the plan that follows is more honest for it.

sections.heading: What each phase costs, and what we will not claim
paragraphs: Tutoring costs more per grade point in the spring than in the Year 10 autumn, which is a pricing reality rather than a judgement. Demand concentrates before papers, the formats wanted then are intensive, and the specialists able to work on a named paper are the scarcest part of the market. Buying the same outcome earlier is simply cheaper.

The Abu Dhabi market, with sources named, runs as follows. University-student tutors online advertise from around AED 33 to 52 at Tutopiya and AED 45 to 65 at EdFlik on their own pages. A qualified subject tutor online sits at roughly AED 150 to 300, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and TutorChase quoting around AED 270. Specialists run AED 200 to 450 and above, and in-home visits AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel priced in.

Those bands map onto the calendar in a predictable way. The budget band is good value in Year 9 and Year 10, where supervision and fluency are what is needed, and poor value in the final twelve weeks, where it cannot address paper technique. The specialist band is the reverse. Most of the overspending in this market comes from pairing a band with the wrong phase, which is a mistake the table below is meant to prevent.

What we will not claim: no provider can guarantee a grade, a score or an improvement, including us. No regulator or examination board accredits IB Gram, we hold no ADEK or MoHRE approval, and there is no Abu Dhabi office. Every dirham figure here carries its source and date. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years, and we will show you how to verify a tutor's.

whyPoints.description: Every plan starts from the series, the mock or the entry deadline and works back in weeks. That is the difference between a schedule a Year 11 student can hold in their head and a term of good intentions that runs out of road in March.

faqs.question: How many weeks does an IGCSE maths tutor in Al Raha Gardens need to make a difference?
faqs.answer: Twelve focused weeks is enough for a real change in mathematics, which responds to technique work better than most subjects. Eight weeks can clear two or three self-contained topics and install shown working. Three weeks is pacing and recall only. The reason mathematics does comparatively well in a short window is that the common losses are procedural: reverse percentages, scale factors, bounds and unshown working, each removable in a week or two of deliberate practice rather than months.

faqs.question: Which maths series do Abu Dhabi IGCSE students sit?
faqs.answer: June and November with Cambridge International, and May, June or November with Pearson Edexcel International GCSE. Cambridge's February and March series is offered to India only, so no candidate in Abu Dhabi sits it however many revision sites list its deadlines. Pearson's November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. Check your own school's timetable on the board's site, because Cambridge allocates centres to six administrative zones with different timetables.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a maths tutor to Al Raha Gardens homes?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Lessons here are one to one over live video with a shared whiteboard, which suits mathematics because every line of working stays visible and is saved for later. In-home visits in Abu Dhabi are quoted in the market at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel priced into the figure.

faqs.question: When is the maths tier decided, and can it still be changed?
faqs.answer: Provisionally from Year 10 attainment, and fixed when final entries are submitted months before the papers. Once entered, a Cambridge Core entry caps the grade at C and a Pearson Foundation entry caps it at 5 for that series whatever happens afterwards. Email the school in the Year 10 spring and ask three things in writing: the tier in each examined subject, the maximum grade it allows, and the last date on which a change can be submitted.

faqs.question: What should be secure before my child starts past papers?
faqs.answer: Algebraic manipulation first, because nearly every upper-tier question routes through it and slow rearrangement costs time in every question rather than marks in one topic. Then the three topics taught once in Year 10 and rarely revisited: upper and lower bounds, similar shape scale factors, and reverse percentages. Starting past papers before those are secure produces a long error list dominated by the same four things, which is demoralising and wastes the papers.

faqs.question: How should we read the mock script rather than just the grade?
faqs.answer: Go through it mark by mark and sort every lost mark into four boxes: content not known, question wording misread, working not shown, or ran out of time. Then count the boxes. In mathematics the working box is usually larger than families expect, because multi-stage questions award method marks for visible steps. A student with most losses in the timing box needs pacing work, not more content, and the tally almost always contradicts what the student guessed.

faqs.question: Is a November maths resit a sensible plan after a poor June?
faqs.answer: Often yes, and mathematics is one of the better subjects for it. The topics are already known, the gap is usually technique, and technique improves quickly with three months of timed practice. The timing caveat is that November results arrive the following January, as happened when November 2025 Pearson results reached students on 22 January 2026. That suits a post-16 place that can hold a conditional grade and does not suit one needing a firm grade in September.

faqs.question: Why does my daughter get right answers and still lose marks?
faqs.answer: Because the working is not visible. Multi-stage mathematics questions allocate method marks to steps, so a student who computes mentally and writes a single line collects the answer mark and forfeits the rest. On a paper with several such questions that habit alone can be worth a grade boundary. It is also the cheapest thing on any error list to change: every line written, enforced session by session, usually becomes automatic within a month.

faqs.question: How many teaching weeks are actually left before the maths papers?
faqs.answer: Fewer than the calendar implies. Take the paper date, subtract the spring break, subtract the weeks your school has reserved for study leave, subtract Ramadan if your household reduces sessions then, and subtract travel you already know about. Most Abu Dhabi families find the usable figure is four to six weeks below their first estimate. Doing that arithmetic before agreeing a plan is the difference between a schedule that holds and one that collapses in March.

faqs.question: Can tutoring continue through Ramadan in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the timing changed. Schools shorten the day during Ramadan, which frees the afternoon, but the freed afternoon is a poor teaching window because the household is fasting and preparing. A post-Iftar slot, commonly between 20:30 and 22:00, works far better and is straightforward to staff on video because nobody is driving late at night. Families who would rather pause can do that instead; the important thing is deciding in advance rather than losing the weeks by accident.

faqs.question: Does mock fortnight suit Al Raha Gardens families particularly?
faqs.answer: It does, for a specific local reason. Many students here commute to Khalifa City or as far as Al Bateen and Al Mushrif, and schools across Abu Dhabi release students for parts of mock season. That fortnight therefore removes the journey and produces a fresh marked script at the same time, which makes a daytime session possible for the only time in the year. Three or four sessions in that window beat twelve in October built from a checklist.

faqs.question: Is it worth clearing small topics or focusing on the big ones?
faqs.answer: Clear the small self-contained ones first, especially with twelve weeks or fewer. Similar shapes, upper and lower bounds and probability without replacement can each be fixed in about a week and each appears regularly, so the marks are reliable and the student gets visible wins early. Large interdependent topics need the manipulation underneath them to be secure first, which is a longer job and a poor use of the final month if it is not already done.

faqs.question: What should be dropped from a short mathematics revision plan?
faqs.answer: Two things, and dropping them is harder than adding anything. Topics that appear rarely and are not understood should be abandoned deliberately rather than learned badly, because the hours they consume are worth more on high-frequency marks. And re-reading notes should stop entirely, since at this stage it produces a strong feeling of progress with almost no measurable return. Both decisions feel wrong and both reliably raise the final mark.

faqs.question: Why does spring tutoring cost more than Year 10 tutoring?
faqs.answer: Demand concentrates before the papers, the formats families want then are intensive, and the specialists who can work on a named paper are the scarcest part of the market. Published Abu Dhabi bands run from about AED 33 to 65 for student tutors, AED 150 to 300 for qualified subject tutors and AED 200 to 450 and above for specialists. The same outcome bought in the Year 10 autumn costs materially less, which is the strongest practical argument for starting early.

faqs.question: What if no maths tutor is free in our window before the papers?
faqs.answer: We tell you plainly rather than filling the slot with a generalist. The final twelve weeks are the tightest part of the year for availability, and Al Raha Gardens competes with Saadiyat, Al Reem and Yas families for the same evening hours. Common tiers usually match within a few days; a fixed weekday slot in the pre-paper window can take a week or more. Hearing that early leaves you time to look elsewhere while it still matters.

intro.heading: Nine content areas, and the small set of places marks actually disappear
paragraphs: IGCSE mathematics is a wide syllabus and a narrow set of failures. The content spans number, algebra, coordinate geometry, mensuration, trigonometry, transformations and vectors, probability, statistics and multi-step problem solving. The marks, though, go missing in a handful of recurring places that are the same across Abu Dhabi schools and across both boards. A tutor who knows that list can diagnose a student from one marked paper; a tutor who does not will work through the textbook in order and hope.

The recurring list looks like this. Reverse percentages, where a student multiplies when the question requires division. Upper and lower bounds, rounded away at the last step and so defeating the whole question. Histograms with unequal class widths, where frequency density is forgotten entirely. Tree diagrams without replacement, where the second denominator is left unchanged and every subsequent mark falls with it. Transformation descriptions that name a rotation without the centre and direction, forfeiting marks the student had earned. Sign errors in a subtracted bracket. Perpendicular gradients where the negative reciprocal is skipped. A calculator left in degrees for a radian-adjacent calculation. Units lost after a cubic conversion.

None of those is a conceptual failure. They are habits, and that is the most useful thing a parent in Al Rawdah can know, because habits respond to targeted practice in weeks rather than terms. A student predicted a 4 who needs a 6 is usually not missing two years of understanding; they are losing three or four marks per paper to the same five errors, which is a different and much cheaper problem.

Two structural facts sit underneath all of it. First, the syllabus code: Cambridge 0580 and 0607 and Pearson 4MA1 are genuinely different examinations with different paper structures, and Cambridge has revised the 0580 assessment model including the balance of calculator and non-calculator papers, so the structure should be read at source for the series your child is entered for. Second, the tier: Cambridge Core and Extended, or Pearson Foundation and Higher, where Foundation caps at grade 5 and Higher runs from 9 to 4 with a grade 3 safety net. Tier entry sets a ceiling the student cannot pass however well the papers go.

IB Gram teaches this as live one-to-one video tuition on Gulf Standard Time. We do not offer home visits in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. For mathematics the format earns its place: the paper and its mark scheme sit open on a shared screen, working is built line by line where both people can see it, graphs are plotted live, and the recording lets a student return to the exact moment a method was explained rather than to whatever they managed to copy down.

Entry is usually conditional on a minimum IGCSE grade, and the step up in algebraic fluency is steep: a student who relied on a calculator through IGCSE meets a wall in the first AS term.

An IGCSE Extended or Higher student arrives with strong algebra and no calculus, which is a narrow and predictable first-term gap.

abu-dhabi/igcse-maths-tutor-in-al-rawdah.subjectsIntro: Below is the syllabus split into the units a tutor actually plans around, each with the specific error that costs marks in it. A first session should narrow this to two or three live items.

subjects.name: Number, fractions and standard form
subjects.description: Operations with fractions and decimals, standard form, ratio and proportion. Non-calculator fluency is the live issue: a student who cannot divide fractions on paper without hesitating will lose time they need later in the paper, and time pressure is itself a mark loss.

subjects.name: Percentages and reverse percentages
subjects.description: Increase, decrease, repeated change, compound interest, and finding the original amount. The reverse case is the reliable trap: given a price after a 20% increase, students multiply by 0.8 instead of dividing by 1.2. It is one mistake and it recurs in every series.

subjects.name: Bounds and accuracy
subjects.description: Upper and lower bounds and calculations with them. The usual failure is rounding the final answer, which destroys the purpose of the question, and the second is using the lower bound where the upper is needed in a division. Both are procedural and fixable in one session.

subjects.name: Algebraic manipulation
subjects.description: Expanding, factorising, rearranging formulae, algebraic fractions and simultaneous equations. Sign errors in a subtracted bracket account for more lost marks than any conceptual gap, and the fix is mechanical practice rather than explanation.

subjects.name: Equations, inequalities and sequences
subjects.description: Linear and quadratic equations, the quadratic formula, completing the square, inequalities on a number line, and nth-term rules for linear and quadratic sequences. Students who solve a quadratic correctly often fail to identify which root the context requires, which is a reading failure.

subjects.name: Coordinate geometry and graphs
subjects.description: Gradients, midpoints, parallel and perpendicular lines, and sketching quadratics, reciprocals and exponentials. Perpendicular gradients cost marks where the negative reciprocal is skipped, and graph sketches lose marks for unlabelled axes and missing intercepts.

subjects.name: Mensuration and compound measures
subjects.description: Area, surface area and volume of prisms, cylinders, cones, spheres and composite solids, plus speed, density and pressure. Two reliable errors: using slant height where vertical height is required, and leaving an answer in the wrong unit after a cubic conversion.

subjects.name: Trigonometry, Pythagoras and bearings
subjects.description: Right-angled trigonometry, the sine and cosine rules, bearings, angles of elevation and depression, and three-dimensional applications at the higher tiers. Bearings lose marks through the diagram rather than the calculation, and the cosine rule is frequently rearranged incorrectly under pressure.

subjects.name: Transformations and vectors
subjects.description: Translation, reflection, rotation and enlargement with negative and fractional scale factors, plus column vectors and vector geometry. Describing a transformation fully, with centre, scale factor and direction, carries marks students routinely forfeit by naming the transformation only.

subjects.name: Probability, including conditional cases
subjects.description: Single and combined events, tree and Venn diagrams, and probability without replacement. The replacement condition is effectively the whole question in most tree items: a student who does not change the second denominator loses every mark downstream of that point.

subjects.name: Statistics and data handling
subjects.description: Averages from frequency and grouped tables, estimated means, cumulative frequency, box plots, scatter diagrams and histograms with unequal class widths. The histogram is the single most reliably mishandled item at the higher tiers, because frequency density is forgotten rather than misunderstood.

subjects.name: Multi-step problem solving
subjects.description: Questions combining two or three topics where method marks reward a sensible route even when the final value is wrong. Strong students lose marks here by producing an answer with no written setup, which gives the marker nothing to credit.

sections.heading: The nine content areas and what a tutor should be able to say about each
paragraphs: Answering the search first: an IGCSE maths tutor in Al Rawdah through IB Gram is a mathematics specialist matched to your child's syllabus code and tier, teaching one-to-one over live video at a time that fits an Abu Dhabi school day, with a free trial lesson used as a diagnosis. We do not offer home visits in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India.

The test of a maths tutor is whether they can talk about the syllabus at the level of question types rather than topic names. Anybody can say they cover algebra. A tutor who has marked papers will tell you that the recurring algebra loss is a sign error in a subtracted bracket, that it is mechanical rather than conceptual, and that the fix is twenty short expansions rather than an explanation of why brackets work.

That specificity is what turns a plan into a diagnosis. Over a term, a student who loses four marks a paper to the same five errors is losing roughly a grade boundary's worth of marks to habit. Identifying those five and drilling them is cheaper, faster and more certain than any general programme of revision, and it is the work most tutoring does not do because it requires marking rather than teaching.

The table below is the version of the syllabus a tutor should be working from: content area, the question type it appears in, the specific trap, and what fixes it. It is also a tool for a parent. Take a marked paper, find the lost marks, and see how many land in this table. In most Year 11 papers from this catchment, most of them do.

sections.heading: Non-calculator fluency: what has to be automatic before the series
paragraphs: Cambridge has revised the 0580 assessment model, including the balance of calculator and non-calculator assessment, so the first job is to confirm at source which papers your child's series actually includes. Where a non-calculator paper is sat, it examines a separate skill set, and it is the one students most often arrive without because a calculator has absorbed the work since Year 7.

The content of that skill set is short and specific. Fractions added, subtracted, multiplied and divided without hesitation. Index laws applied in both directions. Surds simplified and rationalised where the tier requires it. Standard form handled in multiplication and division. Percentages of awkward amounts done mentally. Exact values retained rather than converted to decimals. Estimation used as a checking habit, so an answer three orders of magnitude out is caught before it is written down.

The reason this matters beyond the paper itself is time. A student who hesitates over fraction division spends thirty seconds per occurrence, and a paper can contain a dozen occurrences buried inside larger questions. Six minutes of hesitation is the difference between finishing a paper and abandoning the last two questions, which is a mark loss attributed to not knowing the topic when the real cause was arithmetic drag.

The training is unglamorous and short. Fifteen minutes of timed drills inside a wider session, repeated weekly, measured on speed as well as accuracy. It feels like primary-school work to a Year 11 student and it produces one of the clearest gains available, particularly for students heading towards A-Level or Diploma mathematics where paper fluency is assumed from the first week.

sections.heading: Calculator-paper discipline, and why method marks are the cheapest marks available
paragraphs: On a calculator-permitted paper the mark scheme awards method marks for a written setup even when the final value is wrong. That is the single most valuable piece of examination knowledge in IGCSE mathematics, and a large number of students do not have it. They type into the calculator, write the answer, and when the answer is wrong they score zero on a question where they had earned two of the three marks.

The discipline is mechanical: write the equation or expression being evaluated before evaluating it. On a cosine rule question, write the rule with the values substituted. On a compound interest question, write the expression before computing it. On a trigonometry question, write the ratio being used. None of this takes meaningful time and all of it converts near-misses into part marks.

A second calculator-paper habit is checking the mode. A calculator left in the wrong angular mode produces consistent, confident, wrong answers through an entire question and often through a whole paper. It is worth training a student to check mode at the start and again whenever an answer looks implausible, which is a thirty-second habit protecting several marks.

The third is accuracy and rounding. Mark schemes specify degrees of accuracy, and answers rounded too early inside a multi-step calculation drift outside the accepted range. The rule to train is to keep full accuracy in the calculator through the working and round only at the final line, with the rounding stated. Students who round at each step produce an answer that is nearly right, which earns nothing.

sections.heading: How a grade is actually built, and why boundaries move
paragraphs: Parents often ask what mark a particular grade needs, and the honest answer is that it varies by series and is published by the board after each one. Grade boundaries are set for each paper and each series rather than fixed in advance, which is why no tutoring page should print a boundary as though it were permanent. Cambridge and Pearson publish them, and your child's school can access them.

What is stable is the arithmetic of a near-miss. A student one grade below the target is typically a small number of marks short across two papers, not a large number. That is why error-type analysis beats topic revision for a student in that position: four marks recovered from habitual losses can cross a boundary, while a week spent re-reading a topic the student already knows recovers nothing.

The second stable thing is the distribution of where those marks sit. In this catchment the recoverable marks cluster in the places the first table on this page names, plus the last two questions of a paper that time pressure caused the student to abandon. A paper abandoned with eight accessible marks remaining is a pacing failure, and pacing is trainable.

A caution about any claim of outcomes. No tutor can guarantee a grade, because the result depends on a student's own work on a specific morning, and nobody should publish a percentage of students achieving anything without a sample size, a date and a method attached. What a tutor can honestly offer is a diagnosis, a plan aimed at recoverable marks, marking against the published scheme and an error log that shows whether anything has changed.

sections.heading: Statistics and probability: four losses that repeat in every series
paragraphs: Statistics and probability deserve a section of their own because they produce more recoverable marks than any other part of the syllabus in this catchment. Four items account for most of it, and each is procedural rather than conceptual, which is exactly the profile that responds to a short block of work.

The histogram with unequal class widths is first. Students who understand frequency perfectly plot frequency rather than frequency density, and the whole question falls. The fix is a rule rather than an explanation: when class widths differ, compute a density column before touching the axes. Second is the estimated mean from grouped data, where midpoints are mishandled or the division is done by the number of classes rather than the total frequency.

Third is the tree diagram without replacement, where a student writes the first set of branches correctly and leaves the second denominator unchanged. Everything downstream is then wrong, and the marks are gone even though the method was understood. The training is to write every branch's denominator before multiplying anything, which makes the change impossible to miss. Fourth is cumulative frequency, where students read a median from the wrong axis or plot at the lower boundary of a class instead of the upper.

Scatter diagrams and correlation add a fifth, smaller loss: describing a correlation without referring to the context, or drawing a line of best fit that ignores the data's spread. These are easy marks for a trained student and routinely dropped by an untrained one. Across all five, a Year 11 student in Al Rawdah can commonly recover several marks a paper in two or three sessions, which is as close to a certain return as tutoring offers.

sections.heading: What repairing one topic costs, against a year of general tutoring
paragraphs: The cost conversation reads differently once the work is specific. A student losing three marks a paper to histograms and tree diagrams needs two or three sessions, not a year. At the published band for a qualified subject tutor working online, AED 150 to 300 an hour with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150, that repair costs a few hundred dirhams in total. A year of weekly general tutoring at the same rate costs a multiple of it and may never address the same errors.

The other bands, read in October 2026 for comparison: budget online tuition at AED 45 to 150 an hour, with EdFlik publishing AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52; in-home visits at AED 180 to 500 with travel included, Bestimate quoting AED 180 to 350 and independent home tutors AED 200 to 500; specialists at AED 200 to 450 and upwards, TutorChase publishing AED 270; premium examiner-led tuition at AED 500 to 650 and above, BartyED publishing AED 650. Monthly packages advertised include AED 799 for eight online sessions.

What makes the targeted approach cheaper is not a lower rate but fewer hours aimed better. That is an argument against our own revenue in the short run and it is still the right advice, because a family who gets a specific result from three sessions comes back when there is a genuine need. The alternative, selling a term to a student who needed a fortnight, works once.

Every figure above is a market rate from a named published source rather than an IB Gram price; ours is quoted after the free trial lesson once code, tier and session length are known. And the obvious caution: a premium rate does not improve a wrong diagnosis. Examiner-level money spent on a student whose actual problem is frequency density is an expensive route to a cheap fix.

sections.heading: Why a shared screen suits maths, and what it cannot do
paragraphs: Mathematics is the subject where online delivery is easiest to defend on its merits rather than on price. A past paper and its mark scheme sit open for both people. Working is built line by line in a space both can write in. A graph is plotted live and transformed while the student watches the effect. A histogram's density column is added in front of them rather than described. And the recording means the student can return to the exact moment a method appeared, which matters because the homework usually happens two days later.

In-home tuition has a genuine advantage with attention. A tutor in the room notices a student drifting and reads the page over their shoulder without being asked. For a Year 7 or Year 8 student, that can decide whether a session works at all. By Year 11, with a marked paper on the table and a specific list of errors to repair, the decisive variable is whether the tutor knows the mark scheme.

What online delivery cannot do is supply motivation a student does not have, and it is worth being plain about that. A student who will not attempt the questions between sessions will not improve in either format, and no tutor should imply otherwise. Where engagement is the actual problem, shorter and more frequent sessions with smaller, checkable tasks work better than longer ones, and that is a scheduling change rather than a format change.

sections.heading: Getting started, and what the first session should produce
paragraphs: The useful first message contains four things: the syllabus code, the tier, the school, and a photograph of a recent marked paper. With those, a tutor can arrive at the first session already knowing which error types to test, which is the difference between a diagnostic lesson and an introductory chat.

The free trial lesson is one full lesson with the matched tutor, with no card required and no block of hours bought in advance. Its job is to produce three things: a named list of recurring errors, a judgement on whether the tier looks right on the evidence, and an honest estimate of how many sessions the work needs. That estimate should sometimes be very small, and a provider unwilling to say so is not diagnosing.

After that, the plan is short and written: which errors in which order, what the student does between sessions, and when the plan will be re-tested. Six to eight weeks later a fresh paper is worked and the new error log compared with the first. If the logged failures have gone, the recommendation is to reduce or stop, and the next item in the queue moves up.

Availability is finite and worth stating. Mathematics specialists are in heaviest demand in the weeks before mock windows and before the June series, when every school needs the same people at once. If nobody is free for your code and tier, you are told the expected wait and given the alternatives in writing, including where a tutor is based outside the UAE, which you hear before booking rather than afterwards.

process.title: Send the code, the tier and a marked paper
process.description: 0580, 0607 or 4MA1, the tier, and a photograph of recent annotated work. The marker's comments usually name the real problem faster than any description of how the term has gone, and they tell the tutor which error types to test first.

process.title: Diagnosis against the published scheme
process.description: The paper is marked exactly as the scheme is written rather than generously, and every lost mark is classified by topic and by type: content, method, command reading, arithmetic, units or pacing. The counts, not the student's instinct, set the plan.

process.title: Free trial lesson with the matched tutor
process.description: One full lesson, no card required, no hours bought first. It produces a named list of recurring errors, a view on whether the tier is right, and an honest estimate of how many sessions are needed, including when that number is two or three.

process.title: Repair in order of recoverable marks
process.description: The errors carrying the most recoverable marks are worked first, each with a before and after test. Non-calculator drills run inside the sessions as short timed sets rather than as separate lessons, because they need maintaining rather than completing.

process.title: Re-test, then reduce or stop
process.description: After six to eight weeks a fresh paper is worked and the new log compared with the original. When the logged failures have gone, the recommendation is fewer sessions or none. Continuing by default is how tutoring stops producing anything measurable.

whyPoints.title: Diagnosis from marking, not from conversation
whyPoints.description: A marked paper read against the published scheme names the real failures in about twenty minutes. Most Year 11 gaps turn out to be four or five repeated habits rather than missing understanding, which is a far cheaper problem to solve.

whyPoints.title: The syllabus discussed at question-type level
whyPoints.description: Not covers algebra, but names the sign error in a subtracted bracket and the drill that removes it. That specificity is the test of whether a tutor has marked papers or only delivered lessons.

whyPoints.title: Non-calculator fluency treated separately
whyPoints.description: Paper arithmetic has to be automatic, and practising it alongside calculator technique lets the two sets of habits interfere. Short timed drills inside wider sessions build it without consuming a lesson.

whyPoints.title: Method marks taught explicitly
whyPoints.description: Writing the setup before evaluating converts near-misses into part marks on every calculator paper. It is the single most valuable piece of examination knowledge in IGCSE mathematics and a large number of students do not have it.

whyPoints.title: No printed grade boundaries, no promised grades
whyPoints.description: Boundaries are set per paper and per series and published by the boards, so no page should present one as permanent. And no tutor can guarantee an outcome that depends on a student's own work on the day.

whyPoints.title: Fewer hours aimed better
whyPoints.description: A student losing three marks a paper to two topics needs two or three sessions, not a year. Saying so costs us revenue in the short term and is still the right advice, which is the test of whether a provider is selling teaching or hours.

faqs.question: Why does my child keep losing marks on histogram questions?
faqs.answer: Almost always because frequency density is forgotten. When class widths are unequal, the vertical axis must be frequency density rather than frequency, and students who understand frequency perfectly still plot the wrong quantity and lose the whole question. The fix is a rule rather than an explanation: whenever widths differ, build a density column before touching the axes. Two sessions on this one item typically recovers two to four marks per paper, which is among the cheapest gains in the syllabus.

faqs.question: What is the trap in reverse percentage questions?
faqs.answer: The direction of the operation. Given a price after a 20% increase, a student multiplies by 0.8 instead of dividing by 1.2, and the answer is confidently wrong. It is a single structural misunderstanding and it appears in every series, usually worth two or three marks. The training is ten reverse items worked in a row until the structure becomes automatic, with the student writing the multiplier before calculating anything. It is a one-session repair with a lasting effect.

faqs.question: How do we stop losing marks on tree diagrams?
faqs.answer: By writing every branch's denominator before multiplying anything. The usual failure is a question without replacement where the first set of branches is correct and the second denominator is left unchanged, which wipes out every mark downstream even though the method was understood. Making the denominators explicit before any arithmetic makes the change impossible to miss. Three to four marks are typically at stake in a single question, which makes this one of the higher-value items to repair.

faqs.question: Does my child really need to be fast at fractions without a calculator?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the reason is time rather than principle. A student who hesitates over fraction division spends about thirty seconds per occurrence, and a paper can hide a dozen occurrences inside larger questions. Six minutes of arithmetic drag is the difference between finishing and abandoning the last two questions, and the lost marks then get blamed on the topic rather than on the hesitation. Fifteen minutes of timed drills a week fixes it within a term.

faqs.question: What are method marks and why do they matter so much?
faqs.answer: On calculator-permitted papers the scheme awards marks for a written setup even when the final value is wrong. A student who types into the calculator and records only the answer scores nothing on a question where two of three marks had been earned. Writing the cosine rule with values substituted, or the compound interest expression before computing it, takes seconds and protects those marks. It is the most valuable examination habit in the subject and many students have never been told about it.

faqs.question: Can you tell me what mark my child needs for a grade 6?
faqs.answer: No, and nor should any tutoring page. Grade boundaries are set for each paper and each series rather than fixed in advance, and the boards publish them after each series. Your child's school can access them. What is stable is the arithmetic of a near-miss: a student one grade below target is usually a small number of marks short across two papers, which is why recovering habitual losses matters more than re-reading topics the student already understands.

faqs.question: My child understands the maths but runs out of time. What do we do?
faqs.answer: Treat pacing as its own training rather than as a symptom. The routine is practising sections against the clock, learning to leave a stuck question and return to it, and treating the final questions as accessible marks rather than a lost cause. A paper abandoned with eight marks still reachable is a pacing failure, and it is trainable in a few sessions. Non-calculator fluency drills also help, because much of the lost time is arithmetic hesitation rather than thinking.

faqs.question: Which maths topics should a Year 11 student prioritise with six weeks left?
faqs.answer: Whatever a marked paper says, in order of recoverable marks. In this catchment that list typically contains histograms with unequal widths, reverse percentages, bounds, tree diagrams without replacement, full transformation descriptions and method-mark discipline. Those are procedural rather than conceptual, so they move quickly. Re-teaching a topic the student has genuinely never grasped is a poor use of six weeks, because the return arrives too slowly to appear in the result.

faqs.question: Is it worth working on surds if the tier does not demand much of them?
faqs.answer: If your child is heading for A-Level or Diploma mathematics, yes, and more than the IGCSE paper itself justifies. Post-16 courses assume exact-value fluency with surds, index laws and rearrangement from the first week, and a student who has leaned on a calculator meets a wall in the first AS or DP1 term. Over-practising it in Year 11 is cheap insurance. If your child is stopping mathematics after IGCSE, prioritise whatever the marked paper names instead.

faqs.question: How many sessions does fixing one recurring error take?
faqs.answer: Two or three in most cases, with a before and after test to confirm it has gone. These are procedural failures rather than conceptual ones, which is why they respond so quickly. A student losing three or four marks a paper to two such errors therefore needs a handful of sessions rather than a term, and at the published qualified-tutor band of AED 150 to 300 an hour that is a few hundred dirhams in total rather than a recurring monthly commitment.

faqs.question: Will a tutor hand us a folder of past papers to work through?
faqs.answer: We cite and link them rather than supplying copies. Syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables are published by Cambridge and Pearson, and reproducing or distributing them is a copyright matter; your child's school can also provide them. What a tutor adds is teaching a student to read a mark scheme properly, awarding marks exactly as written rather than generously, which is a skill that keeps paying across every paper they sit afterwards.

faqs.question: Can maths be taught properly over video?
faqs.answer: For this subject it is arguably easier. The paper and its mark scheme sit open for both people, working is built line by line in a shared space, a graph is transformed live while the student watches the effect, and a density column is added in front of them rather than described. The recording matters too, because homework usually happens two days after the lesson. What video cannot supply is motivation a student does not have, which is true of any format.

faqs.question: Should we switch tier if the marked papers are going badly?
faqs.answer: Possibly, and the decision belongs with the school, which holds the entry deadline as the examination centre. Bring evidence rather than impressions: past papers from both tiers, marked against the published schemes, with the error types classified. Cambridge Core caps the grades available and Pearson Foundation tops out at grade 5, so a tier that cannot reach the grade your child needs is a problem regardless of how the papers feel. Raise it in Year 10 where possible.

faqs.question: What makes a good maths tutor different from a competent one?
faqs.answer: A competent tutor explains topics clearly. A good one marks a paper against the published scheme, tells you that the problem is a sign error in subtracted brackets rather than algebra in general, drills it mechanically for two sessions, re-tests, and then says the work is done. The willingness to finish is the tell. A tutor who never reaches a point where fewer sessions are recommended is managing a subscription rather than solving a problem.

abu-dhabi/igcse-maths-tutor-in-al-rawdah.closingHeading: Send a marked paper and we will name the errors

Each works to a named syllabus - 0580, 0607, 0606 or 4MA1 - and plans the hours around the paper your child is actually entered for, in Gulf Standard Time, over live video.

intro.heading: Start with the invoice, not the brochure
paragraphs: Al Reef is a community built around a price. Families move out past the airport road because the villas and the Downtown apartments cost less per square foot than Al Raha or the island, and because the commute is tolerable if the school is in Khalifa City. That same arithmetic should govern tutoring, and usually it does not. A parent who negotiated hard over rent will hand over AED 300 an hour for maths without asking what the hour contains.

So this page is written from cost outward. The first section publishes the AED bands observed across the Abu Dhabi and Dubai market and names who charges them, because almost nobody ranking for this search publishes a figure at all. The second section is a list of the places a maths budget leaks: hours bought in the wrong tier, travel folded into a rate, group rooms moving at the median, year-long retainers where ten focused weeks would have done. The third establishes which syllabus your child sits, because paying for Cambridge preparation when the school enters for Pearson Edexcel is the most expensive mistake available and the easiest to avoid.

The honest position on delivery comes next, because the URL you clicked says home tutor territory. In-home visits are not part of what IB Gram sells anywhere in the UAE; that is an India-only service. What a family off the Sweihan road gets instead is a one-to-one session over live video with a tutor chosen for the paper rather than for the postcode. The practical consequence is that a child sitting 0580 Extended Paper 2 gets somebody who marks non-calculator algebra for a living, rather than whoever was willing to drive thirty kilometres at five in the afternoon.

Maths rewards this approach more than most subjects. It is the one IGCSE where the diagnosis is almost mechanical: take a past paper, mark it question by question, and the topic list writes itself. Number and algebra fluency problems show up on the non-calculator paper; method and communication problems show up on the calculator paper, where a correct answer with no working still loses marks. A tutor who starts by marking rather than by teaching saves a family money in the first fortnight, and the saving is visible.

Everything below is either checkable or attributed. Where a figure belongs to a competitor, that competitor published it and is named. Where a date belongs to a board, the board publishes the live timetable and this page points at it rather than restating something that gets revised. Where the Ministry of Education sets a rule, the rule is quoted and the authority is named. Nothing here is a promise about a grade, because no tutor can make one, and anyone who does is telling you something about themselves rather than about your child.

abu-dhabi/igcse-maths-tutor-in-al-reef.programmesIntro: Four syllabuses cover almost every maths paper sat in and around Al Reef. They are not interchangeable, and the differences decide how many hours a family needs to buy. Check your child's statement of entry before booking anything, because the code on that sheet is the only version of this question that matters.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics
programmes.description: The most widely sat maths syllabus in Abu Dhabi's British-curriculum schools. It is tiered: Core candidates sit two papers and are capped at grade C, Extended candidates sit two longer papers and can reach A*. One paper in each tier is taken without a calculator and the other with one, and the marks are split evenly between them. The content list runs from number and algebra through trigonometry, vectors and transformations to probability and statistics.
programmes.countryNote: Several schools in the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor that Al Reef children travel to enter for 0580, which is why most tutoring enquiries from this community arrive with an 0580 past paper attached. The tier decision is usually made in the autumn term of Year 11 and locked by the school's internal entry deadline, well before the June series. A family that gets the tier right spends fewer hours; a family that gets it wrong spends a year preparing for a ceiling the child did not need.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A
programmes.description: Two papers of two hours each, worth 100 marks apiece, with a calculator permitted on both. Entry is at Foundation tier, which awards grades 5 to 1, or Higher tier, which awards 9 to 4 with an allowed 3 beneath it. Because no paper is sat without a calculator, the arithmetic pressure that dominates Cambridge preparation moves elsewhere - into problem decoding, multi-step method and the discipline of writing enough working to earn method marks on a question that goes wrong.
programmes.countryNote: Pearson runs International GCSE in May/June and in November, and publishes a provisional timetable ahead of each series. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026 - a useful indication of how long the wait is if a family uses November as a resit route. Always open the live Pearson timetable rather than trusting a date restated on a tutoring page, including this one.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE International Mathematics
programmes.description: The syllabus chosen by schools running the IB Middle Years Programme alongside an IGCSE exit, because it includes a graphics-calculator expectation and an investigation or modelling paper that resembles later IB coursework. Candidates sit a short non-calculator paper, a longer calculator paper and a third paper that asks for extended reasoning. It is a different animal from 0580 and preparing for it with 0580 materials wastes hours.
programmes.countryNote: If your child's school in the Khalifa City or Al Raha cluster runs MYP into Year 11, 0607 is the likely entry, and a tutor who has only taught 0580 will miss the investigation paper entirely. Al Reef families with two children at two different schools quite often need two different maths syllabuses covered in the same week, which is a real reason to ask about the code rather than to book a generic maths hour.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE Additional Mathematics
programmes.description: A separate qualification taken alongside 0580 Extended by students heading for AS and A Level Mathematics or for IB Diploma Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level. It introduces differentiation, integration, binomial expansion, further trigonometry and the factor and remainder theorems. The jump in abstraction is larger than the jump from Core to Extended, and it is the point where strong 0580 students first meet work they cannot do by pattern recognition.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools that teach 0606 usually run it as an option set or an after-school class, which means the teaching time per topic is thin and the support burden lands at home. For an Al Reef family already paying for one subject, the sensible move is a short block of hours on calculus notation and technique rather than a standing weekly slot on everything. Pearson's Further Pure Mathematics (4PM1) plays a similar role on the Edexcel side.

abu-dhabi/igcse-maths-tutor-in-al-reef.subjectsIntro: IGCSE Mathematics is not one subject to a tutor, it is ten strands with very different failure modes. The grid below names them the way the syllabus does, with the specific place marks go missing in each. A first session should establish which three of these are costing your child the most marks, and the rest should be left alone.

subjects.name: Number
subjects.description: Standard form, bounds, ratio, percentage change and reverse percentages, surds and indices. On the non-calculator paper this strand is where grades are quietly lost: a reverse percentage done as a forward percentage costs the whole question, and bounds questions are marked on the inequality signs as much as on the arithmetic.

subjects.name: Algebra and graphs
subjects.description: Expanding, factorising, rearranging, simultaneous and quadratic equations, inequalities, sequences and the shapes of reciprocal and exponential curves. The single largest marks block in the syllabus. Students who can solve a quadratic but cannot form one from a worded context lose the second half of every applied question.

subjects.name: Coordinate geometry
subjects.description: Gradient, midpoint, length of a line segment, equations of straight lines, parallel and perpendicular conditions. Compact, learnable and reliably examined. The common error is a sign slip on a negative reciprocal, which converts a four-mark question into one mark and takes about ten minutes of teaching to fix permanently.

subjects.name: Geometry and circle theorems
subjects.description: Angle facts, polygons, congruence, similarity and the circle theorems. Marks here depend on written reasoning, not on the answer. A correct angle with no theorem named scores less than a wrong angle with the right theorem quoted, and most students have never been told that explicitly.

subjects.name: Mensuration
subjects.description: Area and perimeter of compound shapes, surface area and volume of prisms, cylinders, cones, pyramids and spheres, and arc and sector work. Formula recall plus unit discipline. Cubic and square unit conversions - cm cubed to litres, m squared to cm squared - are where a confident student still drops two marks a paper.

subjects.name: Trigonometry
subjects.description: Right-angled trigonometry, bearings, angles of elevation and depression, and at Extended the sine and cosine rules, the area formula and three-dimensional problems. Bearings questions fail on the diagram rather than the trigonometry: a three-figure bearing measured clockwise from north is a drawing skill, and it is teachable in one session.

subjects.name: Transformations and vectors
subjects.description: Translation, reflection, rotation and enlargement including negative and fractional scale factors, plus column vectors, magnitude and vector geometry proofs. Students lose marks by describing a transformation incompletely - a rotation with no centre, an enlargement with no scale factor sign - rather than by performing it wrongly.

subjects.name: Probability
subjects.description: Single and combined events, tree diagrams, conditional probability and set notation with Venn diagrams. The marks sit in the structure. A tree diagram drawn without replacement when the question said without replacement is almost all of the work; the multiplication afterwards is the easy part and is rarely where the error is.

subjects.name: Statistics
subjects.description: Averages from grouped data, cumulative frequency, histograms with unequal class widths, box plots and scatter graphs with lines of best fit. Frequency density is the reliable trap: students plot frequency against an unequal class width and lose an entire eight-mark question that they understood conceptually.

subjects.name: Calculus and further algebra
subjects.description: Differentiation and integration of polynomials, stationary points, rates of change, the binomial expansion, the factor and remainder theorems and further trigonometric identities. This is the bridge into AS Level and into IB Analysis and Approaches, and notation matters here in a way it has not before.

subjects.name: Problem solving under time
subjects.description: Not a syllabus strand but the thing that decides the grade. Reading a six-mark worded problem, choosing a method, and writing enough to earn method marks when the final answer is wrong. Most students have never been taught to leave a question after four minutes and come back, and it is worth more marks than another topic.

subjects.name: Calculator technique
subjects.description: Fraction and surd modes, stored answers, table mode for checking, standard form input, and the habit of writing an unrounded intermediate value before rounding at the end. Premature rounding costs accuracy marks on nearly every statistics and trigonometry question, and no amount of topic revision fixes it.

abu-dhabi/igcse-maths-tutor-in-al-reef.regionsIntro: Al Reef sits on its own, out past the airport, and that geography is the whole argument for buying tutoring online rather than locally. The communities below are the ones an Al Reef family competes with for a tutor's evening slots, and the drive times between them are what gets priced into an in-home rate.

regions.name: Al Reef Villas and Al Reef Downtown
regions.note: Four villa precincts and an apartment ring, built for families who wanted space at a lower price than the island. School buses leave early and return late, which pushes the realistic start time for a weekday session to around 17:00 or later.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Where most Al Reef children go to school, and the nearest concentration of British-curriculum classrooms. A tutor driving from Khalifa City to Al Reef and back spends the better part of an hour in the car, and that hour appears in the rate whether it is itemised or not.

regions.name: Al Raha Gardens and Al Raha Beach
regions.note: An established villa and waterfront cluster with its own IB and British schools. Rates quoted to Al Raha families are often higher than those quoted to Al Reef families for the same tutor, which tells you how much of a local rate is really about distance.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: Newer family housing with schools attached to the development. Yas sessions compete for the same 17:00 to 19:00 window, and tutors who take a Yas booking first will offer Al Reef a less convenient slot or a higher price.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: High-density towers with a growing school presence. A tutor working towers can fit three in-home sessions into an evening because the travel between them is a lift ride; in Al Reef the same tutor manages one, and prices accordingly.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: The premium end of the Abu Dhabi school market, and where the highest in-home quotes in the emirate are observed. Useful as a benchmark: if a tutor quotes an Al Reef family a Saadiyat rate, the quote is about the driving, not about the maths.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: A large mainland community with several international schools and a deep pool of resident teachers. It is the closest thing Al Reef has to a local supply of subject tutors, though specialist cover for 0607 or 0606 thins out quickly.

regions.name: Al Bateen and Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Older island neighbourhoods with long-established schools. For an Al Reef family these are a 30 to 40 minute drive each way in the evening, which is why island-based tutors rarely offer this community a weekday slot at all.

regions.name: Shakhbout City and Al Shamkha
regions.note: Mainland growth areas on the same side of the airport road as Al Reef. Convenient on a map, but they draw from the same thin pool of local maths specialists, so availability rather than price is the binding constraint.

sections.heading: What an IGCSE maths tutor costs around Al Reef, in AED
paragraphs: A qualified subject tutor working online in the UAE is priced at roughly AED 150-300 an hour. An in-home one-to-one visit is quoted at AED 180-500, and a named IB or IGCSE specialist at AED 200-450 and upward. Those are market bands, not an IB Gram price list, and every one of them is attributable to a published source rather than to a guess.

The spread is wider than most parents expect because three different things are being sold under one word. At the bottom, from about AED 45-150, sit university students and generalist online platforms - EdFlik advertises from AED 45-65 an hour, Tutopiya from around AED 33-52. In the middle, from about AED 150, sit qualified subject teachers; Unitors publishes IGCSE tutoring from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. At the top, TutorChase quotes around AED 270 and BartyED around AED 650 for premium examiner-led work. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai rate table puts in-home visits at AED 180-350 and independent home tutors at AED 200-500.

Monthly packages behave differently again. Around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions appears repeatedly in this market, against AED 1,599-1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. Bestimate's own monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour session run AED 240-600 at the budget end, AED 600-1,200 in the middle and AED 1,000-2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. For an Al Reef family the useful comparison is not hourly but monthly, because that is how the household budget is actually organised.

What a parent should take from the table is the shape rather than any single number. The difference between the budget band and the qualified band buys subject knowledge. The difference between the qualified online band and the in-home band buys driving. One of those is worth paying for in a maths exam year and the other is a logistics cost dressed as a quality signal. IB Gram does not publish an hourly price on this page because the sensible first step is a free trial lesson and a conversation about which paper your child is entered for.

sections.heading: Where an Al Reef maths budget leaks
paragraphs: Most families who feel tutoring did not work did not buy bad tutoring. They bought the right tutoring in the wrong shape. Six leaks account for nearly all of it, and every one is visible on an invoice before the money is spent.

The first is the travel premium. An in-home visit out past the airport road carries thirty to forty minutes of driving each way, and a tutor who does not charge for it will instead price the session at the top of the range or decline the booking. The second is session length: two-hour slots are sold because they are easier to schedule, but a Year 11 working on non-calculator algebra stops absorbing anything after about seventy minutes. The third is tier blindness - paying for a year of Extended preparation for a student the school will enter at Core, or the reverse, which is the single most expensive error on this list.

The fourth is the group room. A class of eight moves at the median student, and if your child's gap is frequency density while the median gap is factorising, four of those hours teach nothing your child needed. The fifth is marking you already own. Schools in the Khalifa City cluster mark past papers as part of normal teaching, and paying a tutor at AED 250 an hour to mark a paper rather than to teach from a marked paper converts specialist time into clerical time. The sixth is the standing retainer. A year-long weekly slot booked in September for a June series means thirty-odd sessions, most of them before the mock that would have told you what to work on.

The counter-move is unglamorous. Get the syllabus code and the tier off the statement of entry. Get one full past paper marked properly, question by question, with the marks lost attributed to topics. Buy hours against that list, highest marks first, and stop when the list is clear. That is usually a shorter and cheaper engagement than the one a family would have booked on instinct, which is why almost nobody in this market recommends it.

sections.heading: Cambridge 0580 or Edexcel 4MA1: settle this before you buy an hour
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi's British-curriculum schools do not all enter for the same maths qualification, and the two dominant options reward different preparation. Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 sits one paper without a calculator. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A (4MA1) allows a calculator on both. That one difference changes what an hour of tutoring should be spent on, and a tutor who does not ask which board your child sits is telling you how the hour will go.

On 0580 the non-calculator paper is where grades move. Fraction arithmetic, surds, indices, standard form by hand, reverse percentages and bounds all have to be fluent, because there is no device to absorb a slip. Students who are conceptually strong and arithmetically rusty lose a grade on that paper and nowhere else, and they are the easiest students in this market to help: four or five sessions of timed non-calculator drilling moves them, and no new content is taught at all.

On 4MA1 the pressure sits elsewhere. With a calculator permitted throughout, the examiner tests whether a student can decode a multi-step worded problem and write enough working to earn method marks when the final figure is wrong. The failure mode is a page with an answer on it and no visible reasoning. Preparation for 4MA1 therefore spends its hours on structure and communication rather than on mental arithmetic, and the tiering differs too: Foundation awards 5 to 1, Higher awards 9 to 4 with an allowed 3.

Cambridge IGCSE International Mathematics 0607 is the third possibility, common where a school runs the Middle Years Programme into Year 11. It adds an investigation or modelling paper that 0580 materials do not prepare a student for at all. Check the code on the statement of entry, and check the board's own published syllabus page rather than a tutoring site's summary, including this one. Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and warns that it cannot accept responsibility for a candidate who misses an exam after using the wrong zone timetable, so the school's version of the timetable is the one that counts.
