sections.heading: Where Extended and Higher candidates lose the marks
paragraphs: Ask a tutor where marks are lost and a generalist will say careless errors. A specialist will name topics, and the list is remarkably consistent across Abu Dhabi cohorts. Algebraic fractions come first: simplifying them, adding them, and changing the subject of a formula in which the subject appears twice. These are mechanical skills, they decay without practice, and they are examined every series.

Reverse percentages come second, and they are worth isolating because the failure mode is total rather than partial. A student who divides by the wrong figure loses every mark in the question rather than most of them. Bounds and limits of accuracy come third, especially in division, where the combination producing the maximum is not the one intuition suggests. Both topics are small, both appear reliably, and both are taught quickly in class because they look easy.

After that come graph transformations, where the sign of a horizontal translation is the recurring trap; frequency density in histograms with unequal class widths, which is the discriminating step and the one most often omitted from revision; transformation descriptions, where a partial description earns a partial mark that students do not realise they have lost; and vector collinearity proofs, where the method is short and the notation is unforgiving.

The reason to name these rather than describe general weakness is that each one is a bounded piece of work. A student with four of these problems has perhaps six hours of targeted repair ahead, not a year of tutoring. The table maps each to the paper it appears on and the habit that fixes it, which is the sort of detail a tutor should be able to produce from your child's marked mock within one session.

sections.heading: What one marked mock paper tells a tutor
paragraphs: The cheapest and most useful thing a Saadiyat Island parent can do before hiring anyone is to send a marked paper. Not a reported grade, not a teacher comment, but the paper itself with the annotations on it. From one marked mock, a tutor who knows the specification can read several things that no description would convey.

The first is whether the losses are clustered or scattered. Clustered losses in two or three topics mean a bounded repair job of a few sessions. Scattered single-mark losses across the whole paper usually mean something structural: arithmetic fluency, time management, or a habit of not writing method. Those are different problems with different fixes, and treating one as the other wastes a term.

The second is whether the student is in the right tier. A Core candidate who has lost almost nothing is in the wrong route and is capping their own grade. An Extended candidate scoring in the low band on the harder paper may be better served by consolidating Core content first, which is a conversation to have with the school rather than a decision a tutor makes.

The third is exam behaviour, which shows up in the shape of the paper. Questions abandoned halfway, later questions left blank while earlier ones are over-worked, answers given with no working, calculator values copied with no method recorded: each of these is visible on the page and each has a specific correction. None of them would appear in a progress report, and all of them cost marks in a terminal examination where method marks are the margin between grades.

sections.heading: Fitting a maths session around the Saadiyat Island day
paragraphs: Coverage is useless if the slot does not work. Most campuses serving Saadiyat Island end their taught day between 14:45 and 15:30, with co-curricular sessions running later on some days. A child at a school on the island is often home before 15:45. A child at a Khalifa City or Al Raha campus is typically home between 15:45 and 16:30, and later on an activity day.

Allowing three quarters of an hour at home to eat and change, that puts the honest earliest session start at about 16:30 for an island school and about 17:30 for a mainland one. Our Abu Dhabi scheduling range runs from 16:30 to 21:00 Gulf Standard Time, and most families settle between 17:30 and 18:30. Later than 20:00 in an exam term is competing with sleep, which costs more than the session gains.

Mathematics specifically rewards a ninety-minute slot over a sixty-minute one, because the useful unit of work is a full past-paper section followed by marking it together. A sixty-minute session can do one or the other well. It can rarely do both, and the marking is where the learning happens. For a Year 10 student building content, sixty minutes is fine. For a Year 11 student in the run-in, ninety is the better buy.

Because the lesson is delivered over live video, a late school finish moves the session rather than cancelling it. That is a small operational point with a large cumulative effect across two years: an arrangement that survives disruption delivers the hours you paid for, and an arrangement that depends on a journey does not.

sections.heading: What the market charges, and what a code match is worth
paragraphs: Published rates in this market, with their sources, are these. Entry-level online tuition runs AED 45-150 an hour, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45-65 and Tutopiya from AED 33-52. A qualified subject tutor working online sits at roughly AED 150-300, and Unitors publishes International GCSE tuition from AED 150. In-home one-to-one with travel included runs AED 180-500, with Bestimate quoting AED 180-350. Specialist IGCSE and A Level tutors run AED 200-450 and upwards, with TutorChase at AED 270.

What is striking about those bands in the context of this page is that none of them is priced on specification knowledge. A tutor who teaches Cambridge 0606 Additional Mathematics every week and a tutor who last saw calculus at university can both sit in the AED 200-300 band and present identically. The code question costs nothing to ask and is the only reliable filter available to a parent.

The in-home premium is the second thing to notice. The gap between AED 150-300 online and AED 180-500 in-home is travel, not teaching, and on Saadiyat Island it is larger because the only road access is across a bridge. A family paying the premium is buying presence, which is a legitimate thing to want, and is paying for it from a smaller pool of tutors. On a specification like 0606 that pool may be empty.

None of these are IB Gram's prices. They are published market figures, attributed, so that a Saadiyat Island parent can test a quote. Our own arrangement begins with a free trial lesson and a conversation about code, tier and how many weeks remain before the series your child is entered for.

sections.heading: The questions to ask before you pay anyone
paragraphs: Five questions separate a specification specialist from a generalist, and all five can be asked in a single message. Which syllabus code do you teach most weeks? Which tier is my child entered for, and how will you confirm it? Which board's past papers will we use from the first session? What will you look for in a marked mock? And do you hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit?

The last one is worth a paragraph. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, MoHRE's own service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time, and eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so treat any figure quoted to you as unverified.

There is an Abu Dhabi-specific caution too. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff have been reported as barring teachers from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with the permit-holder's school. We treat this as press-reported rather than as exact policy wording, and we do not arrange for a child to be tutored privately by a teacher at their own school.

Finally, check claims about standing. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education, MoHRE, Cambridge, Pearson or the IB, and has no UAE office or centre. We name those bodies to explain what they govern. Any tutoring page claiming otherwise about itself is making a checkable statement, and it is worth checking.

sections.heading: The series your child sits, and what that means for timing
paragraphs: Cambridge IGCSE candidates in the UAE sit the June series and the November series. The February and March series is offered to India only, so any page quoting it at an Abu Dhabi parent is quoting the wrong country's calendar. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and in November. Which series your child sits is set by the school's entry and confirmed by its exams officer.

Working backwards from a June sitting: results reach centres in August, final entries close months before the exam window, mocks fall in the spring term, and the last realistic point for a tier change sits earlier still. For a November sitting the pattern repeats shifted; the Pearson November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026.

For maths specifically, the consequence is about paper volume. A student needs to have sat several full timed papers under conditions before the real thing, and each one takes a session to sit and a session to mark properly. Eight weeks of that work has to be scheduled during the spring term, not hoped for after the mocks come back. A November resit decision, by contrast, opens the day August results arrive and closes well before the exam.

Official timetables are revised, and Pearson publishes provisional versions ahead of each series. Read the live timetable on the board's own site rather than a date restated on any tutoring page, including this one, and confirm your centre's administrative zone with the school. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six zones and is explicit that using the wrong zone's timetable is the candidate's risk.

faqs.question: Is there actually an IGCSE maths specialist living near Saadiyat Island?
faqs.answer: Few, and that is the honest answer. Saadiyat has a small resident base and a small number of schools, so the number of adults within a short drive who teach Cambridge 0580 at Extended tier as their regular work is very low, and for Additional Mathematics 0606 it is lower still. Filtering by postcode on a small island produces a near-empty list. Filtering by syllabus code instead produces a deep one, and live video removes the only reason a code specialist could not teach your child.

faqs.question: Which maths syllabus code will my child in Abu Dhabi be sitting?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the school's entry. The common codes are Cambridge 0580 Mathematics, split into Core and Extended; Cambridge 0606 Additional Mathematics, taken alongside it by stronger candidates; Pearson Edexcel 4MA1 Mathematics A, tiered into Foundation and Higher; and Pearson 4MB1 Mathematics B, which is a separate specification rather than a variant. The school's exams officer can confirm the code and the tier in one email, and it is worth sending before you pay anyone.

faqs.question: Does it really matter if a tutor uses Cambridge papers for a Pearson entry?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the damage is invisible until results day. The content overlaps heavily, but Cambridge 0580 Extended papers favour structured multi-part questions with incremental marks, while Pearson 4MA1 Higher includes longer problem-solving items where the method is not signposted. A student drilled only on one style is disoriented by the other even when every technique is secure. Switching the past-paper diet to match the entry is the cheapest correction available in Year 11 and takes one session to set up.

faqs.question: What happens if you have no 0606 Additional Mathematics tutor free?
faqs.answer: We tell you, and we may decline rather than place someone who does not teach it. Additional Mathematics introduces differentiation, integration, binomial expansion and trigonometric identities a year early, with multi-step questions that give no scaffolding. A tutor who last saw that material at university will cover it at the wrong depth. The waiting time for this code is the longest of the four we list, and we would rather give you a date we can meet than a tutor who is merely available.

faqs.question: Is a move from Core to Extended maths still possible for a Year 11 student in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is a school decision rather than a tutor's. The important point is that it is a content change, not a difficulty change: Extended papers draw on algebraic manipulation, graph transformations and harder trigonometry that Core papers never set, so there is real material to acquire. Core also caps the grade that can be awarded, which is why a Core candidate aiming high has to move first. Ask the school in writing which route your child is entered for before planning anything.

faqs.question: What does a marked mock paper tell you that a report card does not?
faqs.answer: Three things. Whether the losses are clustered in two or three topics, which means a short repair job, or scattered as single marks across the paper, which usually means arithmetic fluency, timing or a habit of not writing method. Whether the tier is right, since a Core candidate losing almost nothing is capping their own grade. And how the student behaves in an exam: abandoned questions, later questions left blank, answers given without working. None of that appears in a report.

faqs.question: Which maths topics cost Abu Dhabi Extended candidates the most marks?
faqs.answer: The list is consistent. Algebraic fractions and changing the subject of a formula come first, because the skills are mechanical and decay without practice. Reverse percentages come next, and they are worth isolating because dividing by the wrong base loses the whole question rather than part of it. Then bounds in division, graph transformation signs, frequency density in unequal-width histograms, and transformation descriptions given without the centre or scale factor. Each is a bounded piece of work rather than a general weakness.

faqs.question: How long should an IGCSE maths session be for a Year 11 student?
faqs.answer: Ninety minutes, if the budget allows. The useful unit of work in Year 11 maths is a full past-paper section sat under timed conditions followed by marking it together, and the marking is where most of the learning happens. A sixty-minute session can do one or the other well and rarely both. For a Year 10 student still building content, sixty minutes is appropriate and cheaper. The shift from sixty to ninety usually makes sense around the spring term of Year 10.

faqs.question: What time can a maths session start for a Saadiyat Island student?
faqs.answer: That depends on which campus your child attends rather than where you live. Schools on the island typically finish between 14:45 and 15:15, putting a workable start at about 16:30. A child at a Khalifa City or Al Raha campus is often not home until 16:15 or later, which makes 17:30 the honest earliest. Our Abu Dhabi range runs from 16:30 to 21:00 Gulf Standard Time, and because the lesson is delivered over video, a late school finish moves the session rather than cancelling it.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send maths tutors to Saadiyat Island addresses?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE, and in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Abu Dhabi families are taught one-to-one over live video. On this page the reason is not primarily cost: it is pool depth. An in-home arrangement on an island reached by a single bridge means choosing from whoever will make the journey, and for a specification like Cambridge 0606 that group may contain nobody who teaches it.

faqs.question: How much do IGCSE maths tutors charge in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Published market bands are AED 45-150 an hour at entry level, with EdFlik from AED 45-65 and Tutopiya from AED 33-52; AED 150-300 for a qualified online subject tutor, with Unitors listing International GCSE from AED 150; AED 180-500 for in-home one-to-one with travel included, per Bestimate's AED 180-350 and independent quotes of AED 200-500; and AED 200-450 or more for specialists, with TutorChase at AED 270. None of those rates indicates whether the tutor knows your child's code.

faqs.question: Which exam series does an Abu Dhabi IGCSE maths candidate sit?
faqs.answer: Cambridge candidates in the UAE sit the June series and the November series; the February and March series is offered to India only and does not apply. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and in November. The school's entry determines which, and the exams officer can confirm both the series and your centre's administrative zone. Cambridge allocates each centre to one of six zones and states that using the wrong zone's timetable is the candidate's own risk, so the zone question is worth asking.

faqs.question: My child changed schools mid-course and the board changed too. What now?
faqs.answer: Treat it as a bounded audit rather than a crisis. The tutor compares the two specifications, identifies the handful of topics present in one and absent from the other, switches the past-paper diet to the new board immediately, and rebuilds the exam-technique habits the new papers reward. That is usually a few sessions of work. What makes it expensive is leaving it undone, because the student keeps revising competently for a slightly different examination and nobody can explain the result.

faqs.question: Should we use a tuition centre group class for maths instead?
faqs.answer: It is cheaper per hour and it has a real cost for a Saadiyat Island family: a second evening journey, usually to central Abu Dhabi, at the exact time your child should be eating. A group class also cannot match a syllabus code to one student, because the room contains several entries. For content coverage in Year 10 it can work. For Year 11 paper technique, where the value lies in marking one student's own paper with them, it does not.

faqs.question: What should I ask a maths tutor before the first paid session?
faqs.answer: Five things, all in one message. Which syllabus code do you teach most weeks? Which tier is my child entered for and how will you confirm it? Which board's past papers will we use from session one? What will you look for in a marked mock? And do you hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, which is free and valid for two years? A tutor who answers all five crisply is a specialist. One who answers in generalities is a generalist, whatever the rate.

intro.heading: Count the weeks before you count the money
paragraphs: Shakhbout City is a mainland villa community in the Khalifa City corridor, built as family housing, with most children attending one of the international schools a short drive away in that corridor. The school runs are short, the evenings are quiet, and a maths session at half past four is genuinely possible — which makes this one of the easier places in Abu Dhabi to run a consistent weekly arrangement.

Which is exactly why the mistake here is a calendar mistake rather than a logistics one. Families in this corridor can book a standing hour without difficulty, so they do, and the hour then finds its own content. Across a Year 11 that produces a lot of homework supervision at a specialist's rate and not much movement, because the work was never matched to how far away the paper was.

The distance from the exam changes what a maths hour can achieve, completely. Nine months out, an hour can rebuild algebraic fluency, which is slow work that pays everywhere. Three months out, an hour can install paper technique and calculator discipline. Four weeks out, an hour can only drill a repeating error found on a real script. Try to rebuild algebra four weeks out and you spend specialist money on something that will not land in time.

So this page is written as a countdown rather than as a prospectus. What eight weeks can achieve. What belongs at each distance from the paper. Where mock season sits and why a marked mock is worth more than the grade attached to it. How Ramadan reshapes a revision term in this country. And what the tier decision's own deadline does to the Year 10 calendar.

The exam facts you can plan against are these. Cambridge runs IGCSE in a June series and a November series, and the February and March series is offered to India only — not available to a candidate sitting in Abu Dhabi. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May/June and November. Pearson's published history shows a November window from late October to 19 November 2026, June 2026 results reaching students on 20 August 2026 and November 2025 results on 22 January 2026, which tells you the shape of the wait at each end.

On delivery, plainly: IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE. In-home tutoring is a service we run in India only, and no tutor will travel to a Shakhbout City address. Lessons are live one-to-one video in Gulf Standard Time. The calendar reason that matters is frequency: an online slot can double for three weeks around a mock or a deadline and step back afterwards, which a tutor driving a fixed route through the corridor cannot do.
What follows is the countdown in full, with the AED cost of each window attached so you can place the spending as well as the work.

subjects.description: Expanding, factorising, rearranging, solving. Slow fluency work that pays across every multi-step question. Needs months of short frequent practice, so it belongs early and is close to unfixable four weeks out.

subjects.name: Trigonometry and bearings
subjects.description: Right-angled and non-right-angled triangles, sine and cosine rules, bearings and 3D work. Mostly a diagram habit rather than knowledge, which makes it fixable in a handful of sessions even late.

subjects.name: Geometry and mensuration
subjects.description: Angle reasoning, circle theorems, compound-shape surface area and volume. Circle theorems are learnable in two or three sessions; compound shapes are a working-presentation problem in disguise.

subjects.name: Probability and statistics
subjects.description: Averages from tables, cumulative frequency, histograms, tree diagrams, conditional probability. Self-contained topics with reliable marks, which makes them the best late-stage purchase in the syllabus.

subjects.name: Graphs and functions
subjects.description: Straight lines, quadratics, reciprocal and exponential curves, transformations, function notation at the higher tiers. Marks go on reading values without showing the construction lines a marker expects.

subjects.name: Vectors and transformations
subjects.description: Column vectors, vector geometry, translations, rotations, reflections, enlargements with negative scale factors. Small, dependable and quick to teach — another good late-stage target.

subjects.name: Non-calculator arithmetic
subjects.levels: Where a non-calculator paper is sat
subjects.description: Fractions, percentages, ratio, standard form, bounds, estimation. Needs a few weeks of practice with the machine deliberately off the desk, so plan it at least two months out.

subjects.name: Multi-step problem solving
subjects.description: Questions combining topics with no signposting, which separate the top grades. The skill is planning the route before calculating, and it takes a term to build rather than a fortnight.

sections.heading: What eight weeks can actually achieve in IGCSE maths
paragraphs: Answer first, because this is the question most Shakhbout City families arrive with. Eight weeks of weekly one-to-one maths is enough to fix how working is presented, install calculator discipline, and close two self-contained topics properly. It is not enough to rebuild algebraic fluency, and it is not enough to cover a syllabus the student has not learned.

That sounds limiting and it is actually freeing, because it tells you exactly what to buy. Two topics, chosen from a marked script rather than from a feeling, plus the two habit fixes that pay across every question. A tutor who agrees to "go through the syllabus" in eight weeks is agreeing to something that cannot work, and the student will finish the block having seen everything once and secured nothing.

Choosing the two topics well is most of the value. The best late-stage targets are self-contained and reliably examined: histograms with unequal class widths, conditional probability from tree diagrams, circle theorems, vectors, transformations with negative scale factors, bearings. Each is learnable in two or three sessions and each appears every series. The worst late-stage targets are the ones that sit underneath everything — algebraic manipulation and multi-step problem solving — because they are fluency and fluency takes months.

So an eight-week block looks like this: week one, a full paper under timing and a diagnosis. Weeks two and three, working presentation and calculator discipline. Weeks four to seven, the two chosen topics, each ending in a timed question set. Week eight, another full paper to check. That is a defined purchase with a testable outcome, and it costs less than the open-ended version that achieves less.

sections.heading: What belongs at each distance from the paper
paragraphs: The same money buys different things at different distances from the exam, and matching them is the whole discipline. Nine months out, the right purchase is fluency: algebraic manipulation and non-calculator arithmetic, taught in short frequent sessions, because fluency cannot be installed quickly and pays into every question thereafter. Almost nobody buys at this distance, because nothing has gone wrong yet.

Six months out, the right purchase is content gaps found from a real paper rather than guessed at, plus the start of paper technique. Three months out, it is technique proper: working presentation, calculator discipline, formula-booklet familiarity and timing, all built from marked scripts. This is the highest-return window in the countdown and the one most families spend on topic revision instead, duplicating what the school is already doing.

Four weeks out, the window closes on new content. What remains is timed papers and the drilling of repeating errors, and any hour spent teaching something unfamiliar is an hour spent on material unlikely to survive the paper. Two weeks out the only useful activities are a paper, its review, and sleep.

Afterwards there is a window families forget. Results arrive — roughly eight to nine weeks after a summer series, and the following January after a November one, judging by Pearson's published history of June 2026 results reaching students on 20 August 2026 and November 2025 results on 22 January 2026. If a grade falls short of a sixth-form threshold, the resit decision belongs in that window, and the first action is free: ask the receiving sixth form whether they will accept the original grade.

sections.heading: Mock season in maths, specifically
paragraphs: Mocks generate more worry per unit of information than anything else in Year 11, and in maths the information available is unusually rich. A maths script is a page-by-page record of decisions: which question was abandoned, where the minutes went, whether a sign was lost early and propagated, whether the calculator was in the wrong mode for a whole section.

Sorted properly, every lost mark on a maths mock falls into one of four categories, and they need four different responses. Knowledge: the student did not know the method. Method presentation: they knew it and did not write enough to be credited. Misreading: they answered a different question from the one asked. Timing: they ran out of minutes before reaching marks they could have had. A grade shows none of this. A script shows all of it in twenty minutes.

The categories matter because the proportions are usually surprising. A student described as weak at maths often turns out to be losing more marks to timing and presentation than to knowledge, which means the fix is cheap and fast rather than a term of re-teaching. Equally, a student losing most marks to genuine knowledge gaps in two topics has a clear and narrow brief.

Practically: book one session in the week after mock scripts come back, spend it sorting the marks, and let the result set the plan for the remaining months. Do not book ordinary weekly sessions through the mock fortnight itself, because a student sitting several papers has no capacity to absorb anything new, and those hours are paid for and unused.

sections.heading: Ramadan, breaks and the shape of a UAE revision term
paragraphs: A revision plan written on a European template fails in a predictable place here. Ramadan falls inside the UAE school year, school days shorten, family routines change substantially, and the hours when a teenager concentrates move later. None of that is a problem if it is planned for, and all of it is a problem if it is discovered in week one of the month.

What works in practice is treating the month as a lower-intensity period and loading the weeks either side. Sessions commonly move to post-Iftar timing and the slot is held rather than reassigned, and students are often sharper then than in a compressed school afternoon. What does not work is running the full load unchanged, keeping homework expectations identical, and scheduling a mock immediately afterwards with no adjustment.

The breaks are the opposite case: the only uninterrupted stretches in the year, and therefore the natural home for the slow work. Algebraic fluency responds to daily short practice far better than to weekly hours, and a mid-year break is the one time that is possible. A student who spends twenty minutes a day on algebra across a break arrives in the final term with something no amount of late tutoring could have bought.

Travel is the other local variable. Families in this corridor travel, sometimes for weeks, and an in-home arrangement stops when they do. An online slot follows the family on a shifted clock, which in a Year 11 means a three-week absence need not cost a topic.

sections.heading: The tier decision has a deadline too
paragraphs: The entry tier is the one maths deadline families do not realise they are inside. It is decided during Year 10 by the department, usually on the basis of internal assessment, and once the entry is made the grade ceiling is set. A Core or Foundation entry caps the available grade; an Extended or Higher entry opens it and places harder algebra, trigonometry and multi-step problem solving in front of a student who may not be ready.

The downstream cost lands in Year 12. A Level Mathematics and IB Higher Level maths courses normally require an Extended or Higher tier grade at a reasonable level, with each sixth form setting its own threshold. Several schools across this corridor run both pathways, so the fork is real rather than theoretical, and reopening a closed door means a resit series and another year's planning.

Calendar-wise that pushes the highest-value maths spending into Year 10, which is counter-intuitive because nothing has gone wrong then. Four to six sessions aimed squarely at the content separating the tiers, placed before the entry is fixed, is a small defined cost protecting a large one. The same money in Year 11 buys general revision beneath a ceiling that is already set.

There is a second, earlier deadline worth knowing about in this corridor. Sixth-form applications are often made on predicted grades in the autumn of Year 11, before any real result exists. So the grade that opens the door can be a prediction, which moves the effective deadline months forward. Ask the receiving sixth form when they decide and on what evidence — the answer is free and occasionally changes the whole plan.

sections.heading: What to fix first when the weeks are short
paragraphs: When time is the binding constraint, the order matters more than the content. The priority is not the hardest topic or the one the student dislikes most; it is the one with the best ratio of marks recovered to weeks required. That ranking is stable across both boards and both tiers, and it is almost the reverse of what families choose on instinct.

First, working presentation, because it recovers marks the student has already earned and takes three weeks. Second, calculator discipline, one or two sessions for marks lost to modes and unrecorded commands. Third, the self-contained topics that appear every series and are quick to teach: histograms with unequal class widths, conditional probability, circle theorems, vectors, transformations, bearings. Fourth, timing strategy across a whole paper.

Last — and only if months rather than weeks remain — algebraic manipulation and multi-step problem solving. They are the highest-value things in the syllabus and the slowest to build, which makes them an early-year purchase and a poor late one. A family that funds algebra four weeks before a paper has bought the right thing at the wrong time.

The instinct families follow instead is to start with the topic the student finds hardest, which is usually algebra, and to leave presentation and calculator work as too trivial to pay for. That ordering reliably produces a block of sessions that feels serious and moves nothing before the paper.

There is a useful test if you are unsure. Ask what the student would gain if this item were perfect tomorrow, and how many weeks it would take to get there. Presentation scores high on the first and low on the second, which is why it goes first. Multi-step problem solving scores high on both, which is why it is a Year 10 project and not a March one.

sections.heading: What each window costs in AED
paragraphs: A Shakhbout City family buying IGCSE maths is buying into a market with published prices, read in October 2026, and these are its lines. The cheapest route is budget online tutoring at AED 45 to 150 an hour. A qualified subject tutor working online runs AED 150 to 300. A named IGCSE or A-Level specialist occupies AED 200 to 450 and above, and premium examiner-led provision reaches AED 650. The outlier is the in-home one-to-one visit at AED 180 to 500, where the journey sits inside the fee rather than beside it, so a tutor driving out past the villa blocks is charging for the drive whether the hour goes on quadratics or on vectors. Notice the overlap while you are reading: the bottom of the specialist band sits well inside the ordinary qualified-tutor band, which tells you the word specialist is not by itself the thing you are paying for.

Monthly, Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 estimates for weekly one-hour sessions come out at AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-range, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support. Package rates in this market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions.

Mapped onto the countdown, the spending shape should be uneven rather than flat. Early-year fluency work is cheap per session and wants frequency, so it sits in the mid-range monthly band for a term. Technique work three months out is a short block. The final four weeks is the only period that justifies the exam-year intensity, and it should stop with the series. A family paying exam-year rates for the whole of Year 11 has spent a great deal to arrive at the same place.

IB Gram publishes no hourly price on this page. There is a free trial lesson and a consultation, and the number follows once the board, tier and remaining weeks are known. The figures above are the market's, included so you can price any quote against them.

sections.heading: Why a slot that can double matters, and what a tutor may not do
paragraphs: Stated plainly: IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE. No tutor will travel to a Shakhbout City address. In-home tutoring is a service we run in India only. Lessons are live one-to-one video in Gulf Standard Time.

The calendar reason this matters here is frequency rather than distance, since an in-home tutor in this corridor would only be driving ten to twenty-five minutes. A countdown needs an uneven load: weekly for a term, twice weekly for the three weeks after mocks, nothing through the mock fortnight itself, post-Iftar during Ramadan, three a week in the final month, then stop. A tutor whose week is built around a driving route cannot reshape itself like that, because the route is the business.

For maths over video there is one requirement worth setting up in session one: the tutor must see handwritten working as it happens, through a camera angled at paper or a tablet and stylus. With that in place a shared whiteboard retains every worked line, the exact past-paper question is pasted onto the board, and the student writes on their own paper in their own hand, which is what the exam will ask of them.

On assessed work, the boundary. A tutor may teach content, explain what the mark scheme rewards, question a method until the student finds its weakness, read work the student wrote and name what undersells it, and teach honest method description. A tutor may not write, draft, rewrite or complete assessed work, produce a model answer to the live task, or supply data the student did not collect. We also link board papers and mark schemes to their official source rather than redistributing copyrighted material, and IB Gram holds no regulator approval, accreditation or partnership and runs no UAE office.

faqs.question: We have eight weeks before the maths paper. What can that realistically do?
faqs.answer: It will fix how working is presented, install calculator discipline, and close two self-contained topics properly. It will not rebuild algebraic fluency and it will not cover a syllabus the student has not learned. The shape that works: week one a full paper under timing and a diagnosis, weeks two and three presentation and calculator work, weeks four to seven two chosen topics each ending in a timed set, week eight another full paper. A tutor who agrees to cover the syllabus in eight weeks is agreeing to something that cannot work.

faqs.question: Which maths topics are the best late-stage targets?
faqs.answer: Self-contained ones that appear every series and teach quickly: histograms with unequal class widths, conditional probability from tree diagrams, circle theorems, vectors, transformations with negative scale factors, and bearings. Each is two or three sessions and each is reliably examined. The worst late targets are algebraic manipulation and multi-step problem solving, because they sit underneath everything and are fluency rather than knowledge, which takes months. Those are Year 10 purchases, and buying them four weeks out is the right thing at the wrong time.

faqs.question: What should we stop doing four weeks before the paper?
faqs.answer: Learning new content. Anything unfamiliar taught in the final month rarely survives contact with the paper, and the hour spent on it displaces something that would have paid. What remains useful is timed papers, the drilling of errors that recur across scripts, and rest. In the final fortnight the only sensible activities are one paper, its review and sleep. Families often increase intensity at exactly the point where intensity stops converting into marks, which is expensive and counterproductive.

faqs.question: How should we use a maths mock script rather than the grade?
faqs.answer: Sort every lost mark into four categories: knowledge, where the method was absent or wrong; method presentation, where the answer was right and the working too compressed to credit; misreading, where a different question was answered; and timing, where later marks were never reached. A grade shows none of this and a script shows all of it in twenty minutes. The proportions usually surprise families — a student called weak at maths frequently loses more to timing and presentation than to mathematics, which is a cheap fix.

faqs.question: Should we keep weekly sessions running through mock season?
faqs.answer: No. The fortnight either side of mocks is consumed by them, and a student sitting several papers has no capacity to absorb anything new, so those hours are paid for and unused. The valuable booking is one session in the week after the scripts come back, spent sorting every lost mark into categories and letting the result set the plan for the remaining months. Then resume the normal rhythm with a brief that is based on evidence rather than on what the family assumed in September.

faqs.question: How does Ramadan change a maths revision plan in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Treat the month as a lower-intensity period and load the weeks either side rather than running the usual schedule through it. School days shorten, routines move later, and students often concentrate better after Iftar than in a compressed afternoon, so sessions commonly shift to post-Iftar timing with the slot held rather than reassigned. What fails is keeping the full session load and homework expectations unchanged and then scheduling a mock immediately afterwards with no adjustment for the month that preceded it.

faqs.question: What is the best use of a mid-year break for IGCSE maths?
faqs.answer: Daily short algebra practice, mostly unsupervised. Algebraic fluency responds to twenty minutes a day far better than to a weekly hour, and a break is the only time in the year when daily practice is actually possible. A student who does that arrives in the final term with something no amount of late tutoring could buy. One or two check-in sessions across the break are enough to keep the practice honest and correct the errors creeping in, which is a very cheap way to spend a holiday.

faqs.question: When is the tier entry decided, and can we still influence it?
faqs.answer: During Year 10, by the department, usually on internal assessment evidence. Once the entry is made the grade ceiling is set: a Core or Foundation entry caps what is achievable, and A Level Mathematics or IB Higher Level maths normally require an Extended or Higher grade at a reasonable level. You can influence it before it is fixed. Ask the department which tier your child is provisionally entered for and what specifically would have to improve for the other tier to be viable — the second answer is a precise, free tutoring brief.

faqs.question: Which exam series will our child sit, and is a resit possible?
faqs.answer: Cambridge runs IGCSE in a June series and a November series, and the February and March series is offered to India only, so it is not available to an Abu Dhabi candidate. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May/June and November. November is the resit route for both. Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and warns it is essential to use the correct timetable for your zone. For any series, open the board's live official timetable rather than planning against a restated date.

faqs.question: How long after the paper do results arrive?
faqs.answer: Pearson's published history gives the pattern: June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, roughly eight to nine weeks after the summer window, while November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026, about two months after that series. The November 2026 final timetable itself ran from late October to 19 November 2026. Those are backward-looking dates quoted so you can plan the wait. Future dates get revised, so check the live timetable before acting.

faqs.question: Is a November maths resit worth the time and money?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and the first step costs nothing: ask the receiving sixth form whether they will accept the original grade. If a resit is needed, price three things — the entry fee from your centre, a short targeted block rather than a full re-teach since the content is already covered once, and the time cost of revising through the first sixth-form term. A November result reaches students the following January, which is useful for a conditional place and useless for an application already decided.

faqs.question: Why does the session frequency need to change during the year?
faqs.answer: Because a countdown is uneven. A term of weekly work on fluency, nothing through the mock fortnight, two a week for three weeks after the scripts come back, post-Iftar timing through Ramadan, three a week in the final month, then a stop at the series. A tutor whose week is built around a driving route through this corridor cannot reshape itself like that, so the help tends to be available in the quiet weeks and unavailable in the busy ones. Online, the slot flexes and is held rather than reassigned.

faqs.question: Will a maths tutor come to our house in Shakhbout City?
faqs.answer: Not one of ours. IB Gram runs no home visits anywhere in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we offer only in India. Lessons are live one-to-one video in Gulf Standard Time. In this corridor the argument is not distance, since a visiting tutor would drive only ten to twenty-five minutes. It is that a calendar-driven plan needs frequency that changes through the year, and a fixed route cannot deliver that. For maths the one requirement online is a camera angled at the student's paper.

faqs.question: Can a tutor produce or correct assessed coursework?
faqs.answer: No. A tutor may teach the content, explain what the mark scheme rewards, question a method until the student finds its weakness, read work the student wrote and name which part undersells it, and teach honest method description. A tutor may not write, draft, rewrite or complete assessed work, produce a model answer to the live task for adaptation, or supply data the student did not collect. We also link board papers and mark schemes to their official source rather than handing over copies of copyrighted material.

faqs.question: What is the single most useful free thing to do first?
faqs.answer: Have your child sit a full past paper from the correct board under exam timing, then mark it honestly against the real mark scheme rather than generously. That costs nothing, takes an afternoon, and produces the script every sensible plan is built from. It will also tell you whether paid help is needed at all: a script showing losses almost entirely to presentation and timing points to a two or three session fix rather than a term of hours, and you will know that before spending anything.

abu-dhabi/igcse-maths-tutor-in-shakhbout.closingBody: An IGCSE maths tutor in Shakhbout City is worth exactly what the calendar allows. Nine months out, an hour can rebuild algebraic fluency. Three months out, it installs technique. Four weeks out, it can only drill errors a real script has already named. Have your child sit a paper under timing, sort every lost mark into knowledge, presentation, misreading or timing, and buy a block sized to the weeks remaining. intro.heading: Mathematics decays, which is why the timing matters more here than anywhere else
paragraphs: Mathematics is the one International GCSE subject where a topic learned in Year 10 and not revisited is genuinely gone by Year 11. A student can read a History case study in October and recall it in May with modest effort. A student who last factorised a quadratic in February of Year 10 will struggle with it fifteen months later, not because they misunderstood it but because the skill is procedural and procedural skills decay without retrieval.

That single property changes how tutoring should be timed. In a content subject, late revision works, because the material is still roughly where it was left. In mathematics, late revision has to rebuild as well as remind, and rebuilding takes time that a final term does not have alongside five other subjects. The expensive version of this problem is a Year 11 student who is competent in the topic currently being taught and has quietly lost four earlier ones.

The second timing issue is the tier. Cambridge 0580 splits into Core and Extended and Pearson 4MA1 tiers into Foundation and Higher, and the lower option caps the grade. Mathematics is the subject where this decision is made earliest and reviewed least, usually on the basis of Year 9 performance, and where a change upwards involves the most genuinely new content. By the spring of Year 11 the option has effectively closed.

The third is that mathematics is the subject whose topics are taught in the most varied order across schools. One campus does all the algebra first; another threads it through two years. One finishes trigonometry in Year 10; another leaves the sine and cosine rules until the spring of Year 11, which means a mock sat in the winter examines content the student has not met. A tutor who does not ask for the school's topic sequence cannot tell the difference between a gap and a topic not yet reached.

On Yas Island there is one more calendar factor that is genuinely local rather than national. The island hosts large-scale events, including the Grand Prix weekend at the end of the first term, and access and road management during those periods changes what a weekday evening looks like for residents. For an arrangement that depends on somebody driving, that is lost sessions. For a lesson delivered over live video it is nothing.

IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Abu Dhabi families are taught one-to-one over live video, scheduled to Gulf Standard Time. What follows maps the topic sequence against the moments the gaps surface, sets out a rotation that resists decay, and states the Cambridge and Pearson dates we can source with their sources attached.

Cambridge runs Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October, which means a family can see a weakness in number or algebra two full years before it becomes a grade.

abu-dhabi/igcse-maths-tutor-in-yas-islan.subjectsIntro: These are the mathematics strands, written against the calendar: when each is usually taught, and therefore when the gap it leaves tends to surface.

subjects.name: Number, ratio and percentages
subjects.description: Taught early, often in the first term of Year 10, and then assumed for two years. Reverse percentages are the specific loss, and because they are taught early they are the topic most likely to have decayed entirely by the mock.

subjects.name: Algebraic manipulation
subjects.description: Begun in Year 10 and threaded through everything afterwards, which makes it the one strand where decay is masked: the student keeps using it, badly, inside other topics. Gaps surface as scattered single-mark losses across a whole mock paper.

subjects.name: Equations and simultaneous systems
subjects.description: Usually taught in the middle of Year 10. Quadratics by formula and by completing the square tend to be revisited in Year 11; linear and quadratic simultaneous equations often are not, and that is where the Year 11 surprise comes from.

subjects.name: Bounds and limits of accuracy
subjects.description: A short topic taught quickly, frequently in Year 10, and almost never revisited until revision. Division bounds are the trap. Because the topic is small, it is also the fastest to rebuild, which makes it a good early win in a rotation.

subjects.name: Functions and transformations
subjects.description: Often taught in Year 11, which means a winter mock may examine it thinly or not at all. The sign of a horizontal translation is the recurring error, and transformation descriptions are marked by element rather than as a single recall answer.

subjects.name: Trigonometry beyond right angles
subjects.description: Sequenced very differently between schools: some finish the sine and cosine rules in Year 10, others leave them to the spring of Year 11. This is the single most common reason a mock score misleads, because the student was examined on content not yet taught.

subjects.name: Mensuration and similar figures
subjects.description: Usually Year 10 with an extension in Year 11. Length, area and volume scale factors are the specific loss, and the error is reliable enough that it is worth a dedicated half session in any rotation.

subjects.name: Vectors and vector geometry
subjects.description: Frequently taught late, sometimes in the final two terms, which means it arrives when revision is already under way and competes with it. Short, notation-heavy and high-yield once learned, so it repays being scheduled rather than absorbed.

subjects.name: Probability and set notation
subjects.description: Split across both years in most schemes. Conditional probability without replacement is the discriminating skill, and set notation on Venn diagrams is examinable in its own right, which students discover in a mock rather than in class.

subjects.name: Statistics and cumulative frequency
subjects.description: Often taught in Year 10 and left alone afterwards, making it a reliable decay candidate. Frequency density in unequal-width histograms is the discriminating step and is the piece most often missing when the topic is rebuilt from memory.

subjects.name: Sequences and nth terms
subjects.description: Taught early and examined every series. Quadratic nth term questions carry method marks for the second-difference step, which survives in memory far better than the expression-forming step does, so partial recall still earns something.

subjects.name: Calculus and identities (Additional Mathematics 0606)
subjects.description: Entirely a Year 11 body of content, taught alongside the main course and examined in the same series. No runway, no Year 10 foundation, and multi-step questions with no scaffolding, which is why 0606 is the one maths entry that justifies continuous weekly support.

sections.heading: When each topic is taught, and when its gap surfaces
paragraphs: The most useful document a mathematics tutor can be given is the school's own topic sequence, and almost nobody asks for it. Without it, a mock score is uninterpretable: a student who scored badly on trigonometry may have a gap, or may simply not have been taught the sine and cosine rules yet, and those two situations call for opposite responses.

The general pattern across Abu Dhabi campuses is that number, ratio, percentages, basic algebra, mensuration and descriptive statistics are taught in Year 10, while functions, transformations, vectors, conditional probability and the harder trigonometry arrive in Year 11. The variation sits in the middle: simultaneous equations, bounds, cumulative frequency and sequences move around considerably depending on the scheme of work.

The timing of teaching determines the timing of decay. A topic taught in the first term of Year 10 and never revisited has had fifteen months to fade before the examination, and in mathematics that is enough to remove a procedural skill entirely. A topic taught in the spring of Year 11 has had no time to decay and may instead be insecure because it was taught quickly against a deadline. Those are different problems and a rotation has to handle both.

The table maps the main strands against when they are typically taught, when the gap tends to surface, and what delay costs. Treat it as a template to be corrected against your own school's sequence rather than as a statement about any particular campus, because the variation between schools is the point rather than an inconvenience.

sections.heading: The tier window, and why mathematics closes it first
paragraphs: Mathematics is the subject where the ability decision is made earliest and where it matters most, because the two routes genuinely diverge in content rather than only in difficulty. Cambridge 0580 Core covers less of the syllabus and caps the grade a candidate can be awarded; Extended covers the supplementary statements in every strand and is open to the full range. Pearson 4MA1 tiers into Foundation and Higher with the same effect.

Schools typically set the tier on the basis of Year 9 performance and early Year 10 assessment, which means it is decided before a student has had the chance to respond to secondary mathematics properly. That is a reasonable administrative decision and it is also reviewable for a period. The window is genuinely open through Year 10 and narrows sharply once Year 11 begins, because the content gap has to be closed alongside the rest of the course.

What makes a move upward expensive later is the nature of the gap. Extended papers set algebraic manipulation, function notation, graph transformations, the sine and cosine rules, vector geometry, conditional probability and unequal-width histograms, and a Core student has not met several of those at all. That is a body of teaching, not a change of difficulty, and attempting it in the spring of Year 11 means competing with revision in five other subjects.

The useful intervention is evidence rather than advocacy. A tutor can have the student sit one paper from the target tier under real conditions and produce a written list of the content a move would require, with an honest estimate of the hours involved. That gives a family something concrete to put in front of the school, which is a better conversation than an assertion that the child could do more.

sections.heading: A twelve-week rotation that resists decay
paragraphs: Most mathematics revision is organised by topic block: a week on algebra, a week on trigonometry, a week on statistics. That structure feels orderly and it fights the way the subject is actually retained, because a topic covered intensively for a week and then abandoned for eight weeks has decayed again by the time it is examined.

A rotation works differently. Each session covers short segments of several topics rather than one topic at length, and topics return on a schedule chosen so that each one comes back before it is lost. The first visit to a topic re-teaches; the second retrieves; the third and fourth consolidate with progressively harder questions. The total time spent on a topic is similar. The retention is not comparable.

Twelve weeks is a practical cycle length for Year 11. It allows four visits to the high-risk early-taught topics, three to the middle group, and two to anything taught recently that needs consolidation rather than rebuilding. It also fits between the autumn term and the mock window, or between the mocks and the series, which are the two periods when a rotation is worth running.

The table sets out a twelve-week structure at one session a week. At two sessions a week the same structure runs in six weeks or covers twice as many topics, which is the choice a family makes when deciding how much to spend. The important feature is not the specific weeks but that every topic returns, and that the rotation is written down so both the student and the family can see what has been visited and when.

sections.heading: Scheduling the paper pair separately
paragraphs: Both boards set two papers, and they are different examinations in everything but content. One is shorter and structured, carrying a wide spread of topics in brief multi-part questions. The other carries fewer, longer questions with more steps each. Practising them interchangeably trains neither properly.

The structured paper rewards breadth and speed, and the useful practice is mixed sets of short questions under tight time. The longer paper rewards sustained working and is where method marks matter most, because more steps mean more places a slip can be followed through if the working is visible. The useful practice there is fewer questions with full solutions written out and marked against the scheme.

That distinction should shape a schedule. In a post-mock block, alternate: one session on a structured paper and the targeted repair it produces, the next on a long paper and its marking. A student who only ever practises long questions runs out of time on the short paper; one who only practises short questions loses the thread on the long one.

There is a further consideration where a specification sets a non-calculator component. A non-calculator paper has to be practised genuinely without a calculator, which students resist and which cannot be fudged. Fluency for it is built by short frequent drills across months, so it belongs in the rotation rather than in the final block, and what remains available late is timing: measuring how long the paper takes and deciding question order deliberately.

sections.heading: Why mathematics revision decays and what actually prevents it
paragraphs: Two things are going on when a student forgets how to complete the square. The first is ordinary forgetting, which affects every subject. The second is specific to procedural knowledge: a method is a sequence of decisions, and a sequence that has not been executed recently becomes unreliable in the middle even when the beginning and end are remembered. That is why a student can start a question confidently and stall at step three.

Retrieval, rather than review, is what holds a procedure in place. Reading through worked solutions feels productive and produces very little retention, because recognition is easier than recall and the student mistakes one for the other. Attempting a question cold, getting it wrong, and then correcting it produces far more durable retention than reading the same question's solution twice.

Spacing matters as much as retrieval. A topic revisited after a week, then three weeks, then six, holds better than the same total time spent in one block, and the effect is large enough to be worth structuring a plan around. This is the entire justification for the twelve-week rotation above, and it is also why a tutor who re-teaches the current chapter each week is not building retention even when the sessions go well.

The practical test a family can apply is simple. Ask whether your child could, cold and without warning, complete a reverse percentage question, a bounds-in-division question and a frequency density calculation. If the answer is no for a topic taught a year ago, revision has been review rather than retrieval, and the plan needs changing rather than extending.

sections.heading: The November series for a single subject
paragraphs: UAE candidates have two sittings a year available, which matters more in mathematics than in most subjects because mathematics is frequently the one subject a student wants to improve. Cambridge runs June and November. Pearson runs May/June and November. The February and March series is offered to India only and should be disregarded by an Abu Dhabi family.

A single-subject November entry is the easiest block in this market to scope. Two papers, a known starting performance, and a fixed end date roughly three months after results. The work is specific: identify from the June performance where the marks went, rebuild those strands properly rather than revising everything, and sit several timed papers.

What wastes the opportunity is delay. The decision window opens with results in August and families routinely spend four to six weeks deciding, which converts a comfortable block into a compressed one. The practical rule is to decide within a fortnight of results and begin immediately, even if the formal entry is confirmed slightly later through the exam centre.

Sourced anchors for planning: the Pearson International GCSE November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026. Read the live timetable on the board's own site rather than any date restated here, and confirm the entry route and the centre's zone with the school or the exam centre.

sections.heading: The bridge to the next course, and when to build it
paragraphs: Mathematics is the subject where the transition out of International GCSE is steepest, and the timing of that preparation is a calendar question too. A student going on to Cambridge AS Level or to IB Analysis and Approaches at higher level faces an immediate increase in algebraic demand in the first weeks of the new course, and the students who cope are the ones whose Year 11 foundations were secure rather than crammed.

The window for building that bridge is the summer between the two courses, and it is almost universally unused. A short block across those weeks on algebraic fluency, function notation, trigonometric identities and, where relevant, an introduction to differentiation makes the first term of the next course a consolidation rather than a scramble. Where a school offers Additional Mathematics 0606, that course does most of this work already and is the better route.

There is a specific trap for students moving into the IB Diploma. Analysis and Approaches at higher level assumes fluent algebraic manipulation from the first month and sets a non-calculator paper, and a student arriving from a calculator-heavy Year 11 has never built that fluency. The gap appears in October of the first Diploma year, which is a bad time to discover it, and closing it then competes with five other new subjects.

For a family deciding where to spend, the summer bridge is unusually good value: short, low-pressure, and aimed at the exact skills the next course assumes rather than at content anybody will teach again. It is also the only block on this page that can be scheduled with certainty, because it does not have to fit around a school timetable.

sections.heading: Fitting the rotation into a Yas Island week
paragraphs: A rotation only works if the sessions in it actually happen, week after week, which makes slot resilience more important here than in a block that runs for six weeks. Campuses serving Yas Island finish their taught day between about 14:45 and 15:30, with co-curricular sessions running later on some days. A student at an island campus is often home by 15:45; a student travelling to Khalifa City or Al Raha is typically not home before 16:15 and later on an activity day.

Allowing three quarters of an hour at home, that means a 16:30 start is workable from an island campus and 17:30 is the honest earliest from a mainland one. Our Abu Dhabi scheduling range runs from 16:30 to 21:00 Gulf Standard Time. For a twelve-week rotation the slot to choose is the one that survives an activity day, a busy event weekend and a tired Thursday, which in practice means 18:00 or 18:30.

Two local factors deserve planning. The island's event calendar, including the Grand Prix weekend at the end of the first term, changes access and road conditions and would cost an in-home arrangement several sessions a year. And Ramadan, which shifts roughly eleven days earlier each year and therefore periodically lands in the Year 11 spring, shortens school days and moves the usable window to post-Iftar slots. Both are manageable in a plan and disruptive in an improvised arrangement.

For context on cost, published market bands put in-home one-to-one at AED 180-500 an hour with travel included against AED 150-300 for a qualified subject tutor working online. Bestimate quotes AED 180-350 for in-home, Unitors lists International GCSE from AED 150, TutorChase quotes AED 270, and entry-level online runs AED 45-150 with EdFlik from AED 45-65 and Tutopiya from AED 33-52. Those are attributed market figures, not our prices, and IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE.
