process.description: A marked mock with annotations. It shows whether losses are clustered or scattered, whether the paper was finished, and which early-taught topics have decayed. The grade alone hides every one of those distinctions.

process.title: Choose the shape: rotation or block
process.description: A twelve-week retrieval rotation if the problem is decay across several topics. A post-mock paper block if the problem is technique. A tier evidence piece if the ceiling is the problem. Those are three different purchases and the mock script says which.

process.title: Take the free trial lesson
process.description: A full one-to-one session over live video at no cost and with no card details taken. Judge it on whether the tutor asked for the topic sequence and the tier before anything else, and whether they tested recall cold rather than reviewing worked examples.

process.title: Keep the rotation written down
process.description: A rotation only works if every topic returns on schedule, which means the schedule has to exist on paper and be visible to the family. Ask to see which topics have been visited and when. That is the checkable artefact of this kind of plan.

whyPoints.title: Built around decay, not coverage
whyPoints.description: Mathematics is procedural, so topics taught early and never revisited are gone rather than faded. We plan rotations in which each topic returns before it is lost, which is a different structure from a weekly session that follows the school a few days behind.

whyPoints.title: The school's topic order asked for first
whyPoints.description: A mock score is uninterpretable without it, because a low score on an untaught topic and a low score on a decayed one call for opposite responses. Schools in Abu Dhabi sequence mathematics very differently, so this cannot be assumed.

whyPoints.title: The tier treated as an evidence question
whyPoints.description: Where a grade ceiling is the real problem, a tutor can have the student sit one higher-tier paper under conditions and produce a written list of the content a move would require. That is a better conversation with a school than an assertion.

whyPoints.title: The two papers practised separately
whyPoints.description: A structured paper and a long multi-step paper reward different skills, and practising them interchangeably trains neither. In a block we alternate deliberately, and a non-calculator component is practised genuinely without a calculator.

whyPoints.title: Retrieval rather than review
whyPoints.description: Attempting a question cold and correcting it produces far more durable retention than reading the same worked solution twice. Sessions are built on cold attempts, which is less comfortable and measurably more effective.

whyPoints.title: Delivery and claims stated plainly
whyPoints.description: Lessons for Abu Dhabi families are delivered one-to-one over live video; IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. We hold no approval, accreditation or partnership from ADEK, the Ministry of Education, MoHRE, Cambridge or Pearson, and no UAE office.

faqs.question: Why does my child forget maths topics they once knew well?
faqs.answer: Because mathematics is procedural, and a procedure is a sequence of decisions rather than a fact. A sequence that has not been executed recently becomes unreliable in the middle even when the start and finish are remembered, which is why a student can begin a question confidently and stall at the third step. Ordinary forgetting affects every subject; this specific failure mode is what makes untouched maths topics genuinely gone rather than merely hazy after a year.

faqs.question: Why does a tutor need my Yas Island school's topic sequence?
faqs.answer: Because without it a mock score cannot be interpreted. A low trigonometry score may mean the student has a gap, or it may mean the sine and cosine rules have not been taught yet, and those two situations call for opposite responses. Abu Dhabi campuses sequence mathematics very differently: some finish the harder trigonometry in Year 10, others leave it until the spring of Year 11. One email to the department usually produces the order.

faqs.question: When is the maths tier decision genuinely still open?
faqs.answer: Through Year 10, and it narrows sharply once Year 11 begins. Schools typically set the tier on Year 9 and early Year 10 evidence, and it is reviewable for a period after that. What makes a late move expensive is that Extended and Higher papers set content the lower tier never covers, so a move upward in the spring of Year 11 means acquiring a body of teaching while revising five other subjects. By then the option has effectively closed.

faqs.question: What is a retrieval rotation and why use one instead of topic blocks?
faqs.answer: A rotation covers short segments of several topics in each session and brings each topic back on a schedule chosen so it returns before it is lost. Topic blocks feel orderly and fight the way mathematics is retained, because a topic covered intensively for a week and then abandoned for eight has decayed again by the examination. The total time spent is similar; the retention is not comparable. Twelve weeks at one session a week allows four visits to the highest-risk topics.

faqs.question: Should the two maths papers be practised differently?
faqs.answer: Yes. The shorter structured paper rewards breadth and speed, so the useful practice is mixed sets of short questions under tight time. The longer multi-step paper rewards sustained working and visible method, so the useful practice is fewer questions with full solutions written out and marked against the scheme. A student who only practises long questions runs out of time on the short paper, and one who only practises short questions loses the thread on the long one.

faqs.question: How do I test whether my child's maths revision is actually working?
faqs.answer: Ask them, cold and without warning, to do a reverse percentage question, a bounds-in-division question and a frequency density calculation. All three are typically taught early and examined every series. If they cannot, revision has been review rather than retrieval: reading worked solutions feels productive because recognition is easier than recall, and students mistake one for the other. Attempting cold and correcting is what builds durable retention.

faqs.question: Which maths topics decay fastest in an Abu Dhabi IGCSE cohort?
faqs.answer: The ones taught early and never revisited: reverse percentages, bounds and limits of accuracy, cumulative frequency with unequal-width histograms, and the mechanical side of algebraic manipulation. Algebra is a special case because it is used constantly inside other topics, so its decay is masked and shows up as scattered single-mark losses across a whole paper rather than as a visibly weak topic. That pattern is diagnosable from one marked mock.

faqs.question: Is Additional Mathematics 0606 different in how it should be timed?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the one maths entry where a continuous weekly arrangement is genuinely the right purchase. The content is entirely a Year 11 body: calculus, binomial expansion, trigonometric identities and matrices, met a year earlier than usual, with multi-step questions that offer no scaffolding. There is no Year 10 runway to build on and no realistic late block that can cover it, so the work has to run weekly from the first term.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send maths tutors to Yas Island addresses?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE, including Yas Island; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Abu Dhabi families are taught one-to-one over live video. For a twelve-week rotation that format matters practically: the plan depends on sessions happening every week, and the island's event calendar, including the Grand Prix weekend at the end of the first term, would cost an arrangement that depends on a drive several of them.

faqs.question: How should a November maths resit be planned?
faqs.answer: Decide within a fortnight of August results and start immediately. A single-subject resit is unusually easy to scope: two papers, a known starting performance, and a fixed end date about three months out. The work is to identify from the June performance where the marks went, rebuild those strands properly rather than revising everything, and sit several timed papers. What wastes the opportunity is spending four to six weeks deciding.

faqs.question: What should the summer before AS Level or the IB Diploma be used for?
faqs.answer: A short bridge block on algebraic fluency, function notation, trigonometric identities and, where relevant, an introduction to differentiation. The transition out of International GCSE mathematics is the steepest in the British track, and Analysis and Approaches at higher level in particular assumes fluent algebra from the first month alongside a non-calculator paper. A student arriving from a calculator-heavy Year 11 discovers that gap in October, which is a bad time to find it.

faqs.question: Can sessions keep running during Ramadan and event weekends on the island?
faqs.answer: Yes, and a rotation needs them to. Ramadan shifts roughly eleven days earlier each year and therefore periodically lands in the Year 11 spring, shortening school days and moving the usable window to post-Iftar slots. Yas Island event weekends change access and road conditions at exactly the hours a session would run. Because lessons are delivered over live video, both are a matter of moving a slot rather than losing a session.

faqs.question: How long should an IGCSE maths session be during a rotation?
faqs.answer: Sixty minutes works well for rotation sessions, because the structure is short segments across several topics rather than one long piece of work. Ninety minutes is needed for a post-mock paper block, where the unit is a paper sat under conditions plus the marking, and cutting the marking defeats the purpose. Short frequent drills on non-calculator fluency can be as little as forty-five minutes, because repetition matters more than duration for that specific skill.

faqs.question: What time can a Yas Island student realistically start a maths session?
faqs.answer: A student at a campus on the island itself is often home by about 15:45, which makes 16:30 workable. A student travelling to the Khalifa City or Al Raha corridor is typically not home until 16:15 or later, so 17:30 is the honest earliest. Our Abu Dhabi range runs 16:30 to 21:00 Gulf Standard Time, and for a twelve-week rotation the slot worth choosing is the one that survives an activity day and a tired Thursday, usually 18:00 or 18:30.

faqs.question: What is the single best-timed maths purchase across the two years?
faqs.answer: A short block early in Year 10 on the skills that compound, chiefly algebraic manipulation, followed by a retrieval rotation in Year 11 that keeps the early topics alive. That sequence costs less in total than a continuous two-year weekly arrangement and produces more, because it targets the one property that makes mathematics different from every other subject on the timetable: untouched procedures decay, and rebuilding them late competes with everything else.

abu-dhabi/igcse-maths-tutor-in-yas-islan.closingHeading: Plan for decay, not for coverage
abu-dhabi/igcse-maths-tutor-in-yas-islan.closingBody: Ask your child's school for the mathematics topic sequence and the tier, then test cold recall on one topic taught a year ago. If it has gone, the problem is retention rather than understanding, and the answer is a rotation that brings each topic back before it is lost rather than more hours on the current chapter. IB Gram teaches Abu Dhabi students one-to-one over live video, plans against the school's own sequence, keeps the rotation written down, and starts with a free trial lesson and no card details taken.

abu-dhabi/igcse-may-june-exam-preparatio.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE subjects at Core and Extended tier for candidates sitting the summer series. Each one works from the published syllabus and assessment objectives for the specification your child's centre entered, and marks written work against the same criteria an examiner applies.

intro.heading: What June asks of an Abu Dhabi IGCSE candidate
paragraphs: The summer series is the busiest point in the international school year, and it is also the point at which the smallest administrative details start deciding grades. An Abu Dhabi candidate sitting Cambridge IGCSE in June is entered by their school months earlier, at a tier the school chose, on a timetable version assigned to the centre's administrative zone, with a seating plan that may run two papers in one day. None of that is negotiable in May. What is negotiable is how prepared the candidate is for the specific demands of the papers they have actually been entered for.

Most families arrive at this page with a general worry: the mocks were disappointing, or a subject has drifted, and June is coming. The useful first move is to narrow the worry into a list. Which board, which specification code, which tier, which optional papers, which day. A Year 11 pupil at a British-curriculum school in Al Mushrif may be sitting Cambridge 0580 Extended maths and 0654 Coordinated Sciences, while a classmate who moved from a different system sits Pearson Edexcel International GCSE 4MA1 and separate sciences. Those two candidates need different preparation even though both would describe themselves as doing IGCSE maths and science in June.

Abu Dhabi adds its own rhythm to the term. The emirate's private schools answer to the Department of Education and Knowledge, which licenses them, inspects them and publishes the ADEK inspection rating that most parents in Khalifa City or Saadiyat compare before enrolling. Term dates, study-leave weeks and internal mock windows vary between the island schools and the Khalifa City and Al Raha corridor, so a revision plan copied from a sibling's school two years ago rarely matches this year's calendar. An Abu Dhabi IGCSE revision plan has to be built from the candidate's own centre dates.

There is also the simple matter of where the family is in August. Results for the summer series arrive in the second half of August, when a large share of Abu Dhabi families are travelling. Pearson sent June 2026 International GCSE results to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, which is the kind of date worth putting in a calendar in March rather than discovering from a group chat. Knowing it early changes what you do with the last fortnight of preparation, because a candidate who understands that the summer has a hard stop works differently from one who believes the subject continues in September.

IB Gram's part in this is narrow and deliberate. We match one student to one subject specialist, and that specialist teaches online over live video. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Abu Dhabi or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. For a June candidate that constraint is an advantage rather than a compromise, because the tutor is chosen for having taught the exact specification and tier, not for living within a twenty-minute drive of Al Bateen. The sections below set out the calendar, the papers, the tiering decision, the market rates, the mandatory UAE subjects that keep running alongside, and the boundaries a tutor must not cross.

abu-dhabi/igcse-may-june-exam-preparatio.programmesIntro: Three qualifications sit behind the phrase 'IGCSE' in Abu Dhabi, and a candidate's school may use more than one of them across a timetable. The specification code on the entry confirmation is what decides the papers, so it is the first thing a tutor asks for.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: The four-digit syllabus codes most Abu Dhabi British-curriculum schools use: 0580 Mathematics, 0625 Physics, 0620 Chemistry, 0610 Biology, 0654 Coordinated Sciences, 0500 English First Language. Most subjects are tiered, with Core and Extended routes carrying different grade ceilings and different papers. Cambridge runs the exams in a June series and a November series, with Checkpoint tests in March, May and October.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi centres are assigned to one of six Cambridge administrative zones, and the zone decides which version of the timetable applies. Cambridge is explicit that a centre must use the correct version and states it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after working from the wrong one. For a family juggling two children at two schools on the island, that is a live risk worth checking in writing.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Codes run in the 4xx1 pattern: 4MA1 Mathematics, 4PH1 Physics, 4CH1 Chemistry, 4BI1 Biology, 4EA1 English Language A. Papers are untiered in several subjects, which changes the preparation question from 'which tier' to 'which optional paper'. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE exams are available in May/June and November each year, and Pearson publishes provisional timetables for future series ahead of time.
programmes.countryNote: Several Abu Dhabi schools enter maths with Pearson and sciences with Cambridge, or move a cohort between boards after a curriculum review. A pupil who transferred from Al Reem Island to Khalifa City mid-course can therefore be sitting a different specification from the one they were taught in Year 10. Checking the board on this year's entry confirmation, rather than last year's reports, prevents a term of preparation aimed at the wrong paper.

programmes.name: Cambridge O Level
programmes.description: Still entered by a minority of Abu Dhabi centres, usually alongside IGCSE subjects rather than instead of them. Content overlaps heavily with the matching IGCSE syllabus, but the paper structure, the availability of coursework alternatives and the practical assessment arrangements differ. Cambridge runs O Level in the same June and November series as IGCSE, on the same zoned timetables.
programmes.countryNote: Where an Abu Dhabi school enters a mixed timetable, a candidate can end up with two different paper patterns in one week of June. The practical consequence is scheduling: revision for an O Level paper and an IGCSE paper in the same subject area cannot be treated as interchangeable, and a tutor needs the entry confirmation to tell them apart before the first session rather than halfway through the term.

programmes.name: Cambridge International AS Level
programmes.description: The step most Abu Dhabi IGCSE candidates take next, and the reason a June grade matters beyond the certificate. AS content assumes fluency with the Extended tier material, particularly in maths and the sciences, so a candidate who scraped a grade by avoiding whole topics starts Year 12 with a gap. International AS Level runs in June and November series like IGCSE.
programmes.countryNote: For UAE Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track, a student must show five accredited IGCSE or GCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, plus one accredited Advanced Level subject at grade E or above, or two subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic Education are not counted among the five. That rule is why the June subject spread, not only the headline grades, is worth planning.

abu-dhabi/igcse-may-june-exam-preparatio.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Abu Dhabi families most often ask about in the spring term, with the specification codes and the part of each paper where marks are most often left behind. A tutor's first job is to find which of these applies to your child, not to cover all of them.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: 0580 Paper 4 is the Extended structured paper and the one where method marks are won or lost. Candidates lose marks for unshown working on multi-step questions, for rounding too early in trigonometry and bearings, and for mishandling the inequality and transformation topics that Core candidates never meet. A session typically starts with a marked past paper rather than a topic list.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 / Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.description: Extended candidates sit the long structured paper plus a practical-skills component. The alternative to practical paper rewards experimental reasoning on paper: reading a scale correctly, identifying the controlled variable, explaining why a repeat reading matters. Electricity circuits and moments cause the most repeated errors, usually because the candidate was taught the formula and never the diagram.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 / Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.description: Mole calculations, ionic equations and organic reaction pathways account for a large share of lost Extended marks. Candidates who can recite a definition still drop marks on 'explain' questions because they describe an observation instead of giving a reason. Qualitative analysis tables reward precision in language, and that is teachable in two or three focused sessions.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 / Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.description: The content volume makes Biology feel safe and then costs marks on command terms. 'Describe' and 'explain' carry different mark allocations, and data-response questions on enzymes, transport and osmosis reward candidates who quote figures from the stimulus. Genetics crosses and the carbon cycle are where Extended candidates most often write around the answer.

subjects.name: Coordinated Sciences (Cambridge 0654)
subjects.description: One grade covering biology, chemistry and physics, usually entered where a timetable cannot fit three separate sciences. The trap is uneven preparation: a candidate strong in biology can carry a weak physics section a long way before the papers expose it. Mapping which of the three sections is dragging the mark down is the first diagnostic a tutor runs.

subjects.name: English First Language (Cambridge 0500 / Pearson 4EA1)
subjects.description: Reading questions reward close handling of the passage; directed writing rewards register and audience. Abu Dhabi candidates who read widely in English still lose marks for summarising instead of analysing, and for writing a composition that ignores the stated form. Two marked pieces with criterion-referenced feedback usually move a grade more than a term of general reading.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510)
subjects.description: A different qualification from First Language with a different mark scheme, and the one many Abu Dhabi pupils are entered for after joining a British-curriculum school mid-phase. Listening and speaking components carry real weight, and the writing task is assessed on task fulfilment as much as on accuracy. Work is best split between accuracy drills and timed task practice.

subjects.name: Economics (Cambridge 0455)
subjects.description: The structured data-response paper is where candidates with good notes underperform, because the questions ask for applied analysis of the extract rather than recalled definitions. Elasticity, market failure and the exchange-rate questions reward diagrams drawn and labelled under time pressure. UAE-context examples are usually welcome and rarely rehearsed.

subjects.name: Business Studies (Cambridge 0450)
subjects.description: Case-study questions carry the highest mark tariffs and the highest variance. Candidates lose marks by giving generic advantages and disadvantages instead of judgement grounded in the case material. Evaluation is a skill with a visible structure, and practising it against a marked response is faster than re-reading the textbook chapter.

subjects.name: Computer Science (Cambridge 0478)
subjects.description: Theory paper marks go on data representation, networks and security; the problem-solving paper rewards clean pseudocode and trace tables. Candidates who code fluently in a real language often lose marks for writing that language instead of the pseudocode conventions in the syllabus. Trace-table discipline is the single most repeatable gain here.

subjects.name: Arabic as a First Language (Cambridge 0508)
subjects.description: Sat alongside the mandatory Arabic provision an Abu Dhabi school must deliver, and assessed on comprehension, summary and extended writing in Standard Arabic. Candidates who speak a dialect at home frequently lose marks on register rather than on content. Preparation is best timetabled separately from the school's own Arabic periods so the two do not duplicate.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics (Cambridge 0606)
subjects.description: Entered by Abu Dhabi schools that want a bridge into International AS Level maths. Content reaches calculus, vectors and advanced trigonometry, and the paper gives no credit for a correct answer reached by a method the question did not permit. Candidates sitting 0580 Extended and 0606 in the same June need the two revision streams kept distinct.

abu-dhabi/igcse-may-june-exam-preparatio.regionsIntro: Abu Dhabi's school catchments behave differently in exam term, and the difference is mostly about travel and timetable rather than curriculum. These are the communities families most often name when booking a summer-series plan, with the detail that actually affects session timing.

regions.name: Al Mushrif
regions.note: Long-established island community around some of the emirate's oldest British-curriculum provision. Families here often have two children in different key stages at the same school, so sessions are usually booked back to back in a single evening slot rather than spread across the week.

regions.name: Al Bateen
regions.note: A dense cluster of schools and a correspondingly slow 2.30pm to 3.30pm pick-up window. A 4pm session start is unrealistic for most Al Bateen families in term time; 5pm or later holds up far better once study leave begins and the school run stops.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: Newer international provision with a long bridge commute to the island's business district. Parents frequently work through to 6pm, so summer-series sessions are booked at 6.30pm or 7pm with the parent joining for the last five minutes to hear the week's diagnosis.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: Villa communities feeding several large private schools, with a school-bus run that can take fifty minutes door to door. Afternoon sessions work badly here and mid-morning works well during study leave, which is when most Khalifa City candidates do their best timed-paper practice.

regions.name: Al Raha Gardens and Al Raha Beach
regions.note: A compact corridor with a short school run and a settled 4.30pm rhythm in term time. Families here tend to book two shorter sessions a week rather than one long one, which suits timed-paper work in the final six weeks before the first paper.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: High-rise living with school provision arriving faster than the road network. The practical consequence is that a candidate's quiet study space is often a bedroom rather than a study, so screen-share work and a shared digital whiteboard matter more here than in the villa communities.

regions.name: Yas Island
regions.note: A newer catchment where a sizeable share of pupils joined mid-course from another system. Board and tier checks matter disproportionately on Yas, because a pupil taught one specification in Year 10 may well be entered for another in Year 11.

regions.name: Al Shamkha and Al Falah
regions.note: Mainland communities with longer journeys to the island schools and a strong preference for evening scheduling. Online delivery removes the second commute entirely, which is the difference between four sessions a month and four sessions attempted.

schoolClusters.city: Abu Dhabi island
schoolClusters.note: The island schools carry the longest-established British-curriculum IGCSE cohorts in the emirate, and their internal mock calendars tend to sit in January and again shortly before study leave. Students we support sit Cambridge and Pearson specifications across these centres; the entry confirmation is what tells us which.
schools: American Community School of Abu Dhabi

schoolClusters.city: Khalifa City and the Al Raha corridor
schoolClusters.note: Larger year groups, more mixed-board timetables and a bus-driven day that pushes tutoring into the evening. Several centres here run two-week internal exam blocks in the spring term, which is the natural point to switch a plan from content coverage to timed-paper work.

schoolClusters.city: Saadiyat, Yas and Al Reem
schoolClusters.note: The newer catchments, with a high proportion of pupils who joined mid-phase from another curriculum. Transition gaps show up most clearly in maths and the sciences, where a candidate may never have met a topic the specification assumes was covered in Year 10.

The pattern suits a candidate whose grade is close to the target but inconsistent, because it gives enough contact time to work through a topic properly and still mark a paper every few weeks. It works when the target is specific, and works badly as a substitute for a term of teaching, so a tutor will say plainly if a candidate's gap is too wide for a block to close.

Families use it when a school report says a grade is at risk and gives no detail, or when deciding whether tutoring is needed at all. There is no expectation of booking further sessions and the written diagnosis is yours to take to the school.

sections.heading: The summer series, counted backwards from the first paper
paragraphs: IGCSE May June exam preparation in Abu Dhabi works properly only when it is planned from the end. The first paper is a fixed point, and everything that matters sits at a known distance from it: the entry deadline, the tier decision, the last point at which a coursework or practical component can still be addressed, the final internal exam, the start of study leave. Working forwards from January produces a plan that runs out of time in April. Working backwards from the first paper produces a plan where the timed-paper work happens when the candidate can actually benefit from it.

The dates themselves belong to the centre, not to the family and not to a tutoring platform. Cambridge publishes its series timetables by administrative zone and expects the exams officer to use the correct version; Pearson publishes provisional timetables for future series and final timetables closer to the sitting. Neither publishes a single date that applies to every Abu Dhabi candidate, which is why the table below names who sets each milestone and where to confirm it rather than printing a date that would be wrong for half the readers. Pearson's November 2026 series shows the lead times involved: the final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026, entries close months earlier in the year, and November 2025 results only reached students on 22 January 2026. The Cambridge June series works to the same rhythm from the other half of the calendar, with entries closing in the spring term and the binding date issued to each candidate on a statement of entry rather than announced as one national deadline.

What a family can do in March is narrow. What a family can do in January is wide. The gap between those two statements is the entire argument for starting a summer-series plan in the winter term rather than after the Easter break. A candidate who begins in January can still change how they handle a whole paper; a candidate who begins in April is choosing which two topics to rescue. Both are worth doing, and a tutor should tell you honestly which conversation you are having.

The practical output of this section is a one-page Abu Dhabi IGCSE revision plan with the candidate's own dates on it: board, specification code, tier, paper dates from the centre's timetable version, the school's internal exam block, study leave, and the results date. Every session then has a place on that page. Without it, a term of tutoring becomes a sequence of topics chosen by whatever felt weakest that week.

sections.heading: The timetable-zone trap, and why it bites harder here
paragraphs: Cambridge allocates every exam centre to one of six administrative zones, and each zone gets its own version of the series timetable. The guidance to exams officers is blunt about the consequence: it is essential to use the correct version, and Cambridge states it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam because the wrong zone's timetable was used. That is a sentence worth reading twice, because it places the risk on the centre and the family rather than on the board.

In Abu Dhabi this matters more than it does in a single-country system. Families here routinely compare notes across schools, across emirates and across countries. A cousin in Karachi, a former classmate in Nairobi and a neighbour whose child sits at a different Abu Dhabi centre may all be looking at a Cambridge June timetable with the same subject on a different day or at a different start time. Group chats transmit those differences with great speed and no context, and a candidate who has rehearsed the wrong afternoon has lost something that no amount of content revision recovers.

The fix costs one email. Ask the exams officer for the centre's own timetable version, in writing, with the candidate's seat and session times, and put it on the family calendar rather than in a folder. Then check the pattern for clashes a candidate will feel: two papers in one day, a practical component the morning after a long structured paper, a long gap in the middle of the window where momentum tends to be lost.

A tutor uses that document directly. If 0580 Paper 4 falls on the second morning of the window and the Chemistry structured paper lands two days later, the last fortnight of sessions is sequenced around that, and the final session before each paper is spent on the specific skill that paper opens with. Planning the last three weeks without the real timetable is guesswork dressed up as revision.
bullets: Request the centre's own timetable version in writing from the exams officer
Check for two papers in a single day and for practical components placed after long papers
Do not rely on a timetable shared by a family at another centre or in another country
Put the session times, not just the dates, on the family calendar

sections.heading: Where the June marks actually go, paper by paper
paragraphs: A grade is not lost evenly across a paper. It is lost in identifiable places, and most of those places are about technique rather than knowledge. The pattern repeats year after year across Abu Dhabi cohorts: unshown working in multi-step maths questions, 'explain' answered as 'describe', data-response questions answered from memory instead of from the extract, experimental-reasoning marks dropped because the candidate was never taught to read a question as an experimental design problem.

This is why a first session with a tutor is usually spent marking rather than teaching. A past paper the candidate has already sat, marked question by question against the published mark scheme, produces a ranked list of error types with the marks attached to each. That list is a plan. A topic checklist from the syllabus is not a plan, because it treats a candidate who loses eight marks on rounding and a candidate who loses eight marks on circuit diagrams as if they needed the same term.

The alternative to practical paper in the Cambridge sciences deserves separate mention because it is so widely mis-prepared. It is not a theory paper and it is not a laboratory exam. It rewards a candidate who can describe how an experiment would be controlled, identify the variable that must be held constant, explain why a repeat reading improves reliability and read a scale to the stated precision. Candidates who have done the practical work in school often still lose these marks, because doing an experiment and writing about experimental design are different skills.

sections.heading: Core or Extended: the June ceiling is set before the exam
paragraphs: In a tiered Cambridge subject, the tier decides the grade ceiling, and the decision is made by the school at entry. A Core candidate in 0580 is working towards the grades available on that route; the IGCSE Extended tier opens the higher grades and asks for content the Core papers never touch. By March the decision is usually fixed. By November of the previous year it is still a conversation, which is why families who think about tier early have options that families who think about it late do not.

The honest version of this conversation is uncomfortable but short. An Extended entry that a candidate cannot access produces a low grade and a demoralising summer. A Core entry for a candidate who could have managed Extended produces a ceiling that may block a sixth-form subject choice or complicate a Ministry of Education equivalency file later. Neither error is rare, and both are usually visible in a marked paper months in advance.

What a tutor can contribute here is evidence rather than an opinion. Give a candidate an Extended paper under timed conditions, mark it against the published scheme, and look at where the marks sit. A candidate scoring steadily across the paper and stalling only on the final questions is an Extended candidate who needs the top end taught. A candidate losing marks uniformly from question three onwards is telling you something different. That evidence is what a head of department can act on, and it is more useful to the school than a parental request.

Where the tier is already fixed and is the wrong one, the work changes rather than stops. A Core candidate can still be taught to secure every mark available on the Core papers, which is a real and achievable target. A candidate on an Extended entry they cannot access is taught to bank the accessible half of each paper rather than spreading effort thinly across material that will not yield marks in June.

sections.heading: Online, in-home or a centre group: the comparison for an Abu Dhabi family
paragraphs: Home tutoring is the default assumption in Abu Dhabi, and it is a reasonable one. An in-home tutor is familiar, supervisable and requires no technology. The costs are real too, and they are mostly invisible on a rate card: travel time priced into the hourly rate, a 4pm slot that cannot start until 4.40pm because of the Corniche traffic, a cancelled session when the tutor's own commute fails, and a tutor pool limited to people who happen to live within driving distance of your community.

That last point is the one that decides grades. The pool of people in Abu Dhabi who can teach Cambridge 0606 Additional Mathematics to Extended standard, or mark a 0455 data-response paper the way an examiner would, is small. The pool willing to drive to Al Shamkha on a Tuesday evening for a 5pm start is smaller again. Online delivery removes the geography from the matching problem, so the question becomes who has taught this specification rather than who is nearby.

IB Gram does not send a tutor to an Abu Dhabi address, and does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service exists only in India. Every UAE lesson runs online, one-to-one, over live video with a shared whiteboard and screen sharing, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time. Saying so plainly is better than discovering it after a booking. The comparison below is the honest version, including the parts where in-home has the advantage.

Market rates are included for context and are not IB Gram's prices. The ranges come from published rate cards and cost surveys read in October 2026, and they vary with the tutor's experience, the subject, the level and the session length rather than with the emirate. For IB Gram's own figure, the free first lesson and the consultation that follows are the right place to ask.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies keep running through exam term
paragraphs: A June revision plan built only around IGCSE subjects will collide with the mandatory UAE provision, because that provision does not pause. Federal rules require private schools to deliver Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside whatever international curriculum they are licensed to teach, and to follow the Ministry's general regulations on them. A Year 11 candidate therefore has periods in the week that are not revision periods and cannot be treated as spare capacity.

The most detailed public statement of how this works comes from Dubai's regulator rather than Abu Dhabi's. KHDA's mandatory-subjects guidance sets out that schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. It also sets instructional time on a forty-minute lesson unit, allows schools to vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and advises that no mandatory-subject lesson should run shorter than twenty-five minutes. Those are Dubai requirements; an Abu Dhabi family should ask their own school how ADEK's expectations are applied locally rather than assume the Dubai document governs them.

One rule from that guidance is worth knowing wherever you live, because it shapes what any tutor can offer. For the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited. A tutor supporting Arabic or Islamic Education therefore works with the school's own material and the Ministry's content, not with a parallel course of their own design. KHDA also requires schools to ensure that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold the appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects, which is a credential question a parent is entitled to ask of a school.

Practically, this means two things for a summer-series plan. Arabic as a first language candidates sitting Cambridge 0508 should have that preparation timetabled separately from the school's mandatory Arabic periods, so the two do not duplicate each other. And the weekly hours available for IGCSE revision should be counted after the mandatory periods, not before, which is usually the moment a family discovers that three subjects of tutoring a week was never going to fit.

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not do before the first paper
paragraphs: The line is simple and it is not negotiable. A tutor teaches, explains, marks and gives feedback on work the student has produced. A tutor does not become the author of anything a board will assess. For IGCSE that applies to any coursework or controlled-assessment component a specification still carries, and for students moving on to the Diploma it applies with even more force to internal assessments and the extended essay. Reviewing a draft and telling a student which criterion is unmet is teaching. Supplying the sentences is malpractice, and the consequence falls on the student.

Materials carry a similar boundary. Past papers, mark schemes, syllabus documents and grade-boundary tables belong to Cambridge, Pearson and the IB. A tutor references them, cites them and tells you where the official versions live; a tutor does not reproduce or distribute them as downloads. If your child's school has released a paper the candidate sat, that paper can be marked and discussed in a session. A request for an unreleased mark scheme is a request a tutor should refuse, and the refusal is a good sign about the tutor.

Then there is the permit question, which Abu Dhabi families ask more often than families elsewhere, and rightly. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated: the MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, it is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. MoHRE's own service page, 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing', lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time, applied for through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount should be quoted to you.

One Abu Dhabi-specific rule matters here. Press reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff describes a prohibition on teachers providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, with teachers tutoring outside school hours required to hold the MoHRE permit, whose code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. Verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy document before relying on it, but treat the principle as settled: your child's own classroom teacher is not the right person to hire privately.
bullets: A tutor reviews and marks the student's own work; the student is the sole author of assessed work
Official papers and mark schemes are cited and linked, never reproduced as downloads
The MoHRE private tuition work permit is free of charge and valid for two years
Do not hire your child's own school teacher for paid private lessons

sections.heading: If June does not go the way you planned
paragraphs: Results land in the second half of August, and a disappointing grade arrives at the least convenient moment of the year: the family is often abroad, the school is closed, and the deadline for doing something about it is closer than it looks. Deciding in March what you would do in August is not pessimism. It is the difference between a considered decision and a rushed one taken from a hotel lobby.

There are three routes, and they are not equivalent. A review of marking is a request through the centre, with a deadline set by the board and a cost attached; it makes sense where a grade sits a mark or two below a boundary and the script is out of pattern with everything else the candidate produced. A resit in the next available series is a fresh entry, and because Cambridge runs a November series as well as a June one, and Pearson offers International GCSE in November as well as May/June, a single weak subject does not necessarily cost a year. Repeating the whole year is the heaviest option and is sometimes the right one, usually when the problem is broader than one subject.

The equivalency question sits behind all of this for families who intend to apply to UAE universities. On the British track, the Ministry of Education requires five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic Education not counted among the five, plus one accredited Advanced Level subject at grade E or above or two Advanced Subsidiary Level subjects at the same grade. One ranking competitor page states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects; the sourced requirement is five. Check your own file against the Ministry's current guidance or the emirate's attestation authority, because IB Gram does not perform or guarantee equivalency and no tutoring is required for it.

What one-to-one support can do after a result is narrow and real: diagnose what the script says, decide with you whether a resit is a sensible use of a term, and teach the subject properly in the weeks available if it is. What it cannot do is promise a different grade. Any provider that offers you one in August is telling you something about themselves rather than about your child.

process.title: Send the entry confirmation
process.description: Not the report card. The document that names the board, the specification code, the tier and the optional papers, plus the centre's own timetable version. Five minutes of paperwork prevents a term of preparation aimed at the wrong paper, which is the commonest avoidable failure in summer-series tutoring.

process.title: Free first lesson
process.description: One session with a subject specialist, online over live video, with no card details taken and no obligation to continue. It is a teaching session rather than a sales call: the tutor works on something real and tells you afterwards what they found. If the match is wrong, say so and we change the tutor rather than the student.

process.title: A marked paper, not a topic list
process.description: Early in the engagement the candidate sits a past paper under timed conditions and the tutor marks it against the published scheme. The output is a ranked list of error types with the marks attached. That list, rather than the syllabus contents page, decides what the next six sessions cover.

process.title: Build the plan backwards
process.description: The candidate's own paper dates go on one page, with the school's internal exam block, study leave and the results date. Sessions are then placed against that calendar, so timed-paper work lands in the weeks when it helps and content teaching happens while there is still time to use it.

process.title: Weekly notes to the parent
process.description: After each session you get a short written note: what was covered, what the candidate got wrong, what was set, and whether the plan is still on track. No scores, no grade predictions, no percentages invented to look reassuring. If progress stalls, the note says so and proposes a change.

whyPoints.title: The specification, not the subject
whyPoints.description: A tutor is matched on having taught the exact specification and tier your child was entered for, because 0580 Extended, 4MA1 and 0606 are three different jobs. Online delivery is what makes that possible from Abu Dhabi: the match is made on teaching history rather than on driving distance from your community.

whyPoints.title: Marking against published criteria
whyPoints.description: Written work is marked the way the board's scheme marks it, with the criterion named for every mark awarded and withheld. A candidate who can see which three error types cost them eleven marks knows what to practise. A grade written at the top of a script tells them nothing they can act on.

whyPoints.title: Dates taken from your centre
whyPoints.description: Plans are built on the timetable version your child's centre actually uses, not a generic calendar. Given that Cambridge allocates centres to six administrative zones and states it cannot accept responsibility for candidates working from the wrong version, that is a safeguard rather than a nicety.

whyPoints.title: Honest about what we do not do
whyPoints.description: No home visits anywhere in the UAE, no authorship of assessed work, no reproduction of official papers or mark schemes, no claim to accreditation from ADEK, KHDA, the Ministry of Education, Cambridge or Pearson. IB Gram holds none of those approvals and says so rather than implying otherwise.

whyPoints.title: No grade promises
whyPoints.description: We will tell you what the marked evidence shows and what a term of work could realistically address. We will not promise a grade, a number of points, or an improvement figure, because nobody can honestly promise those and the providers who do are not describing your child's situation.

whyPoints.title: You keep the diagnosis
whyPoints.description: The marked scripts, the error lists and the session notes are yours. Take them to the school, use them in a parents' evening, or use them to decide that tutoring is not what this candidate needs. A diagnostic that only makes sense while you keep paying for it is not a diagnostic.

faqs.question: What does the May June IGCSE series look like from an Abu Dhabi exam centre?
faqs.answer: Your child's school is the exam centre, and it enters candidates with Cambridge, Pearson or both, months before the papers. Cambridge runs the exams as a June series and allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, each with its own timetable version. Pearson offers International GCSE in May/June and November. The practical consequence is that there is no single Abu Dhabi exam timetable: there is your centre's version, held by the exams officer. Ask for it in writing, with session times rather than just dates, and plan the final three weeks of preparation around it.

faqs.question: Why does my son's exam timetable differ from a cousin's in another country?
faqs.answer: Because Cambridge allocates each centre to one of six administrative zones and publishes a different version of the timetable for each. Papers can fall on different days or at different start times depending on the zone the centre sits in. Cambridge's guidance to exams officers is explicit that the correct version must be used and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after working from the wrong one. Timetables shared across family group chats are therefore unreliable. Only the version your child's own centre issues should go on the family calendar.

faqs.question: When do June International GCSE results reach students in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: In the second half of August, which for many Abu Dhabi families falls during travel. Pearson released June 2026 International GCSE results to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026. Cambridge publishes its own release dates per series. Because the window is short and the school may be closed, it is worth deciding in the spring term what you would do about a disappointing grade: request a review of marking through the centre, enter a resit in the November series, or accept the grade. That decision is easier made in March than from a hotel in August.

faqs.question: How many weeks before the June papers should one-to-one lessons start?
faqs.answer: If the aim is to change how a candidate handles a whole paper, start in the winter term, roughly twenty weeks out. That allows content teaching, a marked paper every few weeks, and six to eight weeks of timed work at the end. If you are starting after the Easter break, the honest aim is narrower: secure two or three topics and fix one error pattern that is costing repeated marks. Both are worth doing. A tutor should tell you plainly which of those two conversations your timeline allows rather than implying the shorter one does the work of the longer.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE papers cost Abu Dhabi candidates the most marks each June?
faqs.answer: The structured Extended papers, consistently. In 0580 Paper 4 the losses are method marks: unshown working, early rounding in trigonometry and bearings, and Extended-only topics that were quietly skipped. In the sciences it is the experimental-reasoning paper and the quantitative questions. In Economics and Business it is evaluation, where candidates list advantages instead of reaching a judgement grounded in the extract. Across all of them the single largest category is command-term handling: answering 'explain' as though it said 'describe'. All of those are technique failures, which is why they respond quickly to marked practice.

faqs.question: Is Paper 6 the same thing as a laboratory exam in the IGCSE sciences?
faqs.answer: No. The alternative to practical paper is a written paper about experimental work, not an assessment carried out in a laboratory. It rewards a candidate who can identify the variable that must be controlled, read a scale to the stated precision, explain why a repeat reading improves reliability, and spot the flaw in a described method. Candidates who have done plenty of practical work in school still lose these marks, because performing an experiment and writing about experimental design are separate skills. It is one of the most improvable components on the timetable, and usually one of the least rehearsed.

faqs.question: Can we still move our daughter from Core to Extended before the summer series?
faqs.answer: That is the school's decision, taken at entry, and by the spring term it is usually fixed. The conversation is live in the autumn and effectively closed once final entries are submitted. What helps is evidence rather than a request: give her a full Extended paper under timed conditions, have it marked against the published scheme, and look at where the marks sit. A candidate scoring steadily and stalling only at the top end is an Extended candidate. A head of department can act on a marked script in a way they cannot act on a parent's preference.

faqs.question: How do we confirm which board our Abu Dhabi school enters pupils with?
faqs.answer: Ask the exams officer for the entry confirmation, which names the board, the specification code, the tier and any optional papers for every subject. Do not infer it from the textbook, from an older sibling's experience, or from last year's reports, because schools move cohorts between boards after curriculum reviews and may use Cambridge for sciences and Pearson for maths in the same timetable. This matters most for pupils who joined mid-course from another school or another system, where the specification taught in Year 10 may not be the one entered in Year 11.

faqs.question: What may a tutor legally do with a past paper or a published mark scheme?
faqs.answer: Reference it, cite it and point you to the official source on the board's own site. Past papers, mark schemes, syllabus documents and grade-boundary tables are Cambridge's, Pearson's or the IB's property, and reproducing or distributing them is copyright infringement. A paper your child's school has released after they sat it can be marked and discussed in a session. A request for an unreleased mark scheme should be refused, and a tutor who refuses it is showing you something useful about how they work.

faqs.question: Does my child's Arabic and Islamic Education timetable pause for June study leave?
faqs.answer: Treat the answer as no until your school confirms otherwise. Federal rules require private schools to deliver Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies alongside their licensed international curriculum, and schools apply that through to the end of the taught year. The practical effect on planning is that the weekly hours available for IGCSE revision should be counted after the mandatory periods, not before. Families who count the other way round usually discover in April that three tutored subjects a week never fitted the timetable in the first place.

faqs.question: How does one-to-one support fit around an Abu Dhabi school's own revision programme?
faqs.answer: The school's clinics come first, because they are included in the fees and run by the people who know the cohort. Private support should fill what a group cannot: an individual error pattern, a topic the class has moved past, or the timed-paper practice a class of twenty-four cannot mark individually. In practice that means a tutor asks what the school is already covering and deliberately does not duplicate it. It also means that when study leave ends the school's programme stops, which is exactly when one-to-one sessions become most useful.

faqs.question: What happens in a first lesson before the June series work begins?
faqs.answer: It is a teaching session, not a consultation. The tutor works on something real with your child, usually a question or short paper in the weakest area, and then writes you a short note on what they found and what they would do about it. No card details are taken for that first lesson and there is no obligation to book a second. If the subject match or the personality match is wrong, we change the tutor rather than asking your child to adapt to one who does not suit them.

faqs.question: Does the tutor need a MoHRE permit confirmed before the first June session?
faqs.answer: Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers teachers in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Applications go through MoHRE's smart app, website and e-services system, under the service 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing', which lists a two-working-day completion time. Ask any tutor about their permit position directly; it is a fair question and the answer should be straightforward.

faqs.question: If the June result is not the one we need, what are the options from Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Three, and they differ in weight. A review of marking goes through the centre within the board's deadline and suits a grade sitting a mark or two below a boundary. A resit in the next series is a fresh entry, and because Cambridge runs a November series and Pearson offers International GCSE in November as well as May/June, one weak subject need not cost a year. Repeating the year is the heaviest option and sometimes the right one when the problem spans several subjects. Decide the order of preference in spring, not in the week results arrive.

faqs.question: How many subjects can realistically be supported in one spring term?
faqs.answer: One well, two with discipline, three rarely. Each subject needs a weekly session plus the written work between sessions, and a Year 11 candidate already has school homework, mandatory UAE subject periods, and internal exams in the same window. Families who book three subjects usually attend two and resent the third. The better approach is to rank the subjects by marks at risk, start with the one where a term of work moves the most, and add a second only once the first has settled into a rhythm the candidate actually keeps.

faqs.question: Do lessons run on Gulf Standard Time during the June study-leave weeks?
faqs.answer: Yes, and study leave is when scheduling gets easier rather than harder. With no school run, mid-morning sessions open up, which is when most candidates do their best timed-paper work. Lessons are scheduled on Gulf Standard Time whether the tutor is in the UAE or elsewhere, so a 10am slot is 10am for your child. If the family travels during study leave, sessions can follow the trip, which is one practical advantage of online delivery for Abu Dhabi families who leave before results day.

abu-dhabi/igcse-may-june-exam-preparatio.closingHeading: Start with the entry confirmation and one marked paper
abu-dhabi/igcse-may-june-exam-preparatio.closingBody: The useful first step is not booking a term of lessons. It is finding out exactly what your child has been entered for and what a marked paper says about where the marks are going. Send the entry confirmation and the centre's timetable version, take the free first lesson with an online IGCSE tutor in Abu Dhabi who has taught that specification, and read the written diagnosis that follows. If it says a term of one-to-one work would move the grade, you will know which subject and why. If it says the school's own revision programme is enough, you will know that too, and you will have paid nothing to find out.

abu-dhabi/igcse-mock-exam-preparation.tutorsIntro: The tutors here cover Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE at both tiers, with a focus on the weeks either side of a mock: reading the paper against the mark scheme, settling the tier question on evidence, and rebuilding what the marks point at.

intro.heading: Price the whole stack, not the hourly rate
paragraphs: Almost every family who searches for IGCSE mock exam preparation in Abu Dhabi has just received a mark they did not expect, and almost every one of them asks the wrong first question. The question is not what a tutor charges per hour. It is what the total looks like between now and the entry deadline, because that is the sum that lands on a household budget, and because the hourly rate is the smallest of the variables that determines it.

Here is the stack as it actually appears. School fees, already committed, which in Dubai have been held flat for 2026-27 under a decision KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026. Then tuition, which the market prices at AED 150 to AED 300 an hour for a qualified subject tutor online and AED 200 to AED 450 and above for an exam-year specialist, per Bestimate's Dubai rate table, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and TutorChase AED 270. Then, if the tier question goes the wrong way or a grade needs repairing, a resit entry, whose fee is set by the centre and not by us. Then any materials the school does not supply. The decision parents think they are making is about the second line. The one that moves the total most is often the third.

What pushes the figure up in this emirate specifically is a combination of timing and supply. Mock windows in Abu Dhabi schools cluster in a short band, so demand for Extended-tier mathematics and science support spikes in the same three weeks every year. At the same time, a mock mark sits immediately before the centre's internal entry cut-off, which means a family often has a fortnight to decide whether to buy support, change tier, or both. Decisions made in a fortnight are expensive decisions.

The other thing that moves the number is format. In-home one-to-one in the emirate is quoted at AED 180 to AED 350 an hour by Bestimate and AED 200 to AED 500 by independent home tutors, with advertised monthly packages of AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions against AED 799 for eight online sessions. The difference between those two packages is a car crossing Abu Dhabi, priced per hour. Across a six-week post-mock block it is a meaningful share of the total and it reaches nothing on the mark scheme.

IB Gram delivers one-to-one lessons over live video. We do not send a tutor to a UAE address; home visits are a service we offer only in India. On a mock-season booking that is also the practical answer to supply, because the pool of Extended-tier specialists available to a family in Al Shamkha or Al Ain is otherwise whoever can drive there on a Tuesday.

abu-dhabi/igcse-mock-exam-preparation.programmesIntro: A mock has a different meaning at each stage, and so does the money spent after it. These are the stages Abu Dhabi families are usually in when a mock mark triggers a conversation about cost.

programmes.name: Lower Secondary and Checkpoint
programmes.description: Internal assessment weeks at this stage carry no certificate and no entry consequence, which makes them the cheapest useful data a family will ever get. Checkpoint tests run in March, May and October and are diagnostic. Money spent here on algebraic fluency and written explanation costs a fraction of money spent on the same gap two years later under an entry deadline.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools on the Cambridge pathway typically use Year 9 internal data to stream for IGCSE tier. That is the quiet decision point most families miss, and it is far cheaper to influence with evidence in Year 9 than to contest in Year 11 with a mock mark in hand.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: Examined in June and November, with Core and Extended tiers in subjects including Mathematics 0580, Physics 0625 and Chemistry 0620. The Year 11 mock is where the tier question gets settled, because the centre needs a decision before its internal cut-off. The cost consequence is real: a Core entry caps the grade and a wrongly optimistic Extended entry risks a lower grade than a Core one would have produced.
programmes.countryNote: In Abu Dhabi the entry is made by the centre, which for nearly all candidates is the school. Each centre sets its own internal cut-off before the board's deadline, and the school's willingness to revisit a tier decision after mocks varies widely across the emirate. Ask the exams officer, in writing, what the cut-off is.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Available in May/June and November, with codes such as 4MA1 and 4PH1. Some Pearson qualifications are modular, which changes the economics after a weak mock: a candidate may be able to bank or re-sit one paper rather than an entire qualification, and the resit cost drops accordingly. Whether that route applies is a question for the centre.
programmes.countryNote: The November 2026 Pearson final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, with November 2025 results reaching students on 22 January 2026. For an Abu Dhabi family weighing a June entry against a November one after poor mocks, those are the dates the budget has to clear.

programmes.name: AS and A Level
programmes.description: The reason tier matters financially. Abu Dhabi sixth forms publish their own entry grades and several specify tier as well as grade, so a Core entry can close a route that then costs a resit to reopen. Spending on Extended-tier support before the entry deadline is usually cheaper than spending on a November resit after it.
programmes.countryNote: Where a sixth-form place depends on a grade not yet achieved, the November series becomes the fallback and the result arrives in January. Families should factor the cost of holding a place, or of a delayed start, into the comparison rather than treating the resit entry fee as the whole expense.

abu-dhabi/igcse-mock-exam-preparation.subjectsIntro: What a mock paper reveals, subject by subject, and how expensive each revelation is to act on. A technique gap is a small purchase; a tier mismatch is a large one.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: The mock subject where the tier question is sharpest. A candidate who scores respectably on the Extended paper but leaves the final unstructured questions blank has a technique and pacing issue worth a handful of sessions. One who cannot attempt the algebraic fraction questions at all has a content gap that is expensive this late.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 / Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.description: Mock scripts here separate cleanly into two groups: candidates losing marks on electricity and electromagnetism, which takes weeks, and candidates losing them on graph work and anomalous results, which takes a session or two. The mark total looks identical for both, which is why the script decides the spend.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 / Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.description: Moles and stoichiometry under time pressure is the recurring mock failure, and it is cheap to repair because it is arithmetic fluency rather than concept. Qualitative analysis tables are cheaper still, being memorisation. Organic conditions sit in between. None of these justifies a term-long programme.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 / Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.description: The subject where a mock mark most often understates a candidate. Accurate answers written to the wrong command word earn knowledge credit only, and the fix is a short, specific habit change. Families who buy a term of Biology teaching after a weak mock frequently buy the wrong thing.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics / Further Pure
subjects.description: Taken by candidates heading for A Level Mathematics, and the one subject where a weak mock sometimes argues for withdrawing the entry rather than buying support. That is a cheaper and more honest answer than funding an uphill term, and it is worth raising with the school.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: The summary task is where mock marks disappear, through copying rather than compressing, and the directed-writing task through ignoring the register the prompt specifies. Both are inexpensive to fix and respond inside a handful of marked attempts.

subjects.name: First Language English
subjects.description: Marked on reading as much as on writing, and mock scripts commonly show a candidate retelling a passage instead of using it as evidence. A composition that runs long without a controlled structure loses structure marks regardless of quality of expression.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Studies
subjects.description: Data-response questions carry the grade and mock candidates lose them on application, defining a term correctly and never pointing it at the stimulus. This is a low-cost repair and a high-yield one, which makes it a good first purchase after a disappointing mark.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Mock marks concentrate in the written conventions rather than in programming ability: trace tables, pseudocode style, and the precise vocabulary of data representation. A capable coder can lose a grade band here, and it is among the cheapest gaps in the subject list to close.

subjects.name: Arabic and UAE social studies alongside IGCSE
subjects.description: These subjects are taught in UAE private schools alongside the licensed international curriculum and they keep running through mock season. Any costed revision plan has to treat those lessons as fixed load, because a plan that assumes they can be set aside overstates the hours a candidate actually has.

abu-dhabi/igcse-mock-exam-preparation.regionsIntro: Cost is partly geography. Where a family lives in Abu Dhabi determines how long the school run takes, which determines how many usable session slots exist in a week, which determines whether a six-week plan is realistic at all.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: A large mainland catchment with a wide fee spread and a long drive to the island. The in-home travel premium bites hardest here, and families in this community see the largest saving from moving a post-mock block online rather than buying visits.

regions.name: Khalifa City and Al Shamkha
regions.note: Villa catchments feeding several British-curriculum schools, where the term-time school run can add forty minutes each way. Weekday sessions realistically start at 5pm or later, which caps a six-week plan at two weekday slots plus a weekend block.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Short commutes and dense apartment living, so three shorter weekday sessions are feasible where a villa family can manage two. For a candidate whose mock showed a pacing problem, frequent short timed sets beat long weekend sessions.

regions.name: Al Raha and Al Bandar
regions.note: Adjacent to the Khalifa City school cluster and one of the heaviest sources of Extended-tier science demand in the weeks after mocks. Slot availability here is tightest in the same fortnight every year, which is a cost in itself.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: The shortest school runs in the capital, which makes earlier weekday sessions possible and lets a post-mock plan run to three sessions a week without eating the evening. Smaller cohorts mean less internal comparison for a candidate judging a mock mark.

regions.name: Baniyas and Al Wathba
regions.note: Fewer international-curriculum schools nearby and a longer commute to those that exist. For a family here, the choice between an in-home visit and an online session is not marginal: travel is the dominant cost in any in-home quote.

regions.name: Al Ain
regions.note: Same emirate authority, an hour inland, and a thin local pool of IGCSE specialists. A family in Al Ain comparing in-home quotes after a weak mock is usually comparing availability rather than expertise, which is the problem online delivery removes.

schoolClusters.city: Khalifa City, Al Raha and Yas corridor
schoolClusters.note: The largest IGCSE population in the emirate and the source of most post-mock demand. Tier policies after mocks vary noticeably between schools in this corridor, so two families comparing notes may be describing different entry rules rather than different children.

schoolClusters.city: Island, Saadiyat and Al Bateen
schoolClusters.note: Smaller year groups with shorter commutes and longer admission waiting lists. A mock mark here is interpreted against a small cohort, which can make a mid-table result look worse or better than it is.
schools: The British International School Abu Dhabi

schoolClusters.city: Mainland Abu Dhabi and Al Ain
schoolClusters.note: A broad fee range and fewer specialists physically present, so this is where published in-home rates and actual availability diverge most. Families here most often discover that the quoted rate was never the binding constraint.

abu-dhabi/igcse-mock-exam-preparation.modesIntro: Three ways to spend after a mock, with very different totals. The right choice follows from the script, not from the size of the disappointment.

modes.title: Single diagnostic session
modes.description: One session per subject spent entirely on the marked mock paper, producing a written list of marks lost by cause and a straight answer on the tier question. This is the smallest purchase available and frequently the only one needed, because a mock mark that looked alarming often turns out to be a command-word habit rather than a content gap.

Explicit recommendation on Core or Extended entry
A clear statement if nothing further is worth buying

modes.title: Six-week post-mock block
modes.description: One or two subjects, one to two sessions a week, running from the mock to the centre's entry cut-off and on towards the series. Costed as a known total at the start because the week count is fixed. This is the standard shape where a mock showed a genuine but narrow content gap.
bullets: Total stated at the outset rather than billed open-endedly
Marked timed set every second or third session
Topic order set by the mock script, not by the syllabus order
Reviewed at week three against the marked evidence

modes.title: November contingency plan
modes.description: Where the mock makes a June grade unlikely, the cheaper answer is often to plan for the November series rather than to buy an intensive spring. Entries are made by the centre, results reach students in January, and the preparation block is shorter and better targeted than a panicked June push.
