abu-dhabi/igcse-past-papers-practice.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE subjects and mark the student's own scripts against the board's published assessment language. Each records a mark before and after the student's rewrite, so progress is visible rather than asserted.

intro.heading: Before the first paper: which board, which code, which variant
paragraphs: Most Abu Dhabi families searching for IGCSE past papers practice have already downloaded a folder of papers. A good proportion of those papers are the wrong ones. Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel are different boards with different syllabuses, different paper structures and different mark schemes for nominally the same subject. Within Cambridge, subjects are tiered, so Core and Extended candidates sit different components. And within a component, Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, each with its own timetable and its own paper variant.

That last point deserves emphasis because almost nothing written for this market mentions it. Cambridge's own guidance for exams officers states that each centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones and that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for the zone, adding that Cambridge cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam through using the wrong zone timetable. The same logic applies to practice: a student working through a variant their centre does not sit is practising a paper with different questions.

So the first session is administrative and it is the one that saves the most wasted effort. We look at the statement of entry, confirm the board, the syllabus code, the tier and the components, and then establish which variants the student's centre sits. Parents are often surprised at how quickly this resolves confusion that has been running for months, particularly in households where two children attend different schools on different boards.

After that the work is marking, and we treat it as an evidence exercise. A script is marked cold, then marked against the scheme with the losses categorised, then the two highest-value answers are rewritten under time and marked again. Both marks are recorded. Over six weeks that produces a visible trail showing whether technique fixes are holding, which is information a single mock percentage cannot give you.

One boundary to state plainly. We do not supply, host or reproduce Cambridge or Pearson past papers, mark schemes, syllabus documents or grade threshold tables. Those are the boards' copyright material, licensed to centres, and your child's school is the route to them. Everything described on this page assumes the papers arrive that way. Sessions are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE, because home visits are a service we run only in India. A normal arrangement is fortnightly marking across the two or three subjects where the grade gap is widest, with the student producing and self-marking the scripts in between. Nine subjects cannot all be practised at once, and trying is the most common way a Year 11 revision plan collapses.

abu-dhabi/igcse-past-papers-practice.programmesIntro: IGCSE sits between the primary years and post-16 study, and what comes next shapes how paper practice should be used. Here is the picture for a family in this emirate.

programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools typically enter candidates for the June series, using November as the resit route. Mocks usually run in the winter term and again shortly before the real papers, and those mocks are where most families first see a realistic mark.

abu-dhabi/igcse-past-papers-practice.subjectsIntro: Paper technique differs by subject and by board. These are the subjects we mark most often for Abu Dhabi families, with the specific thing practice has to fix in each.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.levels: Cambridge 0580 Core and Extended; Pearson 4MA1 Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: Method marks dominate. Students lose marks for correct answers with no working, for rounding too early, and for answering in the wrong form. Practice targets setting out, and knowing which questions on an Extended or Higher paper are designed to be skipped first.

subjects.name: Additional and Further Mathematics
subjects.description: Taken alongside the main maths syllabus by stronger candidates, often as preparation for A Level. Practice here is almost entirely about question recognition: identifying which technique is being tested from the phrasing before starting.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Structured calculation and the alternative-to-practical or practical component depending on the entry. Marks go missing on units, significant figures, and extended answers where the question asked for an explanation and received a description.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Equation writing, state symbols, mole calculations shown step by step, and the tests-and-observations questions where precision of wording earns the mark. Students who abbreviate their working lose marks they would otherwise keep.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Terminology precision and command word discipline. The most common loss is a correct idea expressed in everyday language where the scheme requires the technical term, which is a vocabulary fix rather than a content one.

subjects.name: English as a First Language
subjects.description: Directed writing, summary and analysis under tight time limits. Practice focuses on planning quickly, matching register to task, and the specific reading question types where marks are awarded for selection rather than for explanation.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Relevant to a large share of Abu Dhabi candidates. Practice targets the exercises where marks follow exact instruction-following, and timed writing tasks where accuracy matters more than ambition.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Economics
subjects.description: Case study application. The frequent loss is a textbook answer that never refers to the business in the stimulus material, and evaluation questions that list points without reaching a judgement.

subjects.name: History and Geography
subjects.description: Source handling and structured extended writing to a tight clock. Practice is largely about question choice, planning in two minutes, and the specific demands of each paper's question types.

subjects.name: Computer Science and ICT
subjects.description: Precision in pseudocode, trace tables and technical definitions, where a nearly-right answer earns nothing. Practice rewards working through the board's own style of question rather than general programming practice.

sections.heading: Syllabus codes, components and variants: the paper your child is actually sitting
paragraphs: A Cambridge IGCSE subject is identified by a four-digit code, and the papers a candidate sits are components within it. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE uses a different code format and a different component structure for the same subject. Mathematics is the clearest example: Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are both widely taught in this emirate, both called IGCSE Maths by every parent, and they are not the same qualification with the same papers.

Within Cambridge, the component number carries a variant digit, and variants exist because centres are allocated to administrative zones. Cambridge's exams officers guide states plainly that each centre sits in one of six zones and that the correct zone timetable must be used, noting that Cambridge cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. Practice material follows the same structure, so a student grinding through a variant their centre does not sit is answering questions their paper will not ask.

None of this is obscure to an exams officer and almost all of it is invisible to students. The fix is to read the statement of entry, which lists the syllabus codes and components the candidate is entered for, and to ask the exams officer or subject teacher which variants the centre sits. Five minutes, once, and every subsequent hour of practice is aimed at the right target.

The table below shows the code structure for subjects we are asked about most often in Abu Dhabi. Codes and component structures are revised by the boards from time to time, so treat it as an illustration of how the identification works rather than as a current catalogue, and confirm the detail against the statement of entry and the board's own published syllabus page.

sections.heading: Core or Extended, Foundation or Higher: half the papers may be irrelevant
paragraphs: Tiering is the second place practice goes wrong. Cambridge offers Core and Extended routes in several subjects, with different papers and different grade ranges available. Pearson uses Foundation and Higher tiers in some subjects. A Core candidate practising Extended papers is attempting content they will not be examined on; an Extended candidate practising Core papers is building confidence on questions easier than the ones they will face.

Both errors are common and the second is more damaging, because it produces a student who is scoring well in practice and is surprised in June. Parents sometimes encourage it without realising, because the marks look encouraging. The honest check is to confirm the tier on the statement of entry and then only use material matched to it.

Tier also changes what a grade ceiling is. On a Core route the top grades available are limited by design, which is a conversation a family should have deliberately rather than discover. Where a student is entered for Core and needs a higher grade for a sixth form condition, that is a discussion with the school about the entry, not something practice can fix, and it needs to happen while entries can still be amended.

Your child's statement of entry and the school's own guidance are the authority on which applies to them.

sections.heading: Three marking passes, and why both marks get recorded
paragraphs: Marking is where a script turns into evidence. We use three passes and record the numbers from each, which is the part families find most useful because it replaces impressions with a trail. Pass one is the student's own cold mark, done before the session. Pass two is our independent mark against the scheme, with every lost mark categorised. Pass three is a mark on the two highest-value answers after the student has rewritten them under time.

The gap between pass one and pass two is the most diagnostic number in the whole exercise. A student who consistently awards themselves eight marks more than the scheme allows has a precise blind spot, usually about what counts as an explanation or about whether implied working earns method marks. Naming that gap is more useful than naming the score, and it closes within a few sessions once the student sees it.

The gap between pass two and pass three tells you whether a fix has taken. If a rewritten answer still loses the same marks, the fault was not understood, and the next session changes approach rather than repeating the instruction. If it gains them, the technique is in place and the next paper tests whether it survives a cold start.

The numbers are there to show the structure of the evidence, not as a prediction: we publish no claims about average grade improvements, because we could not show you the data behind such a claim. What we can show any family is the trail for their own child.

sections.heading: The fault types behind IGCSE lost marks
paragraphs: Across Cambridge and Pearson scripts the same categories recur, and almost none of them are content gaps. Working not shown is the largest in mathematics and the sciences, because a correct final answer earns the answer mark and loses the method marks. Command word misreading is the largest in the humanities and the sciences together: describe answered as explain, or explain answered as describe, each losing marks in a different way.

Precision of wording is the third. Science mark schemes often require a specific term, and an answer that conveys the right idea in everyday language earns nothing. This hits a particular group of students in Abu Dhabi hardest, namely those working in English as an additional language to a high standard, whose understanding is sound and whose technical vocabulary is approximate. It is a learnable, listable fix rather than a reason for concern.

Fourth is the mark allocation ignored, where a student writes a paragraph for a one-mark answer and then runs out of time. Fifth is stimulus material unused, which dominates Business Studies and Geography: a textbook-correct answer that never mentions the company or the figure in the question. Sixth is timing collapse in the final section, which is the most expensive fault of all because the end of a paper usually holds the cheapest marks.

Only the seventh category, genuine content gaps, requires teaching rather than technique. Keeping the log is what lets a family tell the difference. A student whose log is two-thirds technique faults does not need more revision; they need six weeks of marked practice with the faults named. A student whose log is two-thirds content gaps needs subject teaching, and we say so rather than selling marking sessions.

sections.heading: The exam calendar counted backwards, including the resit route
paragraphs: UAE candidates sit the June series and the November series. Cambridge offers a February and March series to India only, so it is not a route available to a student in Abu Dhabi and should be disregarded entirely when planning. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May and June and again in November.

Dates are published by the boards and revised, so the rule we give families is to work from the live official timetable rather than from any date restated on a third-party page. For orientation: the Pearson International GCSE November 2026 timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Those are past, citable dates. For anything forthcoming, check the board's own timetable page, which is also where provisional timetables for future series appear.

The practical shape of the year, counted backwards from the June series, is this: syllabus substantially complete by the winter mocks, mock scripts reviewed properly in the weeks after them, full timed papers from the spring, and the final fortnight on past paper technique rather than new content. The November series exists as a resit route, and a student considering it should know that results arrive in January, which matters for sixth form or college applications with earlier deadlines.

sections.heading: Where the papers come from, and what we will not do
paragraphs: Cambridge and Pearson past papers, mark schemes, syllabus documents and grade threshold tables are the boards' copyright material, licensed to registered centres. We do not supply them, host them, email them or reproduce any part of them. A tutoring provider offering a shared drive of papers is distributing material it does not own, and we will not compete on that basis.

There is a practical argument alongside the legal one. Unofficial collections are frequently mislabelled, mix variants, and include papers from superseded syllabus versions. In subjects where a board has revised the specification, practising a withdrawn paper is worse than not practising, because it teaches question styles that no longer appear. Material supplied through the school is matched to the syllabus the candidate is entered for.

The route we recommend is narrow and usually works. The student asks their subject teacher for questions or a paper on the topics currently being revised, and asks the exams officer which zone variant the centre sits. Schools in this emirate hold their own access and generally release material readily when the request is specific rather than wholesale.

What we do with the material once it is in the student's hands is the entire service: marking, categorising, rewriting and recording. None of that depends on who holds the papers, which is why the boundary costs a family nothing while protecting both them and us. It also means a family is never paying us for access to something their school already holds.

sections.heading: What this costs in Abu Dhabi, and the honest comparison
paragraphs: Published UAE market rates, read in October 2026: Tutopiya advertises from AED 33 to 52 an hour and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65 at the budget online tier. Unitors publishes IGCSE tutoring from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. TutorChase quotes AED 270. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 survey puts IB and IGCSE specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above, in-home visits at AED 180 to 350, and independent home tutors at AED 200 to 500. BartyED publishes AED 650 for a named premium tutor. Those are each provider's own figures.

For IGCSE marking work specifically, the comparison worth making is between a mid-market online hour and an in-home hour at the same nominal rate. The in-home hour includes a travel premium and limits the tutor pool to whoever reaches your address on a weekday evening, which for a family in Al Shamkha or Al Ain is a short list. The online hour at the same price buys a tutor who teaches that board, that subject and that tier.

Where the money is genuinely wasted in this market is on supervision and on content coverage a school is already providing. A student does not need to pay anyone to sit a paper. A student also does not need a tutor to re-teach a syllabus their school is teaching competently, which is what a weekly general session often becomes. The hour worth buying is the marking hour, fortnightly, with the student doing the production work in between.

We quote after a free trial lesson, and the trial is spent marking a script the student has already attempted. If the marking shows content gaps rather than technique faults, we will say so and recommend subject teaching instead, which is a longer and more expensive commitment that we would rather you enter deliberately.

faqs.question: How do I know whether my child sits Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel?
faqs.answer: The statement of entry says so, subject by subject, with the syllabus codes and the components the candidate is entered for. It matters because the boards set different papers for nominally the same subject: Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are both called IGCSE Maths by every parent in Abu Dhabi and they are not the same qualification. Some schools enter candidates with different boards for different subjects, so check per subject rather than assuming the school uses one throughout.

faqs.question: What is a paper variant and why does it matter for practice?
faqs.answer: Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, each with its own timetable, and components carry a variant digit accordingly. Cambridge's own exams officer guidance states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for the zone and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. For practice the consequence is simpler: a variant your centre does not sit asks different questions. The exams officer can tell you which variants apply.

faqs.question: My child is entered for Core. Can they practise Extended papers?
faqs.answer: It is usually counterproductive. Core and Extended are different papers covering different content, and Extended material includes topics a Core candidate will not be examined on, which wastes time and dents confidence. The reverse error is more damaging: an Extended candidate practising Core papers scores encouragingly and is surprised in June. If the tier itself is the problem, because a sixth form condition needs a grade the Core route cannot reach, that is a conversation with the school while entries can still be amended.

faqs.question: Can you give us Cambridge and Edexcel past papers?
faqs.answer: No. Past papers, mark schemes, syllabus documents and grade threshold tables are the boards' copyright material, licensed to registered centres, and we neither supply nor host any of it. Your child's subject teacher and exams officer are the route. There is also a quality argument: unofficial collections routinely mix variants and include papers from superseded specifications, so practising from one can mean learning question styles that no longer appear on the paper your child will sit.

faqs.question: Which series do IGCSE students in the UAE sit?
faqs.answer: June and November. Cambridge offers a February and March series to India only, so it is not available to a candidate in Abu Dhabi and should be left out of any plan. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May and June and again in November. Dates are published by the boards and can be revised, so work from the live official timetable rather than from dates restated elsewhere, and have the exams officer confirm which zone timetable applies to your child's centre.

faqs.question: How does the November resit route work for an Abu Dhabi student?
faqs.answer: It is a full re-sitting of the component in the November series, with results arriving the following January. For Pearson, November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026, which gives a sense of the timing. The important planning point is that January results can fall after some sixth form and college decision deadlines, so a family considering a resit should check the deadlines of the next step before assuming November solves the problem. The school's exams officer handles the entry.

faqs.question: Why is my child scoring well in practice and badly in mocks?
faqs.answer: Three usual causes. The practice papers are the wrong tier or variant, so they are easier or differently structured. The practice is untimed and with notes to hand, so it tests recognition rather than retrieval. Or the self-marking is generous, which is the most common of the three: students award themselves marks for ideas they recognised in the scheme but did not actually write down. Comparing a student's own mark against an independent one usually exposes it within a single session.

faqs.question: What are the most common ways IGCSE marks are lost?
faqs.answer: Working not shown, which loses method marks in maths and the sciences even when the final answer is right. Command words misread, in both directions. Everyday language where the mark scheme requires a technical term. Answer length mismatched to the mark allocation. Stimulus material ignored in Business Studies and Geography. And timing collapse in the final section, which is the most expensive because the end of a paper usually holds the cheapest marks available.

faqs.question: How often should a Year 11 student do a full timed paper?
faqs.answer: Once the syllabus is substantially covered, roughly fortnightly per subject in the spring, and before each set of mocks. Earlier than that, topic-filtered question sets do the same job without the discouragement of meeting untaught content. A student sitting full papers in nine subjects weekly is producing more scripts than anyone can mark or digest, and unmarked scripts teach nothing. Volume is not the variable that matters; what happens after each paper is.

faqs.question: Are sessions online, or does a tutor come to our villa?
faqs.answer: Online, one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send tutors to addresses anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Marking is screen work, with the script, the student's own marking and the error log open together. The practical gain for a family in Al Ain or Al Shamkha is a tutor matched to the exact board, subject and tier rather than whoever can reach the address on a weekday evening, and no travel premium on the hour.

faqs.question: What does IGCSE paper marking cost in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Published UAE rates read in October 2026: AED 33 to 65 an hour at the budget online tier, AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online, AED 200 to 450 and above for specialists, AED 180 to 500 for in-home visits where travel is priced in, and AED 650 at one provider for a named tutor. Those are their figures, not ours. The efficient pattern is fortnightly marking with the student producing and self-marking in between, rather than weekly sessions re-teaching what the school already covers.

faqs.question: Should my child practise papers in all nine subjects?
faqs.answer: Not simultaneously, and not equally. Rank the subjects by the gap between the current mark and the grade actually needed for the next step, then concentrate the marked practice on the two or three where that gap is largest and movable. A student spreading timed papers evenly across nine subjects produces scripts nobody marks and a plan nobody can follow. The error log makes the ranking easy, because it shows which subjects are losing marks to technique and which to missing content.

faqs.question: How should a student mark their own IGCSE script?
faqs.answer: Severely, awarding a mark only where the words on the page would earn it from a marker who will infer nothing. No method mark for working done in the head. No mark for the right idea in the wrong vocabulary where the scheme specifies a term. No mark for a comparison that is implied rather than made. The first two or three papers marked this way feel discouraging and produce an accurate score, which every subsequent decision depends on. Over-marking is comfortable and builds a revision plan on fiction.

faqs.question: Does paper practice help with coursework or practical components?
faqs.answer: Only partly, and it is worth knowing which part of the grade you are working on. Some IGCSE subjects carry a coursework or practical component, and where they do, paper practice influences only the written share of the grade. Check the components on the statement of entry: if a substantial portion sits in coursework, that work needs its own attention and the marking hours should be split accordingly. For the alternative-to-practical papers that several science entries use, past paper technique applies in full.

faqs.question: How should a Year 11 student use a returned IGCSE mock paper?
faqs.answer: Read it question by question alongside the mark scheme, categorise every lost mark, and convert the result into a revision order by marks lost rather than by which topics feel uncomfortable. The mock is usually the only paper a Year 11 student sits under genuinely realistic conditions, so the script carries information no practice paper can: how the timing actually went, what happened in the last section, and which marks were cheapest to recover. Most scripts are glanced at and filed, which wastes the best data available.

abu-dhabi/igcse-past-papers-practice.closingHeading: Start with the statement of entry
abu-dhabi/igcse-past-papers-practice.closingBody: Before buying any tutoring, find your child's statement of entry and check four things: the board, the syllabus code, the tier and the components. Then email the exams officer and ask which zone variants the centre sits. That costs nothing and it is the difference between practice aimed at the right paper and practice aimed near it. Then have your child sit one paper on taught topics, mark it themselves without mercy, and bring both to the free trial lesson. We will mark it independently and show you exactly where the gap is.

abu-dhabi/igcse-private-candidate-regist.tutorsIntro: The tutors here prepare private candidates for Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE papers, working from the exact option codes a centre has entered rather than from a generic syllabus, with particular attention to the written alternatives to practical assessment.

intro.heading: The entry comes first, and the entry decides what you revise
paragraphs: A private candidate is somebody sitting IGCSE or International GCSE papers without being on a school's roll for that qualification. In Abu Dhabi the route is to register through a centre that accepts external candidates, which may be a standalone examination centre or a school willing to take them. Every entry is made by the centre. A parent cannot submit one directly to Cambridge or Pearson, and that single fact restructures the whole project: the first task is finding a centre, not finding a tutor.

The second fact is the one that costs people a term. A private candidate usually cannot submit coursework, and in several subjects the practical assessment is examined through a written alternative rather than a laboratory session. Which of those applies depends on the option code the centre enters. Two candidates sitting the same subject in the same series under different option codes revise different things, and a candidate who prepares for a component they are not entered for has wasted the work.

So the sequence is: find a centre, establish what it will enter and under which codes, get its internal deadline in writing, and only then build a teaching plan. Families routinely do this in reverse, buying tuition in September and discovering in November that the centre's cut-off has passed or that a coursework component is unavailable. Nothing about the teaching fixes either.

On cost, this page prices the whole stack because the tuition line is only part of it. Entry fees are set by the centre and revised between series, so no honest page can publish a figure for them; the correct action is to ask for the current schedule in writing. Tuition sits in a published market range: AED 150 to AED 300 an hour for a qualified subject tutor online, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150, and AED 200 to AED 450 and above for an exam-year specialist per Bestimate's Dubai rate table, with TutorChase at AED 270. Private candidates generally need more hours than school candidates, because there is no classroom doing the first pass.

Teaching is delivered one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a UAE address; home visits are a service we offer only in India. For a private candidate that format is particularly suited to the work: there is no school timetable to fit around, sessions can run at whatever hours suit, and the choice of tutor is not limited to whoever can reach the address. The in-home market in the emirate is quoted at AED 180 to AED 500 an hour because the journey is priced into every lesson, and a private candidate needs hours rather than visits. It also removes the geographic limit on who can teach a subject, which matters most for a family in Al Ain or the Western Region whose nearest option would otherwise be nobody at all.

programmes.name: Preparing without a school behind you
programmes.description: Where a family is home educating or between school systems, the years before IGCSE determine how much teaching the qualification itself needs. A student who has built algebraic fluency and written explanation independently needs far fewer paid hours at IGCSE than one who has not, and that is worth knowing before the budget is set.
programmes.countryNote: Checkpoint tests run in March, May and October and are diagnostic rather than certificating, which makes them a useful external benchmark for a family educating outside a school. Whether a given centre offers them to external candidates is a question to ask directly.

programmes.name: What the certificate is for
programmes.description: Most private IGCSE entries exist to open a next step: a sixth-form place, an A Level programme, a university condition, or recognition inside the UAE. The destination determines which subjects matter and how many, and it is worth confirming before entering subjects that nobody will ask about.
programmes.countryNote: On the published British equivalency track, five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no less than E or grade 3 are counted, with Arabic and Islamic education not included among the five. Verify your own case with the Ministry or the emirate's attestation authority rather than with a tutoring site.

abu-dhabi/igcse-private-candidate-regist.subjectsIntro: What a private candidate should expect in each subject, written around what is actually sittable externally rather than around the syllabus as a whole.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580 / Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: The most straightforward subject to sit externally, since there is no practical or coursework component to replace. The teaching load is the full syllabus plus examination technique, and the marks go on unstructured final questions, bounds and algebraic fractions, plus a steady band of unwritten method lines.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics / Further Pure
subjects.description: Also clean to sit externally and a common choice for a candidate heading towards A Level Mathematics. The paper assumes an algebraic speed that Mathematics alone does not build, so a private candidate taking both needs the sequencing planned rather than assumed.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 / Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.description: Practical assessment is normally met through a written alternative for external candidates, and that paper is where private candidates gain or lose most. It asks for variable identification, method criticism, precise scale reading, graph conventions and justified anomaly identification, none of which is covered by revising theory.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 / Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.description: The same practical position as Physics, with the written alternative adding questions on separation techniques, qualitative analysis and expected observations. A private candidate who has never run the experiments needs to learn what the observations would have been, which is specific teachable content.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 / Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.description: Theory is readily sat externally; the written practical alternative asks about experimental design, controls and food tests. Command-word discipline matters more here than in any other subject, and a private candidate with no classroom feedback loop has to build it through marked practice.

subjects.name: First Language English
subjects.description: Sittable externally, with the caveat that speaking and listening endorsements may not be available to a private candidate depending on the option code. Confirm with the centre which code is being entered, because it changes what appears on the certificate.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Similar position on the speaking component, which is worth checking rather than assuming. The written components reward summary compression and attention to the register the prompt specifies, both of which respond quickly to marked practice.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Studies
subjects.description: Among the most private-candidate-friendly subjects, with no practical requirement and a syllabus that can be covered methodically. The marks live in application to the stimulus and in a supported judgement, which is where self-taught candidates most often fall short.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Check the coursework position carefully, because where a practical programming component exists it may not be submittable externally and the option code changes accordingly. Theory marks concentrate in data representation, logic and the fetch-execute cycle.

subjects.name: Subjects to avoid as a private candidate
subjects.description: Any subject where an unavoidable coursework or performance component cannot be submitted externally is a poor choice for a private entry, and the centre will tell you which those are for its own registration. Establishing the list before choosing subjects saves more money than any decision about tutors.

abu-dhabi/igcse-private-candidate-regist.regionsIntro: A private candidate has no school run, which changes the geography entirely: the only journeys that matter are to the examination centre on the days of the papers. These notes reflect that.

regions.name: Abu Dhabi island and Corniche
regions.note: Where several examination venues and schools accepting external candidates are concentrated, which matters on paper days rather than during preparation. A candidate living here has the shortest and most predictable journey on exam mornings.

regions.name: Khalifa City and Al Raha
regions.note: A long drive to island venues in morning traffic, which is worth rehearsing before the first paper rather than discovering on the day. Cambridge's zone timetable note matters here too: confirm the correct timetable version with the centre.

regions.name: Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: A large mainland catchment where families often choose a centre on travel time rather than on reputation. That is a reasonable basis for choosing, provided the centre's option codes and deadlines have been checked in writing first.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Central and well connected, with short journeys to island venues. For a private candidate studying at home, the practical advantage here is a quiet study environment close to where the papers will be sat.

regions.name: Al Shamkha and Al Falah
regions.note: Newer communities further out, where exam-morning travel is the main logistical issue. Candidates here should establish parking and arrival arrangements at the centre well before the series, since no school is handling it for them.

regions.name: Baniyas and Al Wathba
regions.note: Further from the usual venues, with a longer and less predictable journey on paper days. Families in this area sometimes choose a centre in a different part of the emirate purely for arrival reliability, which is a legitimate reason.

regions.name: Al Ain
regions.note: An hour inland, which makes the choice of centre a significant decision rather than a detail. Confirm early whether a local centre accepts external candidates in your subjects, because the alternative is a long journey on every paper day.

schoolClusters.city: Schools in the emirate that may accept external candidates
schoolClusters.note: Some private schools register external candidates for the series alongside their own cohort, usually with limited places and their own earlier internal deadline. Policies differ year to year and are not always published, so this is a question to ask directly and early rather than to research online.

schoolClusters.city: Where candidates usually come from
schoolClusters.note: Private candidates in the emirate often come from households currently outside a British-curriculum school: home educators, families between systems after a relocation, and students who left a school roll mid-cycle. Their preparation needs differ sharply from a school candidate's.

schoolClusters.city: Al Ain and the Western Region
schoolClusters.note: Fewer venues across a wider geography, which makes centre availability the binding constraint. A family here should settle the centre question before anything else in the project, including the subject list.

sections.heading: What a private candidate can and cannot sit
paragraphs: This is the section families most need and least often find. A private candidate sits written papers, and in most subjects that covers the whole qualification. The exceptions matter. Where a subject carries a coursework component, an external candidate generally cannot submit it, so the centre enters an option code without it, and the written papers carry the grade differently. Where a subject carries practical assessment, external candidates are normally entered for a written alternative that examines practical skills on paper.

The written alternative is not a lesser paper and it is not a formality. It asks candidates to identify independent, dependent and controlled variables; criticise a described method; read a scale or instrument precisely; plot and interpret a graph to the expected conventions; and identify an anomalous result with a reason. A candidate who has never been in a laboratory can learn all of that, but only if someone teaches it deliberately, and it is the single highest-value block of work in a private science entry.

Speaking and listening endorsements in language subjects are the third area to check, because availability varies by subject, board and option code, and the answer changes what the certificate shows. Performance and portfolio subjects are the fourth, and generally a poor choice for an external entry for the obvious reason.

None of this can be settled from a website. The centre knows which codes it will enter and what each includes, and the exams officer will tell you if asked specifically. The question to send is not whether your child can sit Chemistry; it is which Chemistry option code the centre enters for external candidates and which components that code comprises. That phrasing gets a usable answer.

sections.heading: Finding a centre and registering: the order of operations
paragraphs: Centres that accept external candidates in the emirate include standalone examination centres and some private schools that register externals alongside their own cohort. School policies differ year to year, places are limited, and the arrangement is not always published, which means this is a phone-and-email exercise rather than a search-engine one. Start it a series ahead of when you need it, not a term ahead.

The registration itself is the centre's act, not the family's and certainly not ours. What a family does is choose the centre, provide the candidate's details and documents as the centre requires, agree the subject list and codes, pay the centre's fees, and meet the centre's internal deadline. What the centre does is submit the entry to the board, allocate the candidate a number, issue a statement of entry, and run the examinations.

There are six things worth having in writing before any money changes hands, and they are listed in the table below. The two most commonly skipped are the option codes, which determine what is revised, and the Cambridge administrative zone, which determines which timetable version is correct. Cambridge states it is essential to use the correct version for the zone and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. A private candidate has nobody else checking that.

One further practical point. Because a private candidate is not on a school roll, nobody will chase them about deadlines, statements of entry, identification requirements or arrival arrangements. Every reminder a school candidate receives automatically has to be self-generated. Putting the centre's dates into a shared family calendar the day they are received is a small discipline that prevents the most expensive failure in this whole project, which is a missed entry.

sections.heading: The whole cost stack in AED, including the lines nobody mentions
paragraphs: A private candidate's budget has more lines than a school candidate's and families usually plan only one of them. The entry fee is set by the centre, per subject and per series, and it is the line this page deliberately does not quote, because centres publish their own schedules and revise them. Asking for that schedule in writing is the first spending decision, not the last, because it determines how many subjects are affordable.

Then there is late entry. Boards and centres typically charge more for entries submitted after the standard deadline, which turns a missed date into a direct financial penalty on top of the administrative risk. For a private candidate with nobody chasing them, this is a real and avoidable cost, and it is the strongest practical argument for putting the centre's internal deadline into a calendar immediately.

Tuition is the line families focus on, and private candidates need more of it than school candidates because there is no classroom covering the first pass through the syllabus. Market rates are published: budget online tuition at AED 33 to AED 65 an hour per Tutopiya and EdFlik; a qualified subject tutor online at AED 150 to AED 300, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150; exam-year and IGCSE specialists at AED 200 to AED 450 and above per Bestimate's rate table, with TutorChase at AED 270. Monthly estimates for weekly one-hour sessions run AED 240 to AED 600 budget, AED 600 to AED 1,200 mid and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year work.

Two smaller lines complete the stack. Resources, since a private candidate has no school supplying textbooks, and these should be bought legitimately rather than downloaded: syllabus documents, past papers and mark schemes belong to the boards, and the correct behaviour is to use the official sources. And post-results services, where a review of marking is requested; those are charged by the board through the centre and have their own deadlines, which fall surprisingly soon after results.

sections.heading: Counting backwards from the series, with nobody reminding you
paragraphs: A private candidate's calendar has the same fixed points as a school candidate's and none of the support around them. Cambridge International runs IGCSE and O Level exams in a June series and a November series; the February/March series is offered to India only, so it is not available here. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. Results follow in August for the summer series and in January for the autumn one: Pearson's June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026.

Working backwards from the papers, the next fixed point is the board's entry deadline, and before that the centre's internal cut-off, which is the one that actually binds a family. Before that sits the subject and code decision, which has to be made with the centre rather than announced to it. And before all of it sits the choice of centre, which for a family in Al Ain or the Western Region can take longer than expected because availability is limited.

The teaching plan then fills whatever is left, and the honest arithmetic is usually sobering. A full-syllabus private entry in three subjects is not a one-term project; it is two or three terms of consistent work, and choosing the nearest series rather than a realistic one is the commonest way a private candidate underperforms. A candidate who picks the following series and prepares properly nearly always does better than one who picks the next series and rushes.

One structural advantage is worth naming. A private candidate has no school timetable, which means the study week can be designed rather than fitted around lessons. Used well, that is a genuine edge: morning study when concentration is best, timed papers at the hour the real papers will be sat, and no commute. Used badly, it produces a week with no structure at all, which is the characteristic failure mode of self-directed preparation.

sections.heading: Who sits as a private candidate, and why it changes the plan
paragraphs: Four groups make up most private entries in this emirate, and the preparation differs for each. The first is home-educating families, who have usually covered the material in their own way and need the syllabus mapped onto what has been done, plus examination technique from scratch. Their chief risk is a mismatch between what was learned and what the paper asks, which a marked past paper exposes immediately.

The second is families between school systems after a relocation, often where a child joined an Abu Dhabi school too late to be entered or where the new school does not offer a subject the child had been studying. Here the content is largely in place and the work is technique and the specific option codes, which makes it a shorter and cheaper project than families expect.

The third is students who left a school roll mid-cycle, for any of the reasons students do. They typically have partial coverage, a real but patchy content base, and no recent marked work. The diagnostic matters most in this group, because the gap between what has been taught and what has been retained is widest and least predictable.

The fourth is adults and older students returning to add qualifications, often for a specific recognition or admission requirement. Their advantage is motivation and self-management; their constraint is time, and their most common error is entering more subjects than the destination actually requires. Checking the requirement first, in writing, routinely reduces the subject list and therefore the whole budget.

sections.heading: Science without a laboratory: making the written alternative work
paragraphs: This is the part of private candidature that worries families most and is the most tractable. The written alternative to practical assessment does not test whether a candidate has run experiments; it tests whether they understand experimental method, can read instruments and graphs precisely, and can reason about data. All of that can be taught without a laboratory, and taught well it is one of the better-scoring components for a well-prepared external candidate.

The teachable content is specific. Identifying independent, dependent and controlled variables in a described experiment, and explaining why a control matters rather than merely naming it. Reading a scale, a thermometer or a measuring cylinder to the expected precision, including the convention on significant figures. Plotting a graph to the conventions the mark scheme expects, drawing a line of best fit, finding a gradient and interpreting it. Identifying an anomalous point and giving a reason. Criticising a method and suggesting an improvement that addresses the stated weakness.

The content a private candidate genuinely lacks is observational: what a particular reaction looks like, what colour change occurs, what the expected outcome of a food test is. That is a body of knowledge rather than a skill, and it can be learned from the syllabus and from good teaching, supported by video demonstrations from legitimate sources. What it cannot be learned from is theory revision alone, which is why this strand needs its own sessions rather than a mention.

Practically, three or four past alternative-to-practical papers, sat under the real duration and marked strictly against the published mark scheme, is the single highest-yield block of work available in a private science entry. It is also the component school candidates practise least, which means a well-prepared private candidate can be genuinely stronger here than a classroom cohort.

sections.heading: Results, reviews of marking, and what the certificate shows
paragraphs: Results reach a private candidate through the centre, which is worth knowing because it means the centre's own arrangements determine how and when you see them. Ask in advance how results will be released to you and by what route, because a private candidate does not walk into a school hall on results day and nobody will explain the statement to them.

If a grade looks wrong, there is a formal route: a review of marking, requested through the centre and charged by the board, with a deadline that falls soon after results. The deadline is the issue. A family that spends a fortnight deciding has often lost the window, and a private candidate with no school prompting them is especially exposed. Decide the criteria in advance: if a component mark is materially below what marked practice consistently showed, request the review.

On the certificate itself, what appears depends on the option codes entered, which is why the codes matter beyond revision planning. A qualification entered without a coursework component, or without a speaking endorsement, may be reported differently from the school version, and a receiving sixth form or university may or may not care. The only reliable way to know is to ask the receiving institution what it requires, in writing, before entering.

Finally, recognition. For use inside the UAE, the published British-track equivalency rule counts five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education not included among the five, alongside one subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. That process is run by the Ministry and the attestation authority, not by a school or a tutoring service, and nothing here should be read as implying tutoring is required for it.

sections.heading: How teaching runs, and the limits we state plainly
paragraphs: Teaching is one-to-one over live video, with screen sharing, a shared whiteboard and the candidate's own marked work on screen. For a private candidate the scheduling is unusually free, which is an advantage worth using: sessions can run in the morning when concentration is best, and timed papers can be sat at the hour the real papers will be sat rather than late in the evening after school. Gulf Standard Time lessons are set to suit the candidate's own week, and during Ramadan they move to post-Iftar timing.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Home visits are a service we run only in India. For a private candidate the format fits the work: a full-syllabus entry needs many hours across terms, and the in-home market prices the journey into each one at AED 180 to AED 350 per Bestimate and AED 200 to AED 500 for independent home tutors. Buying hours rather than visits is the whole point here, and online delivery also removes the geographic limit on who can teach a subject, which matters in Al Ain and the Western Region.

What we do not do is register anybody. The entry is made by the centre, the fees are paid to the centre, and the responsibility for meeting its deadline sits with the family. What we provide is teaching, marked work, and the written list of questions to put to a centre so that the family asks the right things before paying. Describing that as registration support is accurate; describing it as making the entry would not be.

Three further limits. We do not reproduce or supply board syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes or grade threshold tables; those belong to Cambridge and Pearson and we link the official sources instead. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or partnership from any regulator or board, and in Abu Dhabi private schools are overseen by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises their licensing and accreditation. And where no specialist is free for a subject at the hours you need, we say so and offer a different slot, a later start or a referral rather than filling the hour.

faqs.question: Can my child sit IGCSE in Abu Dhabi without being in a school?
faqs.answer: Yes, as a private candidate registered through a centre that accepts external entries, which may be a standalone examination centre or a private school willing to take externals alongside its own cohort. Every entry is made by the centre; a parent cannot submit one directly to Cambridge or Pearson. School policies on external candidates differ year to year, places are limited, and the arrangement is often unpublished, so this is a phone-and-email exercise started a series ahead rather than a term ahead.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE components can a private candidate not take?
faqs.answer: Usually coursework, which an external candidate generally cannot submit, so the centre enters an option code without it. Science practical examinations are normally replaced by a written alternative that examines practical skills on paper. Speaking and listening endorsements in language subjects vary by subject, board and code. Performance and portfolio subjects are usually impractical externally. The question to send a centre is which option code it enters for your subject and which components that code comprises.

faqs.question: How do we prepare for science practicals with no laboratory?
faqs.answer: Through the written alternative, which tests understanding of experimental method rather than laboratory hours. The teachable content is specific: identifying and justifying controlled variables, reading instruments to the expected precision, plotting and interpreting graphs to the mark scheme's conventions, identifying anomalies with reasons, and criticising a described method. The genuinely missing piece is observational knowledge, such as expected colour changes, which is learned from the syllabus and good teaching. Three or four past papers under the real duration is the highest-yield block available.

faqs.question: What does it cost to sit IGCSE privately in Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: The stack has several lines. Entry fees are set by the centre per subject per series and revised between series, so ask for the written schedule rather than relying on any figure found online, including ours. Add a possible late-entry surcharge, tuition, textbooks and any post-results review. Tuition market rates are AED 150 to AED 300 an hour for a qualified subject tutor online and AED 200 to AED 450 and above for an exam-year specialist, per Bestimate's rate table. Private candidates need more hours than school candidates.

faqs.question: Why does the option code matter so much?
faqs.answer: Because it determines which components are sat, and therefore what has to be revised. Two candidates in the same subject and the same series under different codes prepare for different papers: one may face a written practical alternative while another faces a laboratory examination, and one may have coursework in the grade while another does not. A candidate who revises for a component they were not entered for has wasted the work, and the code is knowable in advance from the centre.

faqs.question: Who reminds a private candidate about deadlines?
faqs.answer: Nobody, and that is the single biggest administrative risk in the project. A school candidate receives automatic reminders about entry deadlines, statements of entry, identification requirements and arrival arrangements. An external candidate receives whatever the centre sends and nothing more. The discipline that prevents the expensive failure is simple: put every date the centre gives you into a shared family calendar the day you receive it, including the centre's internal cut-off, which precedes the board's.

faqs.question: Which series should a private candidate aim for?
faqs.answer: A realistic one rather than the nearest one, and the distinction matters more here than for school candidates. UAE candidates sit the June and November series with Cambridge and May/June and November with Pearson; the Cambridge February/March series is offered to India only. A full-syllabus entry in several subjects is a two or three term project, so a prepared candidate in a later series consistently outperforms a rushed one in the next. Results land in August for the summer series and January for the autumn one.

faqs.question: Do we have to check the Cambridge zone as a private candidate?
faqs.answer: Yes, and more carefully than a school candidate would. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, each with its own timetable version, and states that it is essential to use the correct version for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. A school candidate has staff cross-checking this. An external candidate does not, so ask the centre which zone it sits in and match it to the published timetable yourself.

faqs.question: Can a private candidate choose Core or Extended tier?
faqs.answer: The tier is part of the entry, so it is agreed with the centre before its internal cut-off and fixed once submitted. Extended carries the full grade range and assumes algebraic and analytical fluency the Core papers never test, and most sixth forms expect it for AS sciences and mathematics. Decide it on a marked Extended paper sat under timed conditions rather than on ambition, and have that evidence before the deadline rather than after it.

faqs.question: How do results reach a private candidate?
faqs.answer: Through the centre, by whatever route the centre operates, which is why it is worth asking in advance how and when you will receive them. An external candidate does not walk into a school hall on results day and nobody will explain the statement of results to them. If a grade looks wrong there is a formal review of marking, requested through the centre and charged by the board, with a deadline that falls soon after results. Decide your criteria for requesting one in advance.

faqs.question: Will a privately sat IGCSE be accepted by a sixth form or university?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, and the detail to check is what the option code produced. A qualification entered without a coursework component or without a speaking endorsement may be reported differently from the school version, and whether a receiving institution cares is its decision rather than a general rule. Ask the sixth form or university in writing what it requires, before entering rather than after sitting. For recognition inside the UAE, the Ministry equivalency process applies and is run by the authority.

faqs.question: How many subjects should a private candidate enter?
faqs.answer: As few as the destination actually requires, which is usually fewer than families assume. On the published British equivalency track, five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no less than E or grade 3 are counted, with Arabic and Islamic education not included among the five. A sixth form or university may require a particular subject rather than a number. Check the requirement in writing first; it routinely reduces the subject list and therefore the whole budget.

faqs.question: Do you register candidates or pay the centre on our behalf?
faqs.answer: No. The centre makes the entry, takes the fees and owns its deadline, and the responsibility for meeting it sits with the family. What we provide is teaching from the exact option codes the centre has entered, marked work, and the written list of questions to put to a centre before anything is paid. Calling that registration support is accurate; calling it making the entry would not be, and some providers blur that line in ways families later regret.

faqs.question: Where should a private candidate get syllabus and paper material from?
faqs.answer: We work from them with you and point you at the official sources rather than supplying them. Syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade threshold tables belong to Cambridge and Pearson, and reproducing or distributing them is a copyright matter. A tutor offering a folder of board materials is offering something they are not entitled to distribute, which is a reasonable signal about the rest of their practice. Buy textbooks legitimately, and use the boards' own published materials.

abu-dhabi/igcse-private-candidate-regist.closingHeading: Centre first, codes second, teaching third
abu-dhabi/igcse-private-candidate-regist.closingBody: Private candidature is an administrative project with a teaching project inside it, and families who reverse the order pay for both. Find a centre in the emirate that accepts external candidates in your subjects, then get six things from it in writing: the option codes, its internal deadline, its current fee schedule, its Cambridge administrative zone, the identification requirements and the arrival arrangements. Only then does a teaching plan mean anything, because only then do you know which papers are being sat. Book a free trial lesson with the subject specialist, bring the codes, and expect an honest answer about which series is realistic.

abu-dhabi/igcse-private-tuition.tutorsIntro: The tutors below work on Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE specifications for Abu Dhabi students. Rates depend on subject, tier and tutor, and are quoted after the consultation rather than advertised as a single number.

intro.heading: Why two IGCSE quotes in the same emirate differ by a factor of ten
paragraphs: A parent in Khalifa City who asks three providers for an IGCSE Chemistry price will typically be quoted AED 60, AED 220 and AED 450. All three are real prices for real services and none is being dishonest. They differ because an hour of tuition is not a standardised unit. One is a university student revising alongside your child from a textbook. One is a qualified subject teacher who has taught the specification and will mark a past paper between sessions. One is a specialist with a narrow subject and a thin diary. The comparison is only possible once you know which of the three you are being offered.

The second reason for the spread is what sits outside the hour. Marking a full past paper against the published mark scheme takes a tutor between forty and sixty minutes, and it is the single most useful thing they do in a week. Some rates include it. Some bill it separately. Many providers simply do not do it, which is why a lesson can be sold at AED 60. A written session note, a component tracker and reading a coursework draft outside the lesson are all in the same category: real work, variably priced, and rarely itemised on a quote.

The third reason is specific to this stage. IGCSE is a wide qualification. A Year 11 student in Abu Dhabi usually sits eight to ten subjects across two boards, each with its own papers and its own internally assessed or practical component. That breadth changes the economics completely compared with a two-year Diploma plan in three Higher Levels. A family budgeting for IGCSE tuition is not buying one subject for two years; they are deciding which two of nine subjects deserve the hour, and that decision is worth more than the hourly rate they negotiate.

There are also costs around the tuition that nobody quotes. Examination entry as a private candidate, a November resit after a disappointing June, a replacement set of textbooks for a changed tier, additional practice material. None of these is large on its own and together they routinely exceed a month of lessons. They belong in the same budget conversation, and this page puts them there.

Everything below is priced in AED and attributed. Where a figure comes from a competitor's published page, that provider is named. Where it comes from Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table, that is stated. What you will not find here is an IB Gram price list, because our rate depends on the subject, the tier and the tutor matched, and it is quoted after a consultation. Delivery is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE, so no travel is absorbed into the figure we quote.

abu-dhabi/igcse-private-tuition.programmesIntro: Cost varies by stage more than by district. These are the IGCSE stages Abu Dhabi families buy tuition for, with what each one typically needs in hours and why the price behaves differently.

programmes.name: Year 9, before the course starts
programmes.description: The cheapest hour you will ever buy, because the gaps are small and the clock is not running. Work here is arithmetic fluency, reading stamina and an evidence-based options choice. A term of weekly support in Year 9 regularly removes the need for a far more expensive exam-year block.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi schools run options evenings in the spring of Year 9 and finalise subject lists before any IGCSE paper has been sat. Buying a diagnostic paper at this point costs one session and can prevent a two-year mismatch in a tiered subject.

programmes.name: Year 10, the first course year
programmes.description: Mid-range pricing and the best value in the qualification. Content is being met for the first time, so an hour spent closing a gap now is worth several hours spent unpicking it in the spring of Year 11. Tier decisions in Mathematics and the sciences are usually taken this year.
programmes.countryNote: Families in this emirate overwhelmingly start tuition in Year 11. Those who start in Year 10 buy fewer total hours for the same outcome, which is the clearest saving available and the one almost nobody takes.

programmes.name: Year 11, the examination year
programmes.description: The most expensive hour, for two reasons: demand concentrates between January and May, and the work is remedial rather than developmental. Specialist diaries fill first, so the same tutor who was available in October may not be in March at any price.
programmes.countryNote: Abu Dhabi demand peaks after the autumn mock results are issued and again four weeks before the summer papers. A family wanting a specific specialist for the spring usually has to commit in the autumn term.

programmes.name: The November series and the resit route
programmes.description: Cambridge runs a June and a November series, and Pearson Edexcel offers International GCSE in May/June and November. A resit means a separate entry fee, a short intensive block of tuition, and in some cases a private candidate arrangement at a registered centre.
programmes.countryNote: The resit budget is the one Abu Dhabi families are least prepared for, because it is decided in late August when results arrive and the November entry window is already close. Costing it in advance removes a panic purchase at the worst possible price.

abu-dhabi/igcse-private-tuition.subjectsIntro: Price varies by subject, mostly because supply does. These are the IGCSE subjects Abu Dhabi families ask for, with what makes each one cheap or expensive to cover.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580, Edexcel 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The deepest tutor pool in the emirate and therefore the most competitively priced. The rate rises sharply at the top of the Extended tier, where the work is multi-step method precision rather than content. Tiering is also where the largest free gain sits: a wrong tier caps the grade at no extra cost to anyone.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625, Edexcel 4PH1)
subjects.description: Mid to upper band. Supply is adequate at Core and thinner at Extended, and electricity and waves account for most enquiries. A fifth of the Cambridge mark sits in the practical or alternative-to-practical paper, which is the cheapest marks-per-hour fix in the subject.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620, Edexcel 4CH1)
subjects.description: Upper band at Extended. Moles, electrolysis and organic pathways carry the mark loss, and they need a tutor who can set unfamiliar-substance questions rather than re-explain definitions. That capability is what the higher rate buys.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610, Edexcel 4BI1)
subjects.description: Mid band with good supply. Content volume is the issue rather than difficulty, so the efficient purchase is command-word discipline and recall scheduling rather than a weekly re-teach of the specification.

subjects.name: First Language English (Cambridge 0500, Edexcel 4EA1)
subjects.description: Mid band. The reading paper responds quickly to targeted work on the summary and analysis questions; the writing paper moves more slowly because register and structure are habits. Marking load per session is high, which is why a cheap rate here often excludes it.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510 and 0511)
subjects.description: Lower band, good supply. The expensive mistake is not the rate but the entry: a student placed here who could sit First Language English is capped at a lower ceiling, and sixth forms read the two codes differently.

subjects.name: Business Studies, Economics and Accounting (0450, 0455, 0452, 4BS1, 4EC1)
subjects.description: Mid band. Evaluation marks at the end of the long questions are the unclaimed block, and they are teachable in a handful of sessions. A short targeted purchase usually beats a year of weekly support in these subjects.

subjects.name: Computer Science and ICT (Cambridge 0478, 0417, Edexcel 4IT1)
subjects.description: Upper band because supply is thin. Pseudocode under timed conditions and trace tables are the specific gains, and tutors who can mark Paper 2 to the scheme are a small group in this market.

subjects.name: Additional and Further Pure Mathematics (0606, 4PM1)
subjects.description: The most expensive IGCSE codes to cover locally, simply because almost nobody in a given Abu Dhabi district teaches them. Matching online removes the scarcity premium that a geographic search creates.

subjects.name: Arabic (Cambridge 0508 First Language, 0544 Foreign Language)
subjects.description: Variable pricing and a wide range of quality. Arabic runs alongside the international curriculum as a federally required subject, and the right code depends on whether Arabic is a first or additional language. A placement review costs one session and can change two years of outcomes.

abu-dhabi/igcse-private-tuition.regionsIntro: Where you live in Abu Dhabi changes the cost of tuition in exactly one way: it decides whether travel is in the price. Online delivery removes that variable, which is why the district matters for timing rather than for the rate.

regions.name: Khalifa City
regions.note: The largest source of IGCSE enquiries outside the island. An in-home tutor crossing from the island at 17:00 is paid for the journey one way or another; an online slot at the same hour is not.

regions.name: Al Shamkha and Al Falah
regions.note: Far enough out that visiting tutors either decline or quote a premium. Published in-home bands of AED 180 to 500 sit at the upper end here, which is the clearest case in the emirate for buying the lesson rather than the journey.

regions.name: Saadiyat Island
regions.note: A short crossing but a crowded evening. Families here most often convert to weekend morning blocks, which are cheaper per useful minute because concentration is higher.

regions.name: Al Reem Island
regions.note: Apartment households where the practical spend before the first lesson is a desk and a door that closes, not an extra session. It is the cheapest improvement available to most tower families.

regions.name: Mussafah and Mohammed Bin Zayed City
regions.note: Multi-child households where the budget question is sequencing rather than rate. Two children in back-to-back slots on one evening is materially cheaper than four scattered hours.

regions.note: Schools inside or beside the community hand back most of the commute, so a 90-minute session is feasible. Longer sessions are usually better value per dirham than two short ones.

regions.note: Established island catchment with the earliest realistic start times in the emirate. The practical saving here is scheduling two siblings consecutively from 16:30.

sections.heading: The eight variables that move an IGCSE tuition quote in this emirate
paragraphs: Before comparing numbers it helps to know what the numbers are responding to. Eight variables account for nearly all of the spread in Abu Dhabi, and six of them are things a parent can influence. The tutor's qualification and subject depth is the largest single factor, and it is the one correctly priced: a specialist who has taught Extended Chemistry for a decade is a different purchase from a graduate who sat it four years ago.

Scarcity of the code comes second. Mathematics 0580 has a deep pool and competitive pricing. Edexcel Further Pure 4PM1 and Cambridge Additional Mathematics 0606 have almost no local supply, and a geographic search for them produces either a refusal or a scarcity premium. Timing is third: specialist diaries fill between January and May, so the same hour costs more in March than in October because the alternative is nothing.

Then come the variables inside the service. Whether a full past paper is marked to the published scheme between sessions. Whether a written session note and component tracker are produced. Whether a coursework draft is read outside the lesson. Whether the session is 45, 60 or 90 minutes, and whether a 90-minute session is billed at 1.5 times or at a block rate. And finally, whether travel is in the price, which for in-home tuition in this emirate can be a quarter of what you pay.

The practical use of the list is as a question set. Ask a provider to price the same brief - one 60-minute session a week, one marked Extended paper a fortnight, a written note after each session - and three quotes become comparable for the first time. Most of the apparent price difference in this market disappears once the brief is specified, and what remains is a genuine quality difference you can then decide about.

sections.heading: The published rate card for this market, in AED, with sources
paragraphs: What follows is the market, not our price list. Each band below is taken from a provider's own published page or from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table, and the publisher is named beside the figure. Rates in Abu Dhabi track Dubai closely at the budget and specialist ends, and sit slightly below Dubai in the middle band, where competition between agencies is less intense.

At the budget end, Tutopiya advertises from AED 33 and EdFlik from AED 45 an hour. These are online, generally non-specialist, and marking is rarely included. In the qualified-tutor band, Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. For specialists, Bestimate's table puts IB, IGCSE and A Level at AED 200 to 450 and above, TutorChase quotes AED 270, and BartyED advertises AED 650 for a premium named tutor.

In-home one-to-one carries the travel. Bestimate puts it at AED 180 to 350 and independent home tutors across the UAE advertise AED 200 to 500. Package pricing in the market clusters at around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. Bestimate's monthly estimates for a single weekly hour run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support.

Read the table as a map of what exists rather than as a recommendation. Our own rate for an Abu Dhabi family depends on the subject, the tier and the tutor matched, and is given after a consultation. What we can say in advance is that it contains no travel component, because the lesson is delivered over live video.
